**Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 33, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2)**

**Tafsir (explanation, exegesis) of Surah al-Ahzab**

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab was revealed at Medina." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Abd al-Razzaq in *al-Musannaf*, al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Mani', al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtara* narrated from Zirr, who said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to me, "How many [verses] do you recite Surah al-Ahzab as having, or how many do you count it as?" I said, "Seventy-three verses." He said, "Indeed! I have seen it when it was equal to Surah al-Baqarah, or more than Surah al-Baqarah. We used to recite in it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.'* Then it was abrogated along with what was abrogated." Ibn Kathir said: its chain is *hasan* (good).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up, praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: "As for what follows, O people, Allah sent Muhammad with the truth and revealed the Book to him. Among what was revealed to him was the verse of stoning. We recited it and understood it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely.'* The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned [adulterers], and we stoned after him. I fear that a long time will pass over people and someone will say, 'We do not find the verse of stoning in the Book of Allah,' and thus they will go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed." Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said to me, "How many [verses] do you count Surah al-Ahzab as having?" I said, "Two or seventy-three." He said, "It nearly equals Surah al-Baqarah, and indeed it contains the verse of stoning."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated: "I recited Surah al-Ahzab to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I forgot seventy verses of it, which I could not find."

Abu Ubayd in *al-Fada'il*, Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab used to be recited in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) as two hundred verses. When Uthman copied the codices (*masahif*), he did not keep from it except what is in it now."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

(p. 1156) His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾, meaning: persist in that and increase in it. ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾ from among the people of Mecca and those who are upon their disbelief, ﴿and the hypocrites﴾, meaning those who display Islam and conceal disbelief.

Al-Wahidi said: He, glory be to Him, intended by "the disbelievers" Abu Sufyan, Ikrima, and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami, because they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Abandon the mention of our gods, and say that they have intercession for whoever worships them."

He said: And "the hypocrites" [refers to] Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh.

At the end of the discussion there will come the explanation of the reason for the revelation of the verse. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, meaning: possessing abundant knowledge and wisdom, and perfect in both. Al-Nahhas said: By His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, He indicated that [the Prophet] (ﷺ) used to incline toward them, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to invite them to Islam. The meaning is: if Allah, mighty and majestic, knew that your inclination toward them would be beneficial, He would not have forbidden you from them, for He is Wise. The remoteness of this inference that he claims is not hidden. However, this sentence is a justification for the sentence containing the command to fear Allah and the prohibition against obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites. The meaning is: He does not command you or forbid you except with what He knows to contain righteousness or corruption, because of the abundance of His knowledge and the vastness of His wisdom.

﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, namely from the Qur'an, meaning: follow the revelation in all your affairs, and do not follow anything other than it, such as the counsels of the disbelievers and hypocrites, nor pure personal opinion, for in what has been revealed to you is that which suffices you from that. The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ is a justification for His command to follow what has been revealed to you. The command addressed to him (ﷺ) is a command to his community, so they are commanded to follow the Qur'an just as he is commanded to follow it. For this reason, the address to him and to them is combined in His saying, *"of what you do,"* according to the reading of the majority with the second-person form (*ta'*). Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading.

Abu Amr, al-Sulami, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the third-person form (*ya'*).

﴿And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, meaning: depend upon Him and entrust your affairs to Him, and sufficient is He as a guardian who protects whoever relies upon Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a parable as a preface and preparation for the legal rulings of the Qur'an that follow it, which are part of the revelation that Allah commanded him to follow. He said: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body.﴾

It has been disputed what was the reason for the revelation of this verse, as will come. It was also said: it is a parable that Allah struck for the one who performs *zihar* (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband declares his wife to be unlawful to him by likening her to his mother), meaning: just as a man cannot have two hearts, so also the wife of one who performs *zihar* cannot be his mother unless he has two mothers. Likewise, an adopted son (*da'i*, the one falsely claimed as a son) cannot be the son of two men.

It was also said: one of the hypocrites used to say, "I have a heart that commands me to do this and a heart that commands me to do that." So the verse was revealed to refute hypocrisy and to explain that it does not coexist with Islam, just as two hearts do not coexist. The heart is a small lump in the shape of a pine cone, which Allah created and made the seat of knowledge.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you declare unlawful [by zihar] your mothers﴾. The Kufans and Ibn Amir read *al-la'i* with a silent *ya'* after a *hamza*. Abu Amr and al-Bazzi read it with a silent *ya'* after a pure *alif*.

Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' said: It is the dialect of Quraysh, which the people were commanded to recite in.

Qunbul and Warsh read it with a *hamza* with a kasra, without a *ya'*.

Asim read *tuzahiruna* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *ha'* after an *alif*, the present tense of *zahara*. Ibn Amir read it with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'* and a shadda on the *za'*, the present tense of *tazahara*, and the original form is *tatazahirna*. The rest read *tazzahharun* with a fatha on the *ta'* and a shadda on the *za'*, without an *alif*, and the original form is *tatazahharun*.

*Zihar* (the pre-Islamic form of divorce described above) is derived from *zahr* (back), and its origin is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." The meaning is: Allah has not made your wives, whom you say this statement to, like your mothers in prohibition, but it is a reprehensible speech and a falsehood.

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons.﴾ The *ad'iya'* is the plural of *da'i*, who is the one who claims a son who is not his biological son. The discussion of *zihar* will come in Surah al-Mujadila.

The reference in His saying *"that"* (*dhalikum*) is to what preceded of the mention of *zihar* and adoption, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿your saying with your mouths﴾, meaning: that is nothing but a mere saying with the mouths and has no effect. So a woman does not become a mother by it, nor does the son of another become a son by it, and no ruling of motherhood or sonship follows from it.

It was also said: the reference is to adoption, meaning: your claim that the sons of others are your sons has no reality; rather it is merely a statement with the mouth. Allah speaks the truth, which is worthy of being followed, because it is true in itself and not false, so it includes the calling of sons to their fathers. ﴿And He guides to the way﴾, meaning: He indicates the path that leads to the truth. In this there is guidance for the servants to speak the truth and to abandon speaking falsehood and lies.

Then He, glory be to Him, explicitly stated what is obligatory upon the servants regarding calling sons by their fathers' names. He said: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, meaning: [call them] for their biological fathers, and attribute them to their fathers and do not call them by anything other than their fathers. The sentence ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ is a justification for the command to call sons by their fathers' names. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun of *ud'uhum*, and *aqsat* means *a'dal* (more just). That is: it is more just than every statement related to that. He left out the complement for generality, as in His saying *Allahu akbar* (Allah is greatest). The complement may also be a specific implied one, meaning: more just than your saying, "He is the son of so-and-so," when he was not his biological son.

Then He, glory be to Him, completed the guidance for the servants and said: ﴿And if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients.﴾ That is: then they are your brothers in religion and they are your clients. So say, "My brother" and "My client," and do not say, "the son of so-and-so," since you do not know their fathers in the true sense. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that *mawalikum* means your allies in religion.

It was also said: the meaning is: if they were freed slaves and not free men, then say "client of so-and-so."

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in﴾, meaning: there is no sin upon you for what occurs from you of that by error and without intention. ﴿But [what is sinful is] what your hearts have intended﴾, which is what you say deliberately, such as attributing sons to other than their fathers while knowing that.

Qatada said: If you call a man by someone other than his father while you believe he is his father, there is no harm upon you. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He forgives the one who errs, shows mercy to him, and overlooks him, or [it means]: He is Forgiving of sins and Merciful toward the servants. Among those whom He forgives and has mercy upon is one who calls a man by someone other than his father by mistake. Or [it means] before the prohibition against that.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned to His Messenger a great distinction and a magnificent privilege in which none of the servants shares with him. He said: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves﴾, meaning: he has more right over them in all matters of religion and worldly life, and more worthy of them than they are of themselves, let alone being more worthy of them than others. It is therefore obligatory upon them to prefer him over what he wants from their wealth, even if they are in need of it. It is obligatory upon them to love him more than they love themselves, and obligatory upon them to give precedence to his judgment over their own judgment for themselves.

In summary: when the Prophet (ﷺ) calls them to something and their own souls call them to something else, it is obligatory upon them to give precedence to what he has called them to and to delay what their souls have called them to. It is obligatory upon them to obey him above their obedience to themselves, and to give precedence to his obedience over what their souls incline to and their inner impulses desire.

It was also said: what is meant by "themselves" in the verse is some of them, so the meaning is: the Prophet is more worthy of the believers than some of them are of others.

It was also said: it is specific to judgment, meaning: he is more worthy of them than themselves regarding what he judges between them.

It was also said: he is more worthy of them in jihad before him and in sacrificing the self in his defense. The first is the most correct.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, meaning: they are like their mothers in the ruling of prohibition, and they are placed in the position of mothers regarding the entitlement to honor. So it is not lawful for anyone to marry any one of them, just as it is not lawful for him to marry his own mother. This motherhood is specific to the prohibition of marrying them and to honoring their dignity. The specification of "the believers" indicates that they are not the mothers of the believers' wives, nor their daughters the sisters of the believers, nor their brothers the maternal uncles of the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: What appears to me is that they are the mothers of both men and women, in honor of their right over men and women, as His saying indicates: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves,"* and this necessarily includes men and women.

He said: Moreover, in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b [it reads]: *"And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them."* Ibn Abbas read: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."*

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified that kinship is more worthy for some of them over others. He said: ﴿And those of relationship are more entitled to one another﴾. What is meant by "those of relationship" is the relatives, meaning: they have more right to one another in inheritance. The explanation of this verse has already passed at the end of Surah al-Anfal, and it abrogates what was in the early period of Islam concerning inheritance through emigration and alliance.

Qatada said: When Allah, glorified is He, revealed in Surat al-Anfal, ﴿Those who believed but did not migrate, you owe them no guardianship at all until they migrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], the Muslims inherited from one another on account of migration (hijra, emigration to Medina). Then this was abrogated (naskh) by this verse. Others said the same.

It was said that this verse abrogates inheritance through alliance (hilf) and brotherhood in religion (mu'akhah). The phrase ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ may be connected to the comparative form ﴿closer﴾ in His saying ﴿closer to one another﴾, since the comparative governs the adverbial phrase. It may also be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun, meaning "existing in the Book of Allah." By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the Qur'an, or the verse of inheritance. His saying ﴿of the believers﴾ may be an explanation of ﴿those of the kinship ties (ulu al-arham)﴾, meaning that relatives among the believers and the emigrants are closer to one another. It may also be connected to ﴿closer﴾, meaning that the kinship-holders are closer to one another than the believers and emigrants who are strangers. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another, except for what is permitted to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely that they are like mothers in the prohibition of marriage." There is much weakness in this view, as is well known.

﴿Except that you do kindness to your allies﴾: This exception is either a connected exception from a more general category, and the sense is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another in every matter, including inheritance and other things, except that you do kindness to your allies by way of charity or bequest, for that is permissible." This was said by Qatada, al-Hasan, Ata, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: It was revealed concerning the permissibility of bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian. The disbeliever is a relative by lineage, though not by religion, so it is permissible to make a bequest to him. The exception may also be disconnected (munqati'), and the meaning is: "But doing good to one's allies is not objectionable." The meaning of the verse is that when Allah, glorified is He, abrogated inheritance through alliance and migration, He permitted bequests to them.

Mujahid said: By "kindness" is meant support and preserving the sanctity of the rights of faith and migration. The reference in His saying ﴿that was﴾ is to what was previously mentioned, that is, the abrogation of inheritance by migration, alliance, and pledge, and the return of inheritance to kinship relations. ﴿In the Book, inscribed﴾ means in the Preserved Tablet, or in the Qur'an, written down.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood one day praying, and he had a slip of thought. The hypocrites who prayed with him said: 'Do you not see that he has two hearts, one with you and one with them?' Then ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest﴾ was revealed."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him by another route, with the wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed a prayer in which he made a mistake, and a word escaped him. The hypocrites heard it and said: 'He has two hearts.' Then it was revealed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him, who said: "There was a man of Quraysh called Dhu al-Qalbayn (the Man of Two Hearts) because of his cunning, so Allah revealed this concerning him."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Ibn Umar that "Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we would not call him anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5]. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You are Zayd ibn Harithah ibn Sharahil.'"

al-Bukhari and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no believer but that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. So whichever believer leaves wealth, let his heirs, whoever they are, inherit it. And if he leaves a debt or dependents, let him come to me, for I am his guardian (mawla)."

Ahmad and Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted a similar report from the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Buraydah, who said: "I campaigned with Ali to Yemen, and I saw from him some harshness. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned Ali and disparaged him. I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) change, and he said: 'O Buraydah, am I not closer to the believers than themselves?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla.'"

It is established in the Sahih that he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until I am dearer to him than his own self, his wealth, his child, and all people."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Aisha that a woman said to her: "O mother!" and she said: "I am the mother of your men, but I am not the mother of your women."

Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Umm Salama, who said: "I am the mother of the men among you and of the women."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Dala'il transmitted from Bajala, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by a boy who was reading in the mushaf: 'The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them.' He said: 'O boy, erase it!' The boy said: 'This is the mushaf of Ubayy.' So he went to him and asked him, and he said: 'The Qur'an occupied me, and trading in the markets occupied you.'"

al-Firyabi, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons.﴾ The *ad'iya'* is the plural of *da'i*, who is the one who claims a son who is not his biological son. The discussion of *zihar* will come in Surah al-Mujadila.

The reference in His saying *"that"* (*dhalikum*) is to what preceded of the mention of *zihar* and adoption, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿your saying with your mouths﴾, meaning: that is nothing but a mere saying with the mouths and has no effect. So a woman does not become a mother by it, nor does the son of another become a son by it, and no ruling of motherhood or sonship follows from it.

It was also said: the reference is to adoption, meaning: your claim that the sons of others are your sons has no reality; rather it is merely a statement with the mouth. Allah speaks the truth, which is worthy of being followed, because it is true in itself and not false, so it includes the calling of sons to their fathers. ﴿And He guides to the way﴾, meaning: He indicates the path that leads to the truth. In this there is guidance for the servants to speak the truth and to abandon speaking falsehood and lies.

Then He, glory be to Him, explicitly stated what is obligatory upon the servants regarding calling sons by their fathers' names. He said: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, meaning: [call them] for their biological fathers, and attribute them to their fathers and do not call them by anything other than their fathers. The sentence ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ is a justification for the command to call sons by their fathers' names. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun of *ud'uhum*, and *aqsat* means *a'dal* (more just). That is: it is more just than every statement related to that. He left out the complement for generality, as in His saying *Allahu akbar* (Allah is greatest). The complement may also be a specific implied one, meaning: more just than your saying, "He is the son of so-and-so," when he was not his biological son.

Then He, glory be to Him, completed the guidance for the servants and said: ﴿And if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients.﴾ That is: then they are your brothers in religion and they are your clients. So say, "My brother" and "My client," and do not say, "the son of so-and-so," since you do not know their fathers in the true sense. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that *mawalikum* means your allies in religion.

It was also said: the meaning is: if they were freed slaves and not free men, then say "client of so-and-so."

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in﴾, meaning: there is no sin upon you for what occurs from you of that by error and without intention. ﴿But [what is sinful is] what your hearts have intended﴾, which is what you say deliberately, such as attributing sons to other than their fathers while knowing that.

Qatada said: If you call a man by someone other than his father while you believe he is his father, there is no harm upon you. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He forgives the one who errs, shows mercy to him, and overlooks him, or [it means]: He is Forgiving of sins and Merciful toward the servants. Among those whom He forgives and has mercy upon is one who calls a man by someone other than his father by mistake. Or [it means] before the prohibition against that.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned to His Messenger a great distinction and a magnificent privilege in which none of the servants shares with him. He said: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves﴾, meaning: he has more right over them in all matters of religion and worldly life, and more worthy of them than they are of themselves, let alone being more worthy of them than others. It is therefore obligatory upon them to prefer him over what he wants from their wealth, even if they are in need of it. It is obligatory upon them to love him more than they love themselves, and obligatory upon them to give precedence to his judgment over their own judgment for themselves.

In summary: when the Prophet (ﷺ) calls them to something and their own souls call them to something else, it is obligatory upon them to give precedence to what he has called them to and to delay what their souls have called them to. It is obligatory upon them to obey him above their obedience to themselves, and to give precedence to his obedience over what their souls incline to and their inner impulses desire.

It was also said: what is meant by "themselves" in the verse is some of them, so the meaning is: the Prophet is more worthy of the believers than some of them are of others.

It was also said: it is specific to judgment, meaning: he is more worthy of them than themselves regarding what he judges between them.

It was also said: he is more worthy of them in jihad before him and in sacrificing the self in his defense. The first is the most correct.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, meaning: they are like their mothers in the ruling of prohibition, and they are placed in the position of mothers regarding the entitlement to honor. So it is not lawful for anyone to marry any one of them, just as it is not lawful for him to marry his own mother. This motherhood is specific to the prohibition of marrying them and to honoring their dignity. The specification of "the believers" indicates that they are not the mothers of the believers' wives, nor their daughters the sisters of the believers, nor their brothers the maternal uncles of the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: What appears to me is that they are the mothers of both men and women, in honor of their right over men and women, as His saying indicates: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves,"* and this necessarily includes men and women.

He said: Moreover, in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b [it reads]: *"And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them."* Ibn Abbas read: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."*

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified that kinship is more worthy for some of them over others. He said: ﴿And those of relationship are more entitled to one another﴾. What is meant by "those of relationship" is the relatives, meaning: they have more right to one another in inheritance. Qatada said: When Allah, glorified is He, revealed in Surat al-Anfal, ﴿Those who believed but did not migrate, you owe them no guardianship at all until they migrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], the Muslims inherited from one another on account of migration (hijra, emigration to Medina). Then this was abrogated (naskh) by this verse. Others said the same.

It may also be connected to ﴿closer﴾, meaning that the kinship-holders are closer to one another than the believers and emigrants who are strangers. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another, except for what is permitted to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely that they are like mothers in the prohibition of marriage." There is much weakness in this view, as is well known.

This was said by Qatada, al-Hasan, Ata, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: It was revealed concerning the permissibility of bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian. The disbeliever is a relative by lineage, though not by religion, so it is permissible to make a bequest to him. The exception may also be disconnected (munqati'), and the meaning is: "But doing good to one's allies is not objectionable." The meaning of the verse is that when Allah, glorified is He, abrogated inheritance through alliance and migration, He permitted bequests to them.

Mujahid said: By "kindness" is meant support and preserving the sanctity of the rights of faith and migration. The reference in His saying ﴿that was﴾ is to what was previously mentioned, that is, the abrogation of inheritance by migration, alliance, and pledge, and the return of inheritance to kinship relations. ﴿In the Book, inscribed﴾ means in the Preserved Tablet, or in the Qur'an, written down.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood one day praying, and he had a slip of thought. The hypocrites who prayed with him said: 'Do you not see that he has two hearts, one with you and one with them?' Then ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest﴾ was revealed."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him by another route, with the wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed a prayer in which he made a mistake, and a word escaped him. The hypocrites heard it and said: 'He has two hearts.' Then it was revealed."

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You are Zayd ibn Harithah ibn Sharahil.'"

al-Bukhari and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no believer but that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. So whichever believer leaves wealth, let his heirs, whoever they are, inherit it. Ahmad and Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted a similar report from the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Buraydah, who said: "I campaigned with Ali to Yemen, and I saw from him some harshness. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned Ali and disparaged him. I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) change, and he said: 'O Buraydah, am I not closer to the believers than themselves?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' al-Firyabi, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

**Tafsir (explanation, exegesis) of Surah al-Ahzab**

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab was revealed at Medina." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Abd al-Razzaq in *al-Musannaf*, al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Mani', al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtara* narrated from Zirr, who said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to me, "How many [verses] do you recite Surah al-Ahzab as having, or how many do you count it as?" I said, "Seventy-three verses." He said, "Indeed! I have seen it when it was equal to Surah al-Baqarah, or more than Surah al-Baqarah. We used to recite in it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.'* Then it was abrogated along with what was abrogated." Ibn Kathir said: its chain is *hasan* (good).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up, praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: "As for what follows, O people, Allah sent Muhammad with the truth and revealed the Book to him. Among what was revealed to him was the verse of stoning. We recited it and understood it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely.'* The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned [adulterers], and we stoned after him. I fear that a long time will pass over people and someone will say, 'We do not find the verse of stoning in the Book of Allah,' and thus they will go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed." Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said to me, "How many [verses] do you count Surah al-Ahzab as having?" I said, "Two or seventy-three." He said, "It nearly equals Surah al-Baqarah, and indeed it contains the verse of stoning."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated: "I recited Surah al-Ahzab to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I forgot seventy verses of it, which I could not find."

Abu Ubayd in *al-Fada'il*, Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab used to be recited in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) as two hundred verses. When Uthman copied the codices (*masahif*), he did not keep from it except what is in it now."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

The remoteness of this inference that he claims is not hidden. However, this sentence is a justification for the sentence containing the command to fear Allah and the prohibition against obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites. The meaning is: He does not command you or forbid you except with what He knows to contain righteousness or corruption, because of the abundance of His knowledge and the vastness of His wisdom.

For this reason, the address to him and to them is combined in His saying, *"of what you do,"* according to the reading of the majority with the second-person form (*ta'*). Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading.

Abu Amr, al-Sulami, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the third-person form (*ya'*).

**Tafsir (explanation, exegesis) of Surah al-Ahzab**

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab was revealed at Medina." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Abd al-Razzaq in *al-Musannaf*, al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Mani', al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtara* narrated from Zirr, who said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to me, "How many [verses] do you recite Surah al-Ahzab as having, or how many do you count it as?" I said, "Seventy-three verses." He said, "Indeed! I have seen it when it was equal to Surah al-Baqarah, or more than Surah al-Baqarah. We used to recite in it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.'* Then it was abrogated along with what was abrogated." Ibn Kathir said: its chain is *hasan* (good).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up, praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: "As for what follows, O people, Allah sent Muhammad with the truth and revealed the Book to him. Among what was revealed to him was the verse of stoning. We recited it and understood it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely.'* The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned [adulterers], and we stoned after him. I fear that a long time will pass over people and someone will say, 'We do not find the verse of stoning in the Book of Allah,' and thus they will go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed." Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said to me, "How many [verses] do you count Surah al-Ahzab as having?" I said, "Two or seventy-three." He said, "It nearly equals Surah al-Baqarah, and indeed it contains the verse of stoning."

Abu Ubayd in *al-Fada'il*, Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab used to be recited in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) as two hundred verses. When Uthman copied the codices (*masahif*), he did not keep from it except what is in it now."

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

(p. 1156) His saying: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾, meaning: persist in that and increase in it. ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾ from among the people of Mecca and those who are upon their disbelief, ﴿and the hypocrites﴾, meaning those who display Islam and conceal disbelief.

Al-Wahidi said: He, glory be to Him, intended by "the disbelievers" Abu Sufyan, Ikrima, and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami, because they said to the Prophet (ﷺ), "Abandon the mention of our gods, and say that they have intercession for whoever worships them."

He said: And "the hypocrites" [refers to] Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh.

At the end of the discussion there will come the explanation of the reason for the revelation of the verse. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, meaning: possessing abundant knowledge and wisdom, and perfect in both. Al-Nahhas said: By His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, He indicated that [the Prophet] (ﷺ) used to incline toward them, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to invite them to Islam. The meaning is: if Allah, mighty and majestic, knew that your inclination toward them would be beneficial, He would not have forbidden you from them, for He is Wise. The remoteness of this inference that he claims is not hidden. However, this sentence is a justification for the sentence containing the command to fear Allah and the prohibition against obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites. The meaning is: He does not command you or forbid you except with what He knows to contain righteousness or corruption, because of the abundance of His knowledge and the vastness of His wisdom.

﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, namely from the Qur'an, meaning: follow the revelation in all your affairs, and do not follow anything other than it, such as the counsels of the disbelievers and hypocrites, nor pure personal opinion, for in what has been revealed to you is that which suffices you from that. The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ is a justification for His command to follow what has been revealed to you. The command addressed to him (ﷺ) is a command to his community, so they are commanded to follow the Qur'an just as he is commanded to follow it. For this reason, the address to him and to them is combined in His saying, *"of what you do,"* according to the reading of the majority with the second-person form (*ta'*). Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading.

Abu Amr, al-Sulami, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the third-person form (*ya'*).

﴿And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, meaning: depend upon Him and entrust your affairs to Him, and sufficient is He as a guardian who protects whoever relies upon Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a parable as a preface and preparation for the legal rulings of the Qur'an that follow it, which are part of the revelation that Allah commanded him to follow. He said: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body.﴾

It has been disputed what was the reason for the revelation of this verse, as will come. It was also said: it is a parable that Allah struck for the one who performs *zihar* (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband declares his wife to be unlawful to him by likening her to his mother), meaning: just as a man cannot have two hearts, so also the wife of one who performs *zihar* cannot be his mother unless he has two mothers. Likewise, an adopted son (*da'i*, the one falsely claimed as a son) cannot be the son of two men.

It was also said: one of the hypocrites used to say, "I have a heart that commands me to do this and a heart that commands me to do that." So the verse was revealed to refute hypocrisy and to explain that it does not coexist with Islam, just as two hearts do not coexist. The heart is a small lump in the shape of a pine cone, which Allah created and made the seat of knowledge.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you declare unlawful [by zihar] your mothers﴾. The Kufans and Ibn Amir read *al-la'i* with a silent *ya'* after a *hamza*. Abu Amr and al-Bazzi read it with a silent *ya'* after a pure *alif*.

Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' said: It is the dialect of Quraysh, which the people were commanded to recite in.

Qunbul and Warsh read it with a *hamza* with a kasra, without a *ya'*.

Asim read *tuzahiruna* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *ha'* after an *alif*, the present tense of *zahara*. Ibn Amir read it with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'* and a shadda on the *za'*, the present tense of *tazahara*, and the original form is *tatazahirna*. The rest read *tazzahharun* with a fatha on the *ta'* and a shadda on the *za'*, without an *alif*, and the original form is *tatazahharun*.

*Zihar* (the pre-Islamic form of divorce described above) is derived from *zahr* (back), and its origin is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." The meaning is: Allah has not made your wives, whom you say this statement to, like your mothers in prohibition, but it is a reprehensible speech and a falsehood.

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons.﴾ The *ad'iya'* is the plural of *da'i*, who is the one who claims a son who is not his biological son. The discussion of *zihar* will come in Surah al-Mujadila.

The reference in His saying *"that"* (*dhalikum*) is to what preceded of the mention of *zihar* and adoption, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿your saying with your mouths﴾, meaning: that is nothing but a mere saying with the mouths and has no effect. So a woman does not become a mother by it, nor does the son of another become a son by it, and no ruling of motherhood or sonship follows from it.

It was also said: the reference is to adoption, meaning: your claim that the sons of others are your sons has no reality; rather it is merely a statement with the mouth. Allah speaks the truth, which is worthy of being followed, because it is true in itself and not false, so it includes the calling of sons to their fathers. ﴿And He guides to the way﴾, meaning: He indicates the path that leads to the truth. In this there is guidance for the servants to speak the truth and to abandon speaking falsehood and lies.

Then He, glory be to Him, explicitly stated what is obligatory upon the servants regarding calling sons by their fathers' names. He said: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, meaning: [call them] for their biological fathers, and attribute them to their fathers and do not call them by anything other than their fathers. The sentence ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ is a justification for the command to call sons by their fathers' names. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun of *ud'uhum*, and *aqsat* means *a'dal* (more just). That is: it is more just than every statement related to that. He left out the complement for generality, as in His saying *Allahu akbar* (Allah is greatest). The complement may also be a specific implied one, meaning: more just than your saying, "He is the son of so-and-so," when he was not his biological son.

Then He, glory be to Him, completed the guidance for the servants and said: ﴿And if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients.﴾ That is: then they are your brothers in religion and they are your clients. So say, "My brother" and "My client," and do not say, "the son of so-and-so," since you do not know their fathers in the true sense. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that *mawalikum* means your allies in religion.

It was also said: the meaning is: if they were freed slaves and not free men, then say "client of so-and-so."

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in﴾, meaning: there is no sin upon you for what occurs from you of that by error and without intention. ﴿But [what is sinful is] what your hearts have intended﴾, which is what you say deliberately, such as attributing sons to other than their fathers while knowing that.

Qatada said: If you call a man by someone other than his father while you believe he is his father, there is no harm upon you. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He forgives the one who errs, shows mercy to him, and overlooks him, or [it means]: He is Forgiving of sins and Merciful toward the servants. Among those whom He forgives and has mercy upon is one who calls a man by someone other than his father by mistake. Or [it means] before the prohibition against that.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned to His Messenger a great distinction and a magnificent privilege in which none of the servants shares with him. He said: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves﴾, meaning: he has more right over them in all matters of religion and worldly life, and more worthy of them than they are of themselves, let alone being more worthy of them than others. It is therefore obligatory upon them to prefer him over what he wants from their wealth, even if they are in need of it. It is obligatory upon them to love him more than they love themselves, and obligatory upon them to give precedence to his judgment over their own judgment for themselves.

In summary: when the Prophet (ﷺ) calls them to something and their own souls call them to something else, it is obligatory upon them to give precedence to what he has called them to and to delay what their souls have called them to. It is obligatory upon them to obey him above their obedience to themselves, and to give precedence to his obedience over what their souls incline to and their inner impulses desire.

It was also said: what is meant by "themselves" in the verse is some of them, so the meaning is: the Prophet is more worthy of the believers than some of them are of others.

It was also said: it is specific to judgment, meaning: he is more worthy of them than themselves regarding what he judges between them.

It was also said: he is more worthy of them in jihad before him and in sacrificing the self in his defense. The first is the most correct.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, meaning: they are like their mothers in the ruling of prohibition, and they are placed in the position of mothers regarding the entitlement to honor. So it is not lawful for anyone to marry any one of them, just as it is not lawful for him to marry his own mother. This motherhood is specific to the prohibition of marrying them and to honoring their dignity. The specification of "the believers" indicates that they are not the mothers of the believers' wives, nor their daughters the sisters of the believers, nor their brothers the maternal uncles of the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: What appears to me is that they are the mothers of both men and women, in honor of their right over men and women, as His saying indicates: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves,"* and this necessarily includes men and women.

He said: Moreover, in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b [it reads]: *"And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them."* Ibn Abbas read: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."*

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified that kinship is more worthy for some of them over others. He said: ﴿And those of relationship are more entitled to one another﴾. What is meant by "those of relationship" is the relatives, meaning: they have more right to one another in inheritance. The explanation of this verse has already passed at the end of Surah al-Anfal, and it abrogates what was in the early period of Islam concerning inheritance through emigration and alliance.

Qatada said: When Allah, glorified is He, revealed in Surat al-Anfal, ﴿Those who believed but did not migrate, you owe them no guardianship at all until they migrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], the Muslims inherited from one another on account of migration (hijra, emigration to Medina). Then this was abrogated (naskh) by this verse. Others said the same.

It was said that this verse abrogates inheritance through alliance (hilf) and brotherhood in religion (mu'akhah). The phrase ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ may be connected to the comparative form ﴿closer﴾ in His saying ﴿closer to one another﴾, since the comparative governs the adverbial phrase. It may also be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun, meaning "existing in the Book of Allah." By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the Qur'an, or the verse of inheritance. His saying ﴿of the believers﴾ may be an explanation of ﴿those of the kinship ties (ulu al-arham)﴾, meaning that relatives among the believers and the emigrants are closer to one another. It may also be connected to ﴿closer﴾, meaning that the kinship-holders are closer to one another than the believers and emigrants who are strangers. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another, except for what is permitted to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely that they are like mothers in the prohibition of marriage." There is much weakness in this view, as is well known.

﴿Except that you do kindness to your allies﴾: This exception is either a connected exception from a more general category, and the sense is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another in every matter, including inheritance and other things, except that you do kindness to your allies by way of charity or bequest, for that is permissible." This was said by Qatada, al-Hasan, Ata, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: It was revealed concerning the permissibility of bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian. The disbeliever is a relative by lineage, though not by religion, so it is permissible to make a bequest to him. The exception may also be disconnected (munqati'), and the meaning is: "But doing good to one's allies is not objectionable." The meaning of the verse is that when Allah, glorified is He, abrogated inheritance through alliance and migration, He permitted bequests to them.

At the end of the discussion there will come the explanation of the reason for the revelation of the verse. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, meaning: possessing abundant knowledge and wisdom, and perfect in both. Al-Nahhas said: By His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, He indicated that [the Prophet] (ﷺ) used to incline toward them, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), in order to invite them to Islam. The meaning is: if Allah, mighty and majestic, knew that your inclination toward them would be beneficial, He would not have forbidden you from them, for He is Wise. The remoteness of this inference that he claims is not hidden. However, this sentence is a justification for the sentence containing the command to fear Allah and the prohibition against obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites. The meaning is: He does not command you or forbid you except with what He knows to contain righteousness or corruption, because of the abundance of His knowledge and the vastness of His wisdom.

﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, namely from the Qur'an, meaning: follow the revelation in all your affairs, and do not follow anything other than it, such as the counsels of the disbelievers and hypocrites, nor pure personal opinion, for in what has been revealed to you is that which suffices you from that. The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ is a justification for His command to follow what has been revealed to you. The command addressed to him (ﷺ) is a command to his community, so they are commanded to follow the Qur'an just as he is commanded to follow it. For this reason, the address to him and to them is combined in His saying, *"of what you do,"* according to the reading of the majority with the second-person form (*ta'*). Abu Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading.

Abu Amr, al-Sulami, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with the third-person form (*ya'*).

﴿And rely upon Allah; and sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾, meaning: depend upon Him and entrust your affairs to Him, and sufficient is He as a guardian who protects whoever relies upon Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned a parable as a preface and preparation for the legal rulings of the Qur'an that follow it, which are part of the revelation that Allah commanded him to follow. He said: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body.﴾

It has been disputed what was the reason for the revelation of this verse, as will come. It was also said: it is a parable that Allah struck for the one who performs *zihar* (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband declares his wife to be unlawful to him by likening her to his mother), meaning: just as a man cannot have two hearts, so also the wife of one who performs *zihar* cannot be his mother unless he has two mothers. Likewise, an adopted son (*da'i*, the one falsely claimed as a son) cannot be the son of two men.

It was also said: one of the hypocrites used to say, "I have a heart that commands me to do this and a heart that commands me to do that." So the verse was revealed to refute hypocrisy and to explain that it does not coexist with Islam, just as two hearts do not coexist. The heart is a small lump in the shape of a pine cone, which Allah created and made the seat of knowledge.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you declare unlawful [by zihar] your mothers﴾. The Kufans and Ibn Amir read *al-la'i* with a silent *ya'* after a *hamza*. Abu Amr and al-Bazzi read it with a silent *ya'* after a pure *alif*.

Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' said: It is the dialect of Quraysh, which the people were commanded to recite in.

Qunbul and Warsh read it with a *hamza* with a kasra, without a *ya'*.

Asim read *tuzahiruna* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a kasra on the *ha'* after an *alif*, the present tense of *zahara*. Ibn Amir read it with a fatha on the *ta'* and the *ha'* and a shadda on the *za'*, the present tense of *tazahara*, and the original form is *tatazahirna*. The rest read *tazzahharun* with a fatha on the *ta'* and a shadda on the *za'*, without an *alif*, and the original form is *tatazahharun*.

*Zihar* (the pre-Islamic form of divorce described above) is derived from *zahr* (back), and its origin is that a man says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother." The meaning is: Allah has not made your wives, whom you say this statement to, like your mothers in prohibition, but it is a reprehensible speech and a falsehood.

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons.﴾ The *ad'iya'* is the plural of *da'i*, who is the one who claims a son who is not his biological son. The discussion of *zihar* will come in Surah al-Mujadila.

The reference in His saying *"that"* (*dhalikum*) is to what preceded of the mention of *zihar* and adoption, and it is the subject whose predicate is ﴿your saying with your mouths﴾, meaning: that is nothing but a mere saying with the mouths and has no effect. So a woman does not become a mother by it, nor does the son of another become a son by it, and no ruling of motherhood or sonship follows from it.

It was also said: the reference is to adoption, meaning: your claim that the sons of others are your sons has no reality; rather it is merely a statement with the mouth. Allah speaks the truth, which is worthy of being followed, because it is true in itself and not false, so it includes the calling of sons to their fathers. ﴿And He guides to the way﴾, meaning: He indicates the path that leads to the truth. In this there is guidance for the servants to speak the truth and to abandon speaking falsehood and lies.

Then He, glory be to Him, explicitly stated what is obligatory upon the servants regarding calling sons by their fathers' names. He said: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, meaning: [call them] for their biological fathers, and attribute them to their fathers and do not call them by anything other than their fathers. The sentence ﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ is a justification for the command to call sons by their fathers' names. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun of *ud'uhum*, and *aqsat* means *a'dal* (more just). That is: it is more just than every statement related to that. He left out the complement for generality, as in His saying *Allahu akbar* (Allah is greatest). The complement may also be a specific implied one, meaning: more just than your saying, "He is the son of so-and-so," when he was not his biological son.

Then He, glory be to Him, completed the guidance for the servants and said: ﴿And if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients.﴾ That is: then they are your brothers in religion and they are your clients. So say, "My brother" and "My client," and do not say, "the son of so-and-so," since you do not know their fathers in the true sense. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible that *mawalikum* means your allies in religion.

It was also said: the meaning is: if they were freed slaves and not free men, then say "client of so-and-so."

﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have erred in﴾, meaning: there is no sin upon you for what occurs from you of that by error and without intention. ﴿But [what is sinful is] what your hearts have intended﴾, which is what you say deliberately, such as attributing sons to other than their fathers while knowing that.

Qatada said: If you call a man by someone other than his father while you believe he is his father, there is no harm upon you. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning: He forgives the one who errs, shows mercy to him, and overlooks him, or [it means]: He is Forgiving of sins and Merciful toward the servants. Among those whom He forgives and has mercy upon is one who calls a man by someone other than his father by mistake. Or [it means] before the prohibition against that.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned to His Messenger a great distinction and a magnificent privilege in which none of the servants shares with him. He said: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves﴾, meaning: he has more right over them in all matters of religion and worldly life, and more worthy of them than they are of themselves, let alone being more worthy of them than others. It is therefore obligatory upon them to prefer him over what he wants from their wealth, even if they are in need of it. It is obligatory upon them to love him more than they love themselves, and obligatory upon them to give precedence to his judgment over their own judgment for themselves.

In summary: when the Prophet (ﷺ) calls them to something and their own souls call them to something else, it is obligatory upon them to give precedence to what he has called them to and to delay what their souls have called them to. It is obligatory upon them to obey him above their obedience to themselves, and to give precedence to his obedience over what their souls incline to and their inner impulses desire.

It was also said: what is meant by "themselves" in the verse is some of them, so the meaning is: the Prophet is more worthy of the believers than some of them are of others.

It was also said: it is specific to judgment, meaning: he is more worthy of them than themselves regarding what he judges between them.

It was also said: he is more worthy of them in jihad before him and in sacrificing the self in his defense. The first is the most correct.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, meaning: they are like their mothers in the ruling of prohibition, and they are placed in the position of mothers regarding the entitlement to honor. So it is not lawful for anyone to marry any one of them, just as it is not lawful for him to marry his own mother. This motherhood is specific to the prohibition of marrying them and to honoring their dignity. The specification of "the believers" indicates that they are not the mothers of the believers' wives, nor their daughters the sisters of the believers, nor their brothers the maternal uncles of the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: What appears to me is that they are the mothers of both men and women, in honor of their right over men and women, as His saying indicates: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves,"* and this necessarily includes men and women.

He said: Moreover, in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b [it reads]: *"And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them."* Ibn Abbas read: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."*

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified that kinship is more worthy for some of them over others. He said: ﴿And those of relationship are more entitled to one another﴾. What is meant by "those of relationship" is the relatives, meaning: they have more right to one another in inheritance. The explanation of this verse has already passed at the end of Surah al-Anfal, and it abrogates what was in the early period of Islam concerning inheritance through emigration and alliance.

Qatada said: When Allah, glorified is He, revealed in Surat al-Anfal, ﴿Those who believed but did not migrate, you owe them no guardianship at all until they migrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], the Muslims inherited from one another on account of migration (hijra, emigration to Medina). Then this was abrogated (naskh) by this verse. Others said the same.

It was said that this verse abrogates inheritance through alliance (hilf) and brotherhood in religion (mu'akhah). The phrase ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ may be connected to the comparative form ﴿closer﴾ in His saying ﴿closer to one another﴾, since the comparative governs the adverbial phrase. It may also be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun, meaning "existing in the Book of Allah." By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the Qur'an, or the verse of inheritance. His saying ﴿of the believers﴾ may be an explanation of ﴿those of the kinship ties (ulu al-arham)﴾, meaning that relatives among the believers and the emigrants are closer to one another. It may also be connected to ﴿closer﴾, meaning that the kinship-holders are closer to one another than the believers and emigrants who are strangers. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another, except for what is permitted to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely that they are like mothers in the prohibition of marriage." There is much weakness in this view, as is well known.

﴿Except that you do kindness to your allies﴾: This exception is either a connected exception from a more general category, and the sense is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another in every matter, including inheritance and other things, except that you do kindness to your allies by way of charity or bequest, for that is permissible." This was said by Qatada, al-Hasan, Ata, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: It was revealed concerning the permissibility of bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian. The disbeliever is a relative by lineage, though not by religion, so it is permissible to make a bequest to him. The exception may also be disconnected (munqati'), and the meaning is: "But doing good to one's allies is not objectionable." The meaning of the verse is that when Allah, glorified is He, abrogated inheritance through alliance and migration, He permitted bequests to them.

Mujahid said: By "kindness" is meant support and preserving the sanctity of the rights of faith and migration. The reference in His saying ﴿that was﴾ is to what was previously mentioned, that is, the abrogation of inheritance by migration, alliance, and pledge, and the return of inheritance to kinship relations. ﴿In the Book, inscribed﴾ means in the Preserved Tablet, or in the Qur'an, written down.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood one day praying, and he had a slip of thought. The hypocrites who prayed with him said: 'Do you not see that he has two hearts, one with you and one with them?' Then ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest﴾ was revealed."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him by another route, with the wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed a prayer in which he made a mistake, and a word escaped him. The hypocrites heard it and said: 'He has two hearts.' Then it was revealed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him, who said: "There was a man of Quraysh called Dhu al-Qalbayn (the Man of Two Hearts) because of his cunning, so Allah revealed this concerning him."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Ibn Umar that "Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we would not call him anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5]. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You are Zayd ibn Harithah ibn Sharahil.'"

al-Bukhari and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no believer but that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. So whichever believer leaves wealth, let his heirs, whoever they are, inherit it. And if he leaves a debt or dependents, let him come to me, for I am his guardian (mawla)."

Ahmad and Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted a similar report from the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Buraydah, who said: "I campaigned with Ali to Yemen, and I saw from him some harshness. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned Ali and disparaged him. I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) change, and he said: 'O Buraydah, am I not closer to the believers than themselves?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla.'"

It is established in the Sahih that he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until I am dearer to him than his own self, his wealth, his child, and all people."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Aisha that a woman said to her: "O mother!" and she said: "I am the mother of your men, but I am not the mother of your women."

Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Umm Salama, who said: "I am the mother of the men among you and of the women."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Dala'il transmitted from Bajala, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by a boy who was reading in the mushaf: 'The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them.' He said: 'O boy, erase it!' The boy said: 'This is the mushaf of Ubayy.' So he went to him and asked him, and he said: 'The Qur'an occupied me, and trading in the markets occupied you.'"

al-Firyabi, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 33, verses 1–6 (part 1 of 2)**

**Tafsir (explanation, exegesis) of Surah al-Ahzab**

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated through several chains from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab was revealed at Medina." Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Abd al-Razzaq in *al-Musannaf*, al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Musnad*, Ibn Mani', al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtara* narrated from Zirr, who said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b said to me, "How many [verses] do you recite Surah al-Ahzab as having, or how many do you count it as?" I said, "Seventy-three verses." He said, "Indeed! I have seen it when it was equal to Surah al-Baqarah, or more than Surah al-Baqarah. We used to recite in it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.'* Then it was abrogated along with what was abrogated." Ibn Kathir said: its chain is *hasan* (good).

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that Umar ibn al-Khattab stood up, praised Allah and extolled Him, and then said: "As for what follows, O people, Allah sent Muhammad with the truth and revealed the Book to him. Among what was revealed to him was the verse of stoning. We recited it and understood it: *'The male elder and the female elder, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely.'* The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stoned [adulterers], and we stoned after him. I fear that a long time will pass over people and someone will say, 'We do not find the verse of stoning in the Book of Allah,' and thus they will go astray by abandoning an obligation that Allah revealed." Similar to this has been narrated from him through several chains.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said to me, "How many [verses] do you count Surah al-Ahzab as having?" I said, "Two or seventy-three." He said, "It nearly equals Surah al-Baqarah, and indeed it contains the verse of stoning."

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh* narrated: "I recited Surah al-Ahzab to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I forgot seventy verses of it, which I could not find."

Abu Ubayd in *al-Fada'il*, Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Aisha, who said: "Surah al-Ahzab used to be recited in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) as two hundred verses. When Uthman copied the codices (*masahif*), he did not keep from it except what is in it now."

He said: ﴿The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves﴾, meaning: he has more right over them in all matters of religion and worldly life, and more worthy of them than they are of themselves, let alone being more worthy of them than others. It is therefore obligatory upon them to prefer him over what he wants from their wealth, even if they are in need of it. It is obligatory upon them to love him more than they love themselves, and obligatory upon them to give precedence to his judgment over their own judgment for themselves.

In summary: when the Prophet (ﷺ) calls them to something and their own souls call them to something else, it is obligatory upon them to give precedence to what he has called them to and to delay what their souls have called them to. It is obligatory upon them to obey him above their obedience to themselves, and to give precedence to his obedience over what their souls incline to and their inner impulses desire.

It was also said: what is meant by "themselves" in the verse is some of them, so the meaning is: the Prophet is more worthy of the believers than some of them are of others.

It was also said: it is specific to judgment, meaning: he is more worthy of them than themselves regarding what he judges between them.

It was also said: he is more worthy of them in jihad before him and in sacrificing the self in his defense. The first is the most correct.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, meaning: they are like their mothers in the ruling of prohibition, and they are placed in the position of mothers regarding the entitlement to honor. So it is not lawful for anyone to marry any one of them, just as it is not lawful for him to marry his own mother. This motherhood is specific to the prohibition of marrying them and to honoring their dignity. The specification of "the believers" indicates that they are not the mothers of the believers' wives, nor their daughters the sisters of the believers, nor their brothers the maternal uncles of the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: What appears to me is that they are the mothers of both men and women, in honor of their right over men and women, as His saying indicates: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves,"* and this necessarily includes men and women.

He said: Moreover, in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b [it reads]: *"And his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them."* Ibn Abbas read: *"The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."*

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified that kinship is more worthy for some of them over others. He said: ﴿And those of relationship are more entitled to one another﴾. What is meant by "those of relationship" is the relatives, meaning: they have more right to one another in inheritance. The explanation of this verse has already passed at the end of Surah al-Anfal, and it abrogates what was in the early period of Islam concerning inheritance through emigration and alliance.

Qatada said: When Allah, glorified is He, revealed in Surat al-Anfal, ﴿Those who believed but did not migrate, you owe them no guardianship at all until they migrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72], the Muslims inherited from one another on account of migration (hijra, emigration to Medina). Then this was abrogated (naskh) by this verse. Others said the same.

It was said that this verse abrogates inheritance through alliance (hilf) and brotherhood in religion (mu'akhah). The phrase ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ may be connected to the comparative form ﴿closer﴾ in His saying ﴿closer to one another﴾, since the comparative governs the adverbial phrase. It may also be connected to an omitted word that serves as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun, meaning "existing in the Book of Allah." By "the Book" is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or the Qur'an, or the verse of inheritance. His saying ﴿of the believers﴾ may be an explanation of ﴿those of the kinship ties (ulu al-arham)﴾, meaning that relatives among the believers and the emigrants are closer to one another. It may also be connected to ﴿closer﴾, meaning that the kinship-holders are closer to one another than the believers and emigrants who are strangers. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another, except for what is permitted to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), namely that they are like mothers in the prohibition of marriage." There is much weakness in this view, as is well known.

﴿Except that you do kindness to your allies﴾: This exception is either a connected exception from a more general category, and the sense is: "And those of kinship are closer to one another in every matter, including inheritance and other things, except that you do kindness to your allies by way of charity or bequest, for that is permissible." This was said by Qatada, al-Hasan, Ata, and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: It was revealed concerning the permissibility of bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian. The disbeliever is a relative by lineage, though not by religion, so it is permissible to make a bequest to him. The exception may also be disconnected (munqati'), and the meaning is: "But doing good to one's allies is not objectionable." The meaning of the verse is that when Allah, glorified is He, abrogated inheritance through alliance and migration, He permitted bequests to them.

Mujahid said: By "kindness" is meant support and preserving the sanctity of the rights of faith and migration. The reference in His saying ﴿that was﴾ is to what was previously mentioned, that is, the abrogation of inheritance by migration, alliance, and pledge, and the return of inheritance to kinship relations. ﴿In the Book, inscribed﴾ means in the Preserved Tablet, or in the Qur'an, written down.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in al-Mukhtara transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood one day praying, and he had a slip of thought. The hypocrites who prayed with him said: 'Do you not see that he has two hearts, one with you and one with them?' Then ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest﴾ was revealed."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from him by another route, with the wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed a prayer in which he made a mistake, and a word escaped him. The hypocrites heard it and said: 'He has two hearts.' Then it was revealed."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted from him, who said: "There was a man of Quraysh called Dhu al-Qalbayn (the Man of Two Hearts) because of his cunning, so Allah revealed this concerning him."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others transmitted from Ibn Umar that "Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed slave of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we would not call him anything but Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by their fathers' names﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5]. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'You are Zayd ibn Harithah ibn Sharahil.'"

al-Bukhari and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "There is no believer but that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. So whichever believer leaves wealth, let his heirs, whoever they are, inherit it. And if he leaves a debt or dependents, let him come to me, for I am his guardian (mawla)."

Ahmad and Abu Dawud and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted a similar report from the hadith of Jabir.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ahmad, and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Buraydah, who said: "I campaigned with Ali to Yemen, and I saw from him some harshness. When I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I mentioned Ali and disparaged him. I saw the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) change, and he said: 'O Buraydah, am I not closer to the believers than themselves?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Whoever I am his mawla, then Ali is his mawla.'"

It is established in the Sahih that he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, none of you believes until I am dearer to him than his own self, his wealth, his child, and all people."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Aisha that a woman said to her: "O mother!" and she said: "I am the mother of your men, but I am not the mother of your women."

Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Umm Salama, who said: "I am the mother of the men among you and of the women."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Dala'il transmitted from Bajala, who said: "Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by a boy who was reading in the mushaf: 'The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them.' He said: 'O boy, erase it!' The boy said: 'This is the mushaf of Ubayy.' So he went to him and asked him, and he said: 'The Qur'an occupied me, and trading in the markets occupied you.'"
