al-Firyabi, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 7–23 (part 1 of 3):

His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾. The verb governing the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning "and mention" (wa-dhkur). It is as if He said: "O Prophet, fear Allah, and mention that Allah took the covenant of the prophets."

Qatadah said: Allah took the covenant from the prophets specifically that each of them would confirm the others and that they would follow one another.

Muqatil said: He took their covenant that they would worship Allah, call to the worship of Allah, confirm one another, and give sincere counsel to their peoples.

The covenant (mithaq) is an oath. It was said that it is the acknowledgment of Allah, but the first view is preferable, and its verification has already passed.

Then, after the general statement that encompasses them and others, He (glory be to Him) singled out some of the prophets by mention, saying: ﴿and from you, and from Noah, and Abraham, and Moses, and Jesus son of Mary﴾. The purpose of singling them out is to inform that they have a special excellence and virtue, being among the possessors of well-known laws (shara'i') and among the "Ulu al-'Azm" (the steadfast messengers). Mentioning our Prophet (ﷺ) first, despite his coming later in time, carries an honour and exaltation for him that is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: He took the covenant at the time when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam like particles (al-dharr).

Then He reinforced the covenant He took from the prophets by repeating its mention and describing it as ghaliz (firm), saying: ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, meaning a strong pledge to fulfil what they bore and what Allah had taken from them. It is also permissible that Allah took the covenant from them twice: the first time He took it from them as a mere covenant without emphasis or strictness, then He took it from them a second time, emphasized and strengthened. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there will come to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you will surely believe in him and surely support him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81].

The lam in His saying: ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: in order that He may ask the truthful among the prophets about their truthfulness in conveying the message to their peoples. In this there is a warning to others, for if they are questioned about that, then how about others?

It was said: that He may ask the prophets about what their peoples answered them with, as in His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. It is also permissible that it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: He did that in order to ask. ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ is coordinated with what is indicated by "that He may ask the truthful," since the sense is: He rewarded the truthful and prepared for the disbelievers. It is also permissible that it is coordinated with "We took," since the meaning is: He emphasized to the prophets the call to His religion, so that He might reward the believers and prepare for the disbelievers.

It was said: the second part has omitted what has its counterpart stated in the first, and the first has omitted what has its counterpart stated in the second, and the sense is: that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness, so He rewarded them, and that He may ask the disbelievers about what they answered their messengers, and He prepared for them a painful punishment.

It was said: it is coordinated with the implied governing verb as we mentioned. It is also permissible that the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾, and the clause ﴿and He has prepared for them﴾ is a new sentence explaining what He prepared for the disbelievers.

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾. This is a verification of the earlier command to fear Allah, to such a degree that no fear of anyone remains with it. The phrase ʿalaykum is connected to "favour" if it is a verbal noun (masdar), or to an omitted state (hal) meaning: existing upon you. The sense of ﴿when there came to you soldiers﴾ is "at the time when soldiers came to you." It is an adverbial phrase governed either by "favour," or by the implied verb governing ʿalaykum, or by an omitted "remember." By "soldiers" is meant the armies of the confederates (al-ahzab) who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and attacked him at Medina, which is the expedition known as "the Battle of the Trench" (Ghazwat al-Khandaq). They were: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb with the Quraysh and those who were with them of the mixed tribes, ʿUyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari and those with him of his people, Ghatafan, and the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir. They besieged the Muslims with a severe siege, as Allah the Glorified described in these verses. This expedition took place in Shawwal in the fifth year of the Hijra. This is what Ibn Ishaq said, while Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik, said it was in the fourth year.

The people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) have expounded on this event in what is well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it. ﴿So We sent upon them a wind﴾ is coordinated with "came to you."

Mujahid said: It was the east wind (al-Saba), sent upon the confederates on the day of the Trench, until it overturned their cooking pots and uprooted their tents. What supports this is what is established from him (ﷺ) in his saying: "I was helped by the Saba, and ʿAd were destroyed by the Dabur." By His saying ﴿and soldiers you did not see﴾ are meant the angels.

The commentators said: Allah sent upon them the angels, who uprooted the tent pegs, cut the ropes of the tents, extinguished the fires, overturned the pots, the horses ran about among one another, Allah sent terror upon them, and the angels' takbir increased on the sides of the camp, until the chief of each people would say to his people: "O Banu so-and-so, come to me!" When they gathered, he would say to them: "Escape! Escape!"

﴿And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do﴾. Most readers read taʿmalun with the second-person (ta), meaning: of what you do, O Muslims, of arranging the war, digging the trench, seeking victory through Him, and putting your trust in Him. Abu ʿAmr read it with the third-person (ya), meaning: of what the disbelievers do of enmity toward Allah and His Messenger, and of banding together against the Muslims and gathering against them from every side.

﴿When they came upon you from above you﴾. This "when" and what follows it is a substitution (badal) for the first "when," and the governing verb of this one is the governing verb of that one. It was also said that it is in the accusative governed by an omitted "remember." The meaning of "from above you" is from the upper part of the valley, which is from the direction of the east. Those who came from this direction were Ghatafan, whose chief was ʿUyayna ibn Hisn; Hawazin, whose chief was ʿAwf ibn Malik; and the people of Najd, whose chief was Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi; ʿAwf ibn Malik and the Banu al-Nadir joined them. The meaning of ﴿and from below you﴾ is from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west, from the side of Mecca. These were the Quraysh and those with them of the Ahabish, whose chief was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. Abu al-Aʿwar al-Sulami came with Huyayy ibn Akhtab the Jew among the Jews of Banu Qurayza from the side of the trench, and with them ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl.

The clause ﴿and when the eyes deviated﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: the eyes turned away from everything, so they looked at nothing but their enemy approaching from every side. It was said: they stared in astonishment from the extreme of the terror and bewilderment. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾: "hanajir" is the plural of "hanjara," which is the cavity of the windpipe. The meaning is that the hearts rose from their places and reached the throats from fear and dread, so that had the windpipe not been too narrow for them, which is where it ends at the hanjara, they would have come out. Thus said Qatadah.

It was said: this is an expression of the familiar hyperbole in the speech of the Arabs, even though the hearts did not rise to that place nor leave their position; rather it is a metaphor for their agitation and cowardice.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is that they became cowardly and most of them panicked. The way of the coward, when his fear intensifies, is that his lungs swell, and when the lungs swell the heart rises to the throat; for this reason it is said of a coward: "his lungs swelled (intansha sahruhu)."

﴿And you were thinking about Allah with assumptions﴾, that is, diverse assumptions. Some of them thought victory and hoped for triumph, while others thought otherwise.

Al-Hasan said: The hypocrites thought that Muhammad and his companions would be wiped out, while the believers thought that he would be given victory.

It was said: the verse is addressed to the hypocrites, but the better view is what al-Hasan said, so the address is to whoever professes Islam in general, whether he is a believer in reality or a hypocrite.

The readers differed concerning this alif in "al-zununa" (the assumptions). Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr kept it both in connection and in pause; this reading is also reported from Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i. They relied on the script of the ʿUthmanic Mushaf and all the copies in all the regions, in which the alif is present throughout. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading, but he said: the reader should not run on from them, rather he should pause upon them. They also relied on what occurs in Arabic poetry of this kind.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read it without the alif both in connection and in pause, and they said: it is one of the additions of the script, so it was written thus, and it should not be pronounced.

As for poetry, it permits for necessity what is not permitted otherwise.

Ibn Kathir, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with the alif in pause and without it in connection; this reading is preferred from the standpoint of the Arabic language. This alif is what the grammarians call the alif of extension (alif al-itlaq), and its discussion is well known in the science of grammar. Likewise the readers differed concerning the alif in His saying "al-Rasula" and "al-Sabila," as will come at the end of this surah.

﴿There the believers were tested﴾. The adverb is governed by the verb that follows it. It was said that it is governed by "you think," but Ibn ʿAtiyya considered this weak. It is an adverb of place; just as "hunalika" is said for a distant place, "huna" for a near place, and "hunaka" for an intermediate one, it can also be an adverb of time, meaning: at that time the believers were tested. From this is the poet's saying:

"And when affairs grow great and become intertwined, then there they acknowledge: where is the refuge?"

meaning: at that time. The sense is that in that place or at that time the believers were tested by fear, fighting, hunger, siege and combat, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite.

﴿And they were shaken with a severe shaking﴾. Most readers read "zululu" with a damma on the first zay and a kasra on the second, according to the original form of the passive. It is reported from Abu ʿAmr that he read it with a kasra on the first, and al-Zamakhshari reported from him that he read it with an intonation (ishmam) of kasra. Most readers read "zilzalan" with a kasra on the first zay, while ʿAsim, al-Jahdari and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it with a fatha.

Al-Zajjaj said: every verbal noun of a doubled root on the pattern fi'lal may be read with kasra or fatha, such as "qalqaltuhu qilqalan" and "zulzilu zilzalan," and the kasra is better.

Ibn Salam said: the meaning of "zulzilu" is: they were moved by fear with a severe movement.

Al-Dahhak said: it is their being displaced from their places until there was for them only the spot of the trench. It was said: the meaning is that they were agitated in diverse ways: some were agitated in themselves, and some were agitated in their religion.

﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said﴾. This is coordinated with ﴿and when the eyes deviated﴾. "Disease" (maradun) in the hearts is doubt and suspicion. By "the hypocrites" is meant ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and by "those in whose hearts is a disease" are the people of doubt and agitation: ﴿"Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion"﴾, that is, falsehood of speech. The sayers of this statement were about seventy men of the people of hypocrisy and doubt. This statement attributed to them serves as an explanation of the assumptions mentioned, meaning: the assumption of these was this assumption, just as the assumption of the believers was victory and the elevation of the word of Allah.

﴿And when a faction of them said﴾, that is, of the hypocrites.

Muqatil said: They are the Banu Salim among the hypocrites.

al-Suddi said: They are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. It was said: they are Aws ibn Qibti and his companions. The word "ta'ifa" applies to one or more. The statement that this faction said is: ﴿"O people of Yathrib, there is no station for you"﴾, that is, there is no place of residence for you, or there is no residence for you here in the camp.

Abu ʿUbayd said: Yathrib is the name of the land, and the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) is in one part of it.

Al-Suhayli said: The city was named Yathrib because the one who first settled it from the Amalekites was named Yathrib ibn ʿUmayl. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "لا مَقامَ لَكم" (lā maqāma lakum, "there is no place to stay for you") with a fatḥah on the mīm, while Ḥafṣ, al-Sulamī, al-Jaḥdarī and Abū Ḥaywa read it with a ḍammah, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) from aqāma yuqīmu ("to remain"). On the first reading it is a noun of place (ism makān), meaning "your dwellings." They told them to flee from the army of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims went out in the year of the Trench (al-Khandaq) and placed their backs toward Salʿ, with the trench between them and the enemy. These hypocrites said: "There is no place here for staying," and they ordered the people to return to their homes in Medina. ﴿And a group of them asked permission of the Prophet﴾ is coordinated (maʿṭūf) upon "a group of them said" (qālat ṭāʾifatun minhum), meaning: they asked permission to return to their homes, and they were the Banu Ḥāritha and the Banu Salima. The clause "they say" (yaqūlūna) is either a substitute (badal) for "they ask permission," or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) answering an implied question. The saying they uttered, which is their statement: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed⦆, that is, lost and unprotected, not secure and not defended from the enemy.

Al-Zajjāj said: It is said ʿawira al-makān yaʿwaru ʿawaran wa-ʿawratan, and "buyūtun ʿawiratun wa-ʿawratun," and ʿawra is a verbal noun.

Mujāhid, Muqātil and al-Ḥasan said: They said, "Our houses are unguarded; we fear thieves for them."

Qatāda said: They said, "Our houses are on the side facing the enemy, and we are not safe for our families."

Al-Harawī said: Every place that is not protected or concealed is ʿawra. The root meaning of ʿawra is a defect (khalal), and then it was applied to what has a defect. The intended meaning is "a place with a defect." Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī read ʿawiratun with a kasrah on the wāw, meaning "with walls that are short."

Al-Jawharī said: ʿAwra is every condition feared in a frontier or in war.

Al-Naḥḥās said: It is said aʿwara al-makān when a defect becomes apparent in it, and aʿwara al-fāris when the gap in him becomes apparent. Then He, glorified is He, refuted them with His saying: ﴿But they are not exposed﴾, so Allah, glorified is He, declared them liars in what they claimed. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Then He explained the reason for their seeking permission and what they intend by it, saying: ﴿They intend nothing but flight﴾, that is, they intend only to flee from fighting. It was also said: the intended meaning is that they intend only to flee from the religion.

﴿And if it had been entered upon them from all its sides﴾, meaning their houses or Medina, and the aqṭār (sides) are the directions, plural of quṭr, which is a side and a direction. The meaning: if their houses or Medina had been entered upon them from all its sides together, not from some of them, this severe calamity would have befallen them, their homes would have been plundered, and their sanctities and dwellings violated. ﴿Then they were asked for sedition﴾ from another direction at the arrival of this severe calamity upon them, ﴿they would have given it⦆, that is, they would have come to it or granted it. The meaning of fitna here is either fighting in tribal partisanship, as al-Ḍaḥḥāk said, or association with Allah and return to the disbelief which they conceal while showing the opposite, as al-Ḥasan said. The majority read "la-ātawhā" with the madd, meaning they would have given it from themselves. Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read it with qaṣr, meaning they would have come to it. ﴿And they would not have stayed therein except briefly﴾, that is, in Medina, after they came to sedition, except for a brief stay until they perished. Thus said al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī, al-Farrāʾ and al-Qutaybī.

But most of the exegetes said: the meaning is: they would not have hesitated from the sedition of polytheism except briefly, but rather they would hasten to it, eager for it, and would stop only at the mere fact that the question was put to them, and would not excuse themselves from answering by saying that their houses in this state are exposed, even though they were in fact exposed, just as they excused themselves from answering the Messenger and fighting with him by saying that they were exposed, when they were not exposed at that time.

Then He, glorified is He, related what had occurred from them earlier of the covenant to Allah and His Messenger to remain steadfast in war and not flee from it, saying: ﴿And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs﴾, that is, before the battle of the Trench and after Badr. Qatāda said: This was because they were absent from Badr and saw what Allah gave the people of Badr of honor and victory, so they said: "If Allah makes us witness fighting, we will surely fight." They were the Banu Ḥāritha and the Banu Salima. ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned⦆, that is, it will be questioned about, its holder is demanded to fulfill it, and he will be recompensed for abandoning its fulfillment.

﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing﴾, for whoever his term has come, dies or is killed, whether he flees or does not flee. ﴿And then you will not be given enjoyment except a little﴾, that is, a little enjoyment or a little time after their flight until their terms end, and everything that is coming is near. The majority read "tumattaʿūna" with the second-person form; Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, in the transmission of al-Sājī from him, read it with the third-person (taḥtiyya).

In some transmissions it is "lā tumattaʿū," with the nūn dropped, treating idhan as operative; on the majority's reading, it is cancelled (mulghāh).

﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm﴾, that is, destruction, or loss of wealth, drought and sickness, ﴿or intends for you mercy﴾, by which He shows mercy to you through fertility, victory and well-being. ﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any ally﴾, who would support them and ward off [harm] from them, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who would help them against the punishment of Allah.

Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil have recorded from Abū Maryam al-Ghassānī that "a Bedouin said: O Messenger of Allah, what was the first thing of your prophethood? He said: Allah took my covenant as He took the covenant of the prophets, then he recited" ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, son of Mary, and We took from them a firm covenant﴾, and the supplication of Abraham: (p-1161) ﴿Send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 129], and the glad tidings of Jesus, son of Mary, and the mother of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in her dream that a lamp came out from between her legs, by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when was your covenant taken? He said: While Adam was between the spirit and the body."

Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil recorded from him, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when did you become a prophet? He said: While Adam was between the spirit and the body."

There are other ḥadīths on this subject, some of which have been declared authentic.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil, al-Daylamī and Ibn ʿAsākir recorded through the chain of Qatāda from al-Ḥasan from Abū Hurayra from "the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾, the verse, he said: I was the first of the prophets in creation and the last of them in resurrection, so He began with me before them."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "their covenant" means their pledge.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī recorded with a ṣaḥīḥ chain from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ that he said: Allah only took the covenant of the prophets concerning their peoples.

Al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqī both in al-Dalāʾil, and Ibn ʿAsākir recorded through various chains from Ḥudhayfa who said: "We saw ourselves on the night of the Confederates, while we sat in rows, and Abū Sufyān and those with him of the confederates were above us, and the Jews of Qurayẓa below us; we feared for our offspring from them. No night ever came upon us that was darker or with a harsher wind, its sounds like thunderbolts, and it was such darkness that no one of us could see his finger. The hypocrites began to ask permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed, and they are not exposed﴾, and none of them asked permission without being granted it, and they slipped away, while we were three hundred or so. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to us man by man, until he passed by me, and I had no shield against the enemy nor against the cold except a cloak of my wife's that did not reach beyond my knees. He came to me while I was crouching on my knees, and said: Who is this? I said: Ḥudhayfa. Ḥudhayfa said: I made myself small toward the ground, and I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, out of dislike of standing up. He said: Stand up. So I stood. He said: Among the people there is news, so bring me news of the people. He said: I was among the most fearful of the people and the most shivering with cold. So I went out, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: O Allah, guard him from before him and behind him, from his right and from his left, from above him and from below him. He said: By Allah, no fear and no cold that Allah created was within my belly except that it left my belly, and I found none of it. When I turned away, he said: O Ḥudhayfa, do not do anything among the people until you come back to me. So I went out, until when I drew near the camp of the people I looked by the light of a fire they had kindled, and there was a black, large man who was placing his hand over the fire and wiping his side, saying: Depart, depart. Then I entered the camp, and the nearest of the people to me were the Banu ʿĀmir, saying: O family of ʿĀmir, depart, depart, there is no place to stay for you. And the wind was in their camp, not exceeding a span; by Allah, I heard the sound of stones in their saddles and their bedding, the wind striking them. Then I went out toward the Prophet (ﷺ), and when I had gone half the way, or thereabouts, I saw about twenty riders wrapped in turbans, and they said: Inform your companion that Allah has sufficed him against the people. So I returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, while he was wrapped in a garment and praying, and whenever a matter distressed him he would pray. I informed him of the news of the people, that I had left them preparing to depart. Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when hosts came to you﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying "when hosts came to you," that he said: it was the day of Abū Sufyān, the day of the Confederates.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, Abū al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: When it was the night of the Confederates, the north wind came to the south wind and said: Go forth and help Allah and His Messenger. The south wind said: A free woman does not travel by night. So Allah became angry with it and made it barren, and He sent upon them the eastern wind (al-ṣabā), which extinguished their fires and cut their tent ropes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I was given victory by the ṣabā, and ʿĀd was destroyed by the dabūr. That is His saying: ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others recorded from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was given victory by the ṣabā, and ʿĀd was destroyed by the dabūr."

Al-Bukhārī and others recorded from ʿĀʾisha concerning His saying: ﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you﴾, the verse, she said: That was the day of the Trench. There are other ḥadīths in describing this campaign and what occurred in it, and the books of campaigns and biographies (sīra) contain them.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others recorded from Abū Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to [a city] that devours the other towns; they call it Yathrib, and it is Medina; it expels impurities as the furnace expels the dross of iron."

Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever names Medina Yathrib, let him seek forgiveness from Allah; it is Ṭāba, it is Ṭāba, it is Ṭāba." The wording of Aḥmad is: "It is only Ṭāba." Its chain is weak.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verse 7–23 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi (in al-Dala'il) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And a faction of them asked permission of the Prophet﴾ (ﷺ), he said: "They are the Banu Harithah. They said: ﴿Our houses are exposed⦆ — that is, vulnerable; we fear theft for them." Ibn Mardawayh also narrated a similar report from Jabir.

Al-Bayhaqi (in al-Dala'il) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The fulfilment (ta'wil) of this verse came about sixty years later: ﴿And if they had been entered from its surroundings, then they had been asked for sedition, they would have given it⦆." He said: "They would have given it" — meaning the admission of the Banu Harithah, the people of Syria, into Medina.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 7–23 (part 1 of 3):

His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾. The verb governing the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning "and mention" (wa-dhkur). It is as if He said: "O Prophet, fear Allah, and mention that Allah took the covenant of the prophets."

Qatadah said: Allah took the covenant from the prophets specifically that each of them would confirm the others and that they would follow one another.

Muqatil said: He took their covenant that they would worship Allah, call to the worship of Allah, confirm one another, and give sincere counsel to their peoples.

The covenant (mithaq) is an oath. It was said that it is the acknowledgment of Allah, but the first view is preferable, and its verification has already passed.

Then, after the general statement that encompasses them and others, He (glory be to Him) singled out some of the prophets by mention, saying: ﴿and from you, and from Noah, and Abraham, and Moses, and Jesus son of Mary﴾. The purpose of singling them out is to inform that they have a special excellence and virtue, being among the possessors of well-known laws (shara'i') and among the "Ulu al-'Azm" (the steadfast messengers). Mentioning our Prophet (ﷺ) first, despite his coming later in time, carries an honour and exaltation for him that is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: He took the covenant at the time when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam like particles (al-dharr).

Then He reinforced the covenant He took from the prophets by repeating its mention and describing it as ghaliz (firm), saying: ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, meaning a strong pledge to fulfil what they bore and what Allah had taken from them. It is also permissible that Allah took the covenant from them twice: the first time He took it from them as a mere covenant without emphasis or strictness, then He took it from them a second time, emphasized and strengthened. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there will come to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you will surely believe in him and surely support him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81].

The lam in His saying: ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: in order that He may ask the truthful among the prophets about their truthfulness in conveying the message to their peoples. In this there is a warning to others, for if they are questioned about that, then how about others?

It was said: that He may ask the prophets about what their peoples answered them with, as in His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. It is also permissible that it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: He did that in order to ask. ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ is coordinated with what is indicated by "that He may ask the truthful," since the sense is: He rewarded the truthful and prepared for the disbelievers. It is also permissible that it is coordinated with "We took," since the meaning is: He emphasized to the prophets the call to His religion, so that He might reward the believers and prepare for the disbelievers.

It was said: the second part has omitted what has its counterpart stated in the first, and the first has omitted what has its counterpart stated in the second, and the sense is: that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness, so He rewarded them, and that He may ask the disbelievers about what they answered their messengers, and He prepared for them a painful punishment.

It was said: it is coordinated with the implied governing verb as we mentioned. It is also permissible that the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾, and the clause ﴿and He has prepared for them﴾ is a new sentence explaining what He prepared for the disbelievers.

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾. This is a verification of the earlier command to fear Allah, to such a degree that no fear of anyone remains with it. The phrase ʿalaykum is connected to "favour" if it is a verbal noun (masdar), or to an omitted state (hal) meaning: existing upon you. The sense of ﴿when there came to you soldiers﴾ is "at the time when soldiers came to you." It is an adverbial phrase governed either by "favour," or by the implied verb governing ʿalaykum, or by an omitted "remember." By "soldiers" is meant the armies of the confederates (al-ahzab) who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and attacked him at Medina, which is the expedition known as "the Battle of the Trench" (Ghazwat al-Khandaq). They were: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb with the Quraysh and those who were with them of the mixed tribes, ʿUyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari and those with him of his people, Ghatafan, and the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir. They besieged the Muslims with a severe siege, as Allah the Glorified described in these verses. This expedition took place in Shawwal in the fifth year of the Hijra. This is what Ibn Ishaq said, while Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik, said it was in the fourth year.

The people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) have expounded on this event in what is well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it. ﴿So We sent upon them a wind﴾ is coordinated with "came to you."

Mujahid said: It was the east wind (al-Saba), sent upon the confederates on the day of the Trench, until it overturned their cooking pots and uprooted their tents. What supports this is what is established from him (ﷺ) in his saying: "I was helped by the Saba, and ʿAd were destroyed by the Dabur." By His saying ﴿and soldiers you did not see﴾ are meant the angels.

The commentators said: Allah sent upon them the angels, who uprooted the tent pegs, cut the ropes of the tents, extinguished the fires, overturned the pots, the horses ran about among one another, Allah sent terror upon them, and the angels' takbir increased on the sides of the camp, until the chief of each people would say to his people: "O Banu so-and-so, come to me!" When they gathered, he would say to them: "Escape! Escape!"

﴿And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do﴾. Most readers read taʿmalun with the second-person (ta), meaning: of what you do, O Muslims, of arranging the war, digging the trench, seeking victory through Him, and putting your trust in Him. Abu ʿAmr read it with the third-person (ya), meaning: of what the disbelievers do of enmity toward Allah and His Messenger, and of banding together against the Muslims and gathering against them from every side.

﴿When they came upon you from above you﴾. This "when" and what follows it is a substitution (badal) for the first "when," and the governing verb of this one is the governing verb of that one. It was also said that it is in the accusative governed by an omitted "remember." The meaning of "from above you" is from the upper part of the valley, which is from the direction of the east. Those who came from this direction were Ghatafan, whose chief was ʿUyayna ibn Hisn; Hawazin, whose chief was ʿAwf ibn Malik; and the people of Najd, whose chief was Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi; ʿAwf ibn Malik and the Banu al-Nadir joined them. The meaning of ﴿and from below you﴾ is from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west, from the side of Mecca. These were the Quraysh and those with them of the Ahabish, whose chief was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. Abu al-Aʿwar al-Sulami came with Huyayy ibn Akhtab the Jew among the Jews of Banu Qurayza from the side of the trench, and with them ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl.

The clause ﴿and when the eyes deviated﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: the eyes turned away from everything, so they looked at nothing but their enemy approaching from every side. It was said: they stared in astonishment from the extreme of the terror and bewilderment. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾: "hanajir" is the plural of "hanjara," which is the cavity of the windpipe. The meaning is that the hearts rose from their places and reached the throats from fear and dread, so that had the windpipe not been too narrow for them, which is where it ends at the hanjara, they would have come out. Thus said Qatadah.

It was said: this is an expression of the familiar hyperbole in the speech of the Arabs, even though the hearts did not rise to that place nor leave their position; rather it is a metaphor for their agitation and cowardice.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is that they became cowardly and most of them panicked. The way of the coward, when his fear intensifies, is that his lungs swell, and when the lungs swell the heart rises to the throat; for this reason it is said of a coward: "his lungs swelled (intansha sahruhu)."

﴿And you were thinking about Allah with assumptions﴾, that is, diverse assumptions. Some of them thought victory and hoped for triumph, while others thought otherwise.

Al-Hasan said: The hypocrites thought that Muhammad and his companions would be wiped out, while the believers thought that he would be given victory.

It was said: the verse is addressed to the hypocrites, but the better view is what al-Hasan said, so the address is to whoever professes Islam in general, whether he is a believer in reality or a hypocrite.

The readers differed concerning this alif in "al-zununa" (the assumptions). Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr kept it both in connection and in pause; this reading is also reported from Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i. They relied on the script of the ʿUthmanic Mushaf and all the copies in all the regions, in which the alif is present throughout. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading, but he said: the reader should not run on from them, rather he should pause upon them. They also relied on what occurs in Arabic poetry of this kind.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read it without the alif both in connection and in pause, and they said: it is one of the additions of the script, so it was written thus, and it should not be pronounced.

As for poetry, it permits for necessity what is not permitted otherwise.

Ibn Kathir, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with the alif in pause and without it in connection; this reading is preferred from the standpoint of the Arabic language. This alif is what the grammarians call the alif of extension (alif al-itlaq), and its discussion is well known in the science of grammar. Likewise the readers differed concerning the alif in His saying "al-Rasula" and "al-Sabila," as will come at the end of this surah.

﴿There the believers were tested﴾. The adverb is governed by the verb that follows it. It was said that it is governed by "you think," but Ibn ʿAtiyya considered this weak. It is an adverb of place; just as "hunalika" is said for a distant place, "huna" for a near place, and "hunaka" for an intermediate one, it can also be an adverb of time, meaning: at that time the believers were tested. From this is the poet's saying:

"And when affairs grow great and become intertwined, then there they acknowledge: where is the refuge?"

meaning: at that time. The sense is that in that place or at that time the believers were tested by fear, fighting, hunger, siege and combat, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite.

﴿And they were shaken with a severe shaking﴾. Most readers read "zululu" with a damma on the first zay and a kasra on the second, according to the original form of the passive. It is reported from Abu ʿAmr that he read it with a kasra on the first, and al-Zamakhshari reported from him that he read it with an intonation (ishmam) of kasra. Most readers read "zilzalan" with a kasra on the first zay, while ʿAsim, al-Jahdari and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it with a fatha.

Al-Zajjaj said: every verbal noun of a doubled root on the pattern fi'lal may be read with kasra or fatha, such as "qalqaltuhu qilqalan" and "zulzilu zilzalan," and the kasra is better.

Ibn Salam said: the meaning of "zulzilu" is: they were moved by fear with a severe movement.

Al-Dahhak said: it is their being displaced from their places until there was for them only the spot of the trench. It was said: the meaning is that they were agitated in diverse ways: some were agitated in themselves, and some were agitated in their religion.

﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said﴾. This is coordinated with ﴿and when the eyes deviated﴾. "Disease" (maradun) in the hearts is doubt and suspicion. By "the hypocrites" is meant ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and by "those in whose hearts is a disease" are the people of doubt and agitation: ﴿"Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion"﴾, that is, falsehood of speech. The sayers of this statement were about seventy men of the people of hypocrisy and doubt. This statement attributed to them serves as an explanation of the assumptions mentioned, meaning: the assumption of these was this assumption, just as the assumption of the believers was victory and the elevation of the word of Allah.

﴿And when a faction of them said﴾, that is, of the hypocrites.

Muqatil said: They are the Banu Salim among the hypocrites.

al-Suddi said: They are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. It was said: they are Aws ibn Qibti and his companions. The word "ta'ifa" applies to one or more. The statement that this faction said is: ﴿"O people of Yathrib, there is no station for you"﴾, that is, there is no place of residence for you, or there is no residence for you here in the camp.

Abu ʿUbayd said: Yathrib is the name of the land, and the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) is in one part of it.

Al-Suhayli said: The city was named Yathrib because the one who first settled it from the Amalekites was named Yathrib ibn ʿUmayl. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "لا مَقامَ لَكم" (lā maqāma lakum, "there is no place to stay for you") with a fatḥah on the mīm, while Ḥafṣ, al-Sulamī, al-Jaḥdarī and Abū Ḥaywa read it with a ḍammah, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) from aqāma yuqīmu ("to remain"). On the first reading it is a noun of place (ism makān), meaning "your dwellings." They told them to flee from the army of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims went out in the year of the Trench (al-Khandaq) and placed their backs toward Salʿ, with the trench between them and the enemy. These hypocrites said: "There is no place here for staying," and they ordered the people to return to their homes in Medina. ﴿And a group of them asked permission of the Prophet﴾ is coordinated (maʿṭūf) upon "a group of them said" (qālat ṭāʾifatun minhum), meaning: they asked permission to return to their homes, and they were the Banu Ḥāritha and the Banu Salima. The clause "they say" (yaqūlūna) is either a substitute (badal) for "they ask permission," or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) answering an implied question. The saying they uttered, which is their statement: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed⦆, that is, lost and unprotected, not secure and not defended from the enemy.

Al-Zajjāj said: It is said ʿawira al-makān yaʿwaru ʿawaran wa-ʿawratan, and "buyūtun ʿawiratun wa-ʿawratun," and ʿawra is a verbal noun.

Mujāhid, Muqātil and al-Ḥasan said: They said, "Our houses are unguarded; we fear thieves for them."

Qatāda said: They said, "Our houses are on the side facing the enemy, and we are not safe for our families."

Al-Harawī said: Every place that is not protected or concealed is ʿawra. The root meaning of ʿawra is a defect (khalal), and then it was applied to what has a defect. The intended meaning is "a place with a defect." Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī read ʿawiratun with a kasrah on the wāw, meaning "with walls that are short."

Al-Jawharī said: ʿAwra is every condition feared in a frontier or in war.

Al-Naḥḥās said: It is said aʿwara al-makān when a defect becomes apparent in it, and aʿwara al-fāris when the gap in him becomes apparent. Then He, glorified is He, refuted them with His saying: ﴿But they are not exposed﴾, so Allah, glorified is He, declared them liars in what they claimed. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Then He explained the reason for their seeking permission and what they intend by it, saying: ﴿They intend nothing but flight﴾, that is, they intend only to flee from fighting. It was also said: the intended meaning is that they intend only to flee from the religion.

﴿And if it had been entered upon them from all its sides﴾, meaning their houses or Medina, and the aqṭār (sides) are the directions, plural of quṭr, which is a side and a direction. The meaning: if their houses or Medina had been entered upon them from all its sides together, not from some of them, this severe calamity would have befallen them, their homes would have been plundered, and their sanctities and dwellings violated. ﴿Then they were asked for sedition﴾ from another direction at the arrival of this severe calamity upon them, ﴿they would have given it⦆, that is, they would have come to it or granted it. The meaning of fitna here is either fighting in tribal partisanship, as al-Ḍaḥḥāk said, or association with Allah and return to the disbelief which they conceal while showing the opposite, as al-Ḥasan said. The majority read "la-ātawhā" with the madd, meaning they would have given it from themselves. Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read it with qaṣr, meaning they would have come to it. ﴿And they would not have stayed therein except briefly﴾, that is, in Medina, after they came to sedition, except for a brief stay until they perished. Thus said al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī, al-Farrāʾ and al-Qutaybī.

But most of the exegetes said: the meaning is: they would not have hesitated from the sedition of polytheism except briefly, but rather they would hasten to it, eager for it, and would stop only at the mere fact that the question was put to them, and would not excuse themselves from answering by saying that their houses in this state are exposed, even though they were in fact exposed, just as they excused themselves from answering the Messenger and fighting with him by saying that they were exposed, when they were not exposed at that time.

Then He, glorified is He, related what had occurred from them earlier of the covenant to Allah and His Messenger to remain steadfast in war and not flee from it, saying: ﴿And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs﴾, that is, before the battle of the Trench and after Badr. Qatāda said: This was because they were absent from Badr and saw what Allah gave the people of Badr of honor and victory, so they said: "If Allah makes us witness fighting, we will surely fight." They were the Banu Ḥāritha and the Banu Salima. ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned⦆, that is, it will be questioned about, its holder is demanded to fulfill it, and he will be recompensed for abandoning its fulfillment.

﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing﴾, for whoever his term has come, dies or is killed, whether he flees or does not flee. ﴿And then you will not be given enjoyment except a little﴾, that is, a little enjoyment or a little time after their flight until their terms end, and everything that is coming is near. The majority read "tumattaʿūna" with the second-person form; Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, in the transmission of al-Sājī from him, read it with the third-person (taḥtiyya).

In some transmissions it is "lā tumattaʿū," with the nūn dropped, treating idhan as operative; on the majority's reading, it is cancelled (mulghāh).

﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm﴾, that is, destruction, or loss of wealth, drought and sickness, ﴿or intends for you mercy﴾, by which He shows mercy to you through fertility, victory and well-being. ﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any ally﴾, who would support them and ward off [harm] from them, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who would help them against the punishment of Allah.

Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil have recorded from Abū Maryam al-Ghassānī that "a Bedouin said: O Messenger of Allah, what was the first thing of your prophethood? He said: Allah took my covenant as He took the covenant of the prophets, then he recited" ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, son of Mary, and We took from them a firm covenant﴾, and the supplication of Abraham: (p-1161) ﴿Send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 129], and the glad tidings of Jesus, son of Mary, and the mother of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in her dream that a lamp came out from between her legs, by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when was your covenant taken? He said: While Adam was between the spirit and the body."

Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil recorded from him, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when did you become a prophet? He said: While Adam was between the spirit and the body."

There are other ḥadīths on this subject, some of which have been declared authentic.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil, al-Daylamī and Ibn ʿAsākir recorded through the chain of Qatāda from al-Ḥasan from Abū Hurayra from "the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾, the verse, he said: I was the first of the prophets in creation and the last of them in resurrection, so He began with me before them."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "their covenant" means their pledge.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī recorded with a ṣaḥīḥ chain from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ that he said: Allah only took the covenant of the prophets concerning their peoples.

Al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqī both in al-Dalāʾil, and Ibn ʿAsākir recorded through various chains from Ḥudhayfa who said: "We saw ourselves on the night of the Confederates, while we sat in rows, and Abū Sufyān and those with him of the confederates were above us, and the Jews of Qurayẓa below us; we feared for our offspring from them. No night ever came upon us that was darker or with a harsher wind, its sounds like thunderbolts, and it was such darkness that no one of us could see his finger. The hypocrites began to ask permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed, and they are not exposed﴾, and none of them asked permission without being granted it, and they slipped away, while we were three hundred or so. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to us man by man, until he passed by me, and I had no shield against the enemy nor against the cold except a cloak of my wife's that did not reach beyond my knees. He came to me while I was crouching on my knees, and said: Who is this? I said: Ḥudhayfa. Ḥudhayfa said: I made myself small toward the ground, and I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, out of dislike of standing up. He said: Stand up. So I stood. He said: Among the people there is news, so bring me news of the people. He said: I was among the most fearful of the people and the most shivering with cold. So I went out, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: O Allah, guard him from before him and behind him, from his right and from his left, from above him and from below him. He said: By Allah, no fear and no cold that Allah created was within my belly except that it left my belly, and I found none of it. When I turned away, he said: O Ḥudhayfa, do not do anything among the people until you come back to me. So I went out, until when I drew near the camp of the people I looked by the light of a fire they had kindled, and there was a black, large man who was placing his hand over the fire and wiping his side, saying: Depart, depart. Then I entered the camp, and the nearest of the people to me were the Banu ʿĀmir, saying: O family of ʿĀmir, depart, depart, there is no place to stay for you. And the wind was in their camp, not exceeding a span; by Allah, I heard the sound of stones in their saddles and their bedding, the wind striking them. Then I went out toward the Prophet (ﷺ), and when I had gone half the way, or thereabouts, I saw about twenty riders wrapped in turbans, and they said: Inform your companion that Allah has sufficed him against the people. So I returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him, while he was wrapped in a garment and praying, and whenever a matter distressed him he would pray. I informed him of the news of the people, that I had left them preparing to depart. Then Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, remember the favor of Allah upon you when hosts came to you﴾, the verse."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His saying "when hosts came to you," that he said: it was the day of Abū Sufyān, the day of the Confederates.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, Abū al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: When it was the night of the Confederates, the north wind came to the south wind and said: Go forth and help Allah and His Messenger. The south wind said: A free woman does not travel by night. So Allah became angry with it and made it barren, and He sent upon them the eastern wind (al-ṣabā), which extinguished their fires and cut their tent ropes. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: I was given victory by the ṣabā, and ʿĀd was destroyed by the dabūr. That is His saying: ﴿So We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others recorded from the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was given victory by the ṣabā, and ʿĀd was destroyed by the dabūr."

Al-Bukhārī and others recorded from ʿĀʾisha concerning His saying: ﴿When they came upon you from above you and from below you﴾, the verse, she said: That was the day of the Trench. There are other ḥadīths in describing this campaign and what occurred in it, and the books of campaigns and biographies (sīra) contain them.

Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others recorded from Abū Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to [a city] that devours the other towns; they call it Yathrib, and it is Medina; it expels impurities as the furnace expels the dross of iron."

Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever names Medina Yathrib, let him seek forgiveness from Allah; it is Ṭāba, it is Ṭāba, it is Ṭāba." The wording of Aḥmad is: "It is only Ṭāba." Its chain is weak.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verse 7–23 (part 3 of 3):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi (in al-Dala'il) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿And a faction of them asked permission of the Prophet﴾ (ﷺ), he said: "They are the Banu Harithah. They said: ﴿Our houses are exposed⦆ — that is, vulnerable; we fear theft for them." Ibn Mardawayh also narrated a similar report from Jabir.

Al-Bayhaqi (in al-Dala'il) narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The fulfilment (ta'wil) of this verse came about sixty years later: ﴿And if they had been entered from its surroundings, then they had been asked for sedition, they would have given it⦆." He said: "They would have given it" — meaning the admission of the Banu Harithah, the people of Syria, into Medina.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 7–23 (part 1 of 3):

His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾. The verb governing the adverbial phrase is omitted, meaning "and mention" (wa-dhkur). It is as if He said: "O Prophet, fear Allah, and mention that Allah took the covenant of the prophets."

Qatadah said: Allah took the covenant from the prophets specifically that each of them would confirm the others and that they would follow one another.

Muqatil said: He took their covenant that they would worship Allah, call to the worship of Allah, confirm one another, and give sincere counsel to their peoples.

The covenant (mithaq) is an oath. It was said that it is the acknowledgment of Allah, but the first view is preferable, and its verification has already passed.

Then, after the general statement that encompasses them and others, He (glory be to Him) singled out some of the prophets by mention, saying: ﴿and from you, and from Noah, and Abraham, and Moses, and Jesus son of Mary﴾. The purpose of singling them out is to inform that they have a special excellence and virtue, being among the possessors of well-known laws (shara'i') and among the "Ulu al-'Azm" (the steadfast messengers). Mentioning our Prophet (ﷺ) first, despite his coming later in time, carries an honour and exaltation for him that is not hidden.

Al-Zajjaj said: He took the covenant at the time when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam like particles (al-dharr).

Then He reinforced the covenant He took from the prophets by repeating its mention and describing it as ghaliz (firm), saying: ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾, meaning a strong pledge to fulfil what they bore and what Allah had taken from them. It is also permissible that Allah took the covenant from them twice: the first time He took it from them as a mere covenant without emphasis or strictness, then He took it from them a second time, emphasized and strengthened. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, then there will come to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you will surely believe in him and surely support him"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81].

The lam in His saying: ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ may be the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: in order that He may ask the truthful among the prophets about their truthfulness in conveying the message to their peoples. In this there is a warning to others, for if they are questioned about that, then how about others?

It was said: that He may ask the prophets about what their peoples answered them with, as in His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-A'raf: 6]. It is also permissible that it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: He did that in order to ask. ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾ is coordinated with what is indicated by "that He may ask the truthful," since the sense is: He rewarded the truthful and prepared for the disbelievers. It is also permissible that it is coordinated with "We took," since the meaning is: He emphasized to the prophets the call to His religion, so that He might reward the believers and prepare for the disbelievers.

It was said: the second part has omitted what has its counterpart stated in the first, and the first has omitted what has its counterpart stated in the second, and the sense is: that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness, so He rewarded them, and that He may ask the disbelievers about what they answered their messengers, and He prepared for them a painful punishment.

It was said: it is coordinated with the implied governing verb as we mentioned. It is also permissible that the speech is complete at His saying: ﴿that He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾, and the clause ﴿and He has prepared for them﴾ is a new sentence explaining what He prepared for the disbelievers.

﴿O you who have believed, remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾. This is a verification of the earlier command to fear Allah, to such a degree that no fear of anyone remains with it. The phrase ʿalaykum is connected to "favour" if it is a verbal noun (masdar), or to an omitted state (hal) meaning: existing upon you. The sense of ﴿when there came to you soldiers﴾ is "at the time when soldiers came to you." It is an adverbial phrase governed either by "favour," or by the implied verb governing ʿalaykum, or by an omitted "remember." By "soldiers" is meant the armies of the confederates (al-ahzab) who banded together against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and attacked him at Medina, which is the expedition known as "the Battle of the Trench" (Ghazwat al-Khandaq). They were: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb with the Quraysh and those who were with them of the mixed tribes, ʿUyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari and those with him of his people, Ghatafan, and the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir. They besieged the Muslims with a severe siege, as Allah the Glorified described in these verses. This expedition took place in Shawwal in the fifth year of the Hijra. This is what Ibn Ishaq said, while Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim, from Malik, said it was in the fourth year.

The people of the biographies (ahl al-siyar) have expounded on this event in what is well known, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it. ﴿So We sent upon them a wind﴾ is coordinated with "came to you."

Mujahid said: It was the east wind (al-Saba), sent upon the confederates on the day of the Trench, until it overturned their cooking pots and uprooted their tents. What supports this is what is established from him (ﷺ) in his saying: "I was helped by the Saba, and ʿAd were destroyed by the Dabur." By His saying ﴿and soldiers you did not see﴾ are meant the angels.

The commentators said: Allah sent upon them the angels, who uprooted the tent pegs, cut the ropes of the tents, extinguished the fires, overturned the pots, the horses ran about among one another, Allah sent terror upon them, and the angels' takbir increased on the sides of the camp, until the chief of each people would say to his people: "O Banu so-and-so, come to me!" When they gathered, he would say to them: "Escape! Escape!"

﴿And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do﴾. Most readers read taʿmalun with the second-person (ta), meaning: of what you do, O Muslims, of arranging the war, digging the trench, seeking victory through Him, and putting your trust in Him. Abu ʿAmr read it with the third-person (ya), meaning: of what the disbelievers do of enmity toward Allah and His Messenger, and of banding together against the Muslims and gathering against them from every side.

﴿When they came upon you from above you﴾. This "when" and what follows it is a substitution (badal) for the first "when," and the governing verb of this one is the governing verb of that one. It was also said that it is in the accusative governed by an omitted "remember." The meaning of "from above you" is from the upper part of the valley, which is from the direction of the east. Those who came from this direction were Ghatafan, whose chief was ʿUyayna ibn Hisn; Hawazin, whose chief was ʿAwf ibn Malik; and the people of Najd, whose chief was Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi; ʿAwf ibn Malik and the Banu al-Nadir joined them. The meaning of ﴿and from below you﴾ is from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west, from the side of Mecca. These were the Quraysh and those with them of the Ahabish, whose chief was Abu Sufyan ibn Harb. Abu al-Aʿwar al-Sulami came with Huyayy ibn Akhtab the Jew among the Jews of Banu Qurayza from the side of the trench, and with them ʿAmir ibn al-Tufayl.

The clause ﴿and when the eyes deviated﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it, meaning: the eyes turned away from everything, so they looked at nothing but their enemy approaching from every side. It was said: they stared in astonishment from the extreme of the terror and bewilderment. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾: "hanajir" is the plural of "hanjara," which is the cavity of the windpipe. The meaning is that the hearts rose from their places and reached the throats from fear and dread, so that had the windpipe not been too narrow for them, which is where it ends at the hanjara, they would have come out. Thus said Qatadah.

It was said: this is an expression of the familiar hyperbole in the speech of the Arabs, even though the hearts did not rise to that place nor leave their position; rather it is a metaphor for their agitation and cowardice.

Al-Farra' said: The meaning is that they became cowardly and most of them panicked. The way of the coward, when his fear intensifies, is that his lungs swell, and when the lungs swell the heart rises to the throat; for this reason it is said of a coward: "his lungs swelled (intansha sahruhu)."

﴿And you were thinking about Allah with assumptions﴾, that is, diverse assumptions. Some of them thought victory and hoped for triumph, while others thought otherwise.

Al-Hasan said: The hypocrites thought that Muhammad and his companions would be wiped out, while the believers thought that he would be given victory.

It was said: the verse is addressed to the hypocrites, but the better view is what al-Hasan said, so the address is to whoever professes Islam in general, whether he is a believer in reality or a hypocrite.

The readers differed concerning this alif in "al-zununa" (the assumptions). Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Bakr kept it both in connection and in pause; this reading is also reported from Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisa'i. They relied on the script of the ʿUthmanic Mushaf and all the copies in all the regions, in which the alif is present throughout. Abu ʿUbayd chose this reading, but he said: the reader should not run on from them, rather he should pause upon them. They also relied on what occurs in Arabic poetry of this kind.

Abu ʿAmr, Hamza, al-Jahdari and Ya'qub read it without the alif both in connection and in pause, and they said: it is one of the additions of the script, so it was written thus, and it should not be pronounced.

As for poetry, it permits for necessity what is not permitted otherwise.

Ibn Kathir, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with the alif in pause and without it in connection; this reading is preferred from the standpoint of the Arabic language. This alif is what the grammarians call the alif of extension (alif al-itlaq), and its discussion is well known in the science of grammar. Likewise the readers differed concerning the alif in His saying "al-Rasula" and "al-Sabila," as will come at the end of this surah.

﴿There the believers were tested﴾. The adverb is governed by the verb that follows it. It was said that it is governed by "you think," but Ibn ʿAtiyya considered this weak. It is an adverb of place; just as "hunalika" is said for a distant place, "huna" for a near place, and "hunaka" for an intermediate one, it can also be an adverb of time, meaning: at that time the believers were tested. From this is the poet's saying:

"And when affairs grow great and become intertwined, then there they acknowledge: where is the refuge?"

meaning: at that time. The sense is that in that place or at that time the believers were tested by fear, fighting, hunger, siege and combat, so that the believer might be distinguished from the hypocrite.

﴿And they were shaken with a severe shaking﴾. Most readers read "zululu" with a damma on the first zay and a kasra on the second, according to the original form of the passive. It is reported from Abu ʿAmr that he read it with a kasra on the first, and al-Zamakhshari reported from him that he read it with an intonation (ishmam) of kasra. Most readers read "zilzalan" with a kasra on the first zay, while ʿAsim, al-Jahdari and ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it with a fatha.

Al-Zajjaj said: every verbal noun of a doubled root on the pattern fi'lal may be read with kasra or fatha, such as "qalqaltuhu qilqalan" and "zulzilu zilzalan," and the kasra is better.

Ibn Salam said: the meaning of "zulzilu" is: they were moved by fear with a severe movement.

Al-Dahhak said: it is their being displaced from their places until there was for them only the spot of the trench. It was said: the meaning is that they were agitated in diverse ways: some were agitated in themselves, and some were agitated in their religion.

﴿And when the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease said﴾. This is coordinated with ﴿and when the eyes deviated﴾. "Disease" (maradun) in the hearts is doubt and suspicion. By "the hypocrites" is meant ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, and by "those in whose hearts is a disease" are the people of doubt and agitation: ﴿"Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion"﴾, that is, falsehood of speech. The sayers of this statement were about seventy men of the people of hypocrisy and doubt. This statement attributed to them serves as an explanation of the assumptions mentioned, meaning: the assumption of these was this assumption, just as the assumption of the believers was victory and the elevation of the word of Allah.

﴿And when a faction of them said﴾, that is, of the hypocrites.

Muqatil said: They are the Banu Salim among the hypocrites.

al-Suddi said: They are ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions. It was said: they are Aws ibn Qibti and his companions. The word "ta'ifa" applies to one or more. The statement that this faction said is: ﴿"O people of Yathrib, there is no station for you"﴾, that is, there is no place of residence for you, or there is no residence for you here in the camp.

Abu ʿUbayd said: Yathrib is the name of the land, and the city of the Prophet (ﷺ) is in one part of it.

Al-Suhayli said: The city was named Yathrib because the one who first settled it from the Amalekites was named Yathrib ibn ʿUmayl. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "لا مَقامَ لَكم" (lā maqāma lakum, "there is no place to stay for you") with a fatḥah on the mīm, while Ḥafṣ, al-Sulamī, al-Jaḥdarī and Abū Ḥaywa read it with a ḍammah, as a verbal noun (maṣdar) from aqāma yuqīmu ("to remain"). On the first reading it is a noun of place (ism makān), meaning "your dwellings." They told them to flee from the army of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims went out in the year of the Trench (al-Khandaq) and placed their backs toward Salʿ, with the trench between them and the enemy. These hypocrites said: "There is no place here for staying," and they ordered the people to return to their homes in Medina. ﴿And a group of them asked permission of the Prophet﴾ is coordinated (maʿṭūf) upon "a group of them said" (qālat ṭāʾifatun minhum), meaning: they asked permission to return to their homes, and they were the Banu Ḥāritha and the Banu Salima. The clause "they say" (yaqūlūna) is either a substitute (badal) for "they ask permission," or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) answering an implied question. The saying they uttered, which is their statement: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed⦆, that is, lost and unprotected, not secure and not defended from the enemy.

Al-Zajjāj said: It is said ʿawira al-makān yaʿwaru ʿawaran wa-ʿawratan, and "buyūtun ʿawiratun wa-ʿawratun," and ʿawra is a verbal noun.

Mujāhid, Muqātil and al-Ḥasan said: They said, "Our houses are unguarded; we fear thieves for them."

Qatāda said: They said, "Our houses are on the side facing the enemy, and we are not safe for our families."

Al-Harawī said: Every place that is not protected or concealed is ʿawra. The root meaning of ʿawra is a defect (khalal), and then it was applied to what has a defect. The intended meaning is "a place with a defect." Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid and Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī read ʿawiratun with a kasrah on the wāw, meaning "with walls that are short."

Al-Jawharī said: ʿAwra is every condition feared in a frontier or in war.

Al-Naḥḥās said: It is said aʿwara al-makān when a defect becomes apparent in it, and aʿwara al-fāris when the gap in him becomes apparent. Then He, glorified is He, refuted them with His saying: ﴿But they are not exposed﴾, so Allah, glorified is He, declared them liars in what they claimed. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Then He explained the reason for their seeking permission and what they intend by it, saying: ﴿They intend nothing but flight﴾, that is, they intend only to flee from fighting. It was also said: the intended meaning is that they intend only to flee from the religion.

﴿And if it had been entered upon them from all its sides﴾, meaning their houses or Medina, and the aqṭār (sides) are the directions, plural of quṭr, which is a side and a direction. The meaning: if their houses or Medina had been entered upon them from all its sides together, not from some of them, this severe calamity would have befallen them, their homes would have been plundered, and their sanctities and dwellings violated. ﴿Then they were asked for sedition﴾ from another direction at the arrival of this severe calamity upon them, ﴿they would have given it⦆, that is, they would have come to it or granted it. The meaning of fitna here is either fighting in tribal partisanship, as al-Ḍaḥḥāk said, or association with Allah and return to the disbelief which they conceal while showing the opposite, as al-Ḥasan said. The majority read "la-ātawhā" with the madd, meaning they would have given it from themselves. Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read it with qaṣr, meaning they would have come to it. ﴿And they would not have stayed therein except briefly﴾, that is, in Medina, after they came to sedition, except for a brief stay until they perished. Thus said al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī, al-Farrāʾ and al-Qutaybī.

But most of the exegetes said: the meaning is: they would not have hesitated from the sedition of polytheism except briefly, but rather they would hasten to it, eager for it, and would stop only at the mere fact that the question was put to them, and would not excuse themselves from answering by saying that their houses in this state are exposed, even though they were in fact exposed, just as they excused themselves from answering the Messenger and fighting with him by saying that they were exposed, when they were not exposed at that time.

Then He, glorified is He, related what had occurred from them earlier of the covenant to Allah and His Messenger to remain steadfast in war and not flee from it, saying: ﴿And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs﴾, that is, before the battle of the Trench and after Badr. Qatāda said: This was because they were absent from Badr and saw what Allah gave the people of Badr of honor and victory, so they said: "If Allah makes us witness fighting, we will surely fight." They were the Banu Ḥāritha and the Banu Salima. ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned⦆, that is, it will be questioned about, its holder is demanded to fulfill it, and he will be recompensed for abandoning its fulfillment.

﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing﴾, for whoever his term has come, dies or is killed, whether he flees or does not flee. ﴿And then you will not be given enjoyment except a little﴾, that is, a little enjoyment or a little time after their flight until their terms end, and everything that is coming is near. The majority read "tumattaʿūna" with the second-person form; Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, in the transmission of al-Sājī from him, read it with the third-person (taḥtiyya).

In some transmissions it is "lā tumattaʿū," with the nūn dropped, treating idhan as operative; on the majority's reading, it is cancelled (mulghāh).

﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm﴾, that is, destruction, or loss of wealth, drought and sickness, ﴿or intends for you mercy﴾, by which He shows mercy to you through fertility, victory and well-being. ﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any ally﴾, who would support them and ward off [harm] from them, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who would help them against the punishment of Allah.

Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil have recorded from Abū Maryam al-Ghassānī that "a Bedouin said: O Messenger of Allah, what was the first thing of your prophethood? He said: Allah took my covenant as He took the covenant of the prophets, then he recited" ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, son of Mary, and We took from them a firm covenant﴾, and the supplication of Abraham: (p-1161) ﴿Send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 129], and the glad tidings of Jesus, son of Mary, and the mother of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw in her dream that a lamp came out from between her legs, by which the palaces of Syria were illuminated.

Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when was your covenant taken? He said: While Adam was between the spirit and the body."

Al-Bazzār, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ and Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil recorded from him, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when did you become a prophet? He said: While Adam was between the spirit and the body."

There are other ḥadīths on this subject, some of which have been declared authentic.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym in al-Dalāʾil, al-Daylamī and Ibn ʿAsākir recorded through the chain of Qatāda from al-Ḥasan from Abū Hurayra from "the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾, the verse, he said: I was the first of the prophets in creation and the last of them in resurrection, so He began with me before them."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "their covenant" means their pledge.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī recorded with a ṣaḥīḥ chain from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ that he said: Allah only took the covenant of the prophets concerning their peoples.

Al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic, Ibn Mardawayh, Abū Nuʿaym, and al-Bayhaqī both in al-Dalāʾil, and Ibn ʿAsākir recorded through various chains from Ḥudhayfa who said: "We saw ourselves on the night of the Confederates, while we sat in rows, and Abū Sufyān and those with him of the confederates were above us, and the Jews of Qurayẓa below us; we feared for our offspring from them. No night ever came upon us that was darker or with a harsher wind, its sounds like thunderbolts, and it was such darkness that no one of us could see his finger. The hypocrites began to ask permission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying, ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed, and they are not exposed﴾, and none of them asked permission without being granted it, and they slipped away, while we were three hundred or so. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to us man by man, until he passed by me, and I had no shield against the enemy nor against the cold except a cloak of my wife's that did not reach beyond my knees. He came to me while I was crouching on my knees, and said: Who is this? I said: Ḥudhayfa. Ḥudhayfa said: I made myself small toward the ground, and I said: Yes, O Messenger of Allah, out of dislike of standing up. He said: Stand up. So I stood. He said: Among the people there is news, so bring me news of the people. He said: I was among the most fearful of the people and the most shivering with cold.
