Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the enjoyment mentioned here is abrogated by the verse in Surah al-Baqarah, which is His saying: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already set a dowry for them, then half of what you have set﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. It was also said: the enjoyment here is more general than being half the dowry, or the enjoyment is specific if no dowry was named for her. So with the naming of the dowry she is entitled to half of what was named, acting upon His saying: "then half of what you have set for them," and without naming she is entitled to enjoyment, acting upon this verse. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them a dowry; but provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236]. This harmonization is necessary, and it takes precedence over preference (tarjih) and over the claim of abrogation.

The widow whose husband has died is specified out of this verse, for if he dies after contracting marriage with her and before consummation, death is like consummation, so she observes a waiting period of four months and ten days.

Ibn Kathir said: by consensus. So the specifier is consensus. Those who take this verse as evidence that there is no divorce before marriage, namely the majority, have relied upon it. Malik and Abu Hanifah held that divorce before marriage is valid if he says: "If I marry so-and-so, she is divorced," so she is divorced when he marries her.

The basis of the evidence of the verse for what the majority said is that He said: ﴿When you marry believing women, then you divorce them﴾, so He followed the divorce with the marriage by the particle thumma (then), which indicates sequence and an interval, ﴿and release them with a fair release﴾, i.e., send them out of your homes, since you have no waiting period for them. The "fair release" here is a metaphor for divorce, but this is far-fetched, because divorce has already been mentioned, followed by the provision of enjoyment, and the fair release is joined to it by conjunction, so it must mean something other than divorce.

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whose bridal payments you have given﴾. In this verse He mentioned the kinds of marriages which He made lawful for His Messenger, and He began with his wives whose dowries (ujur) he had given, i.e., their mahr (bridal gift), for the mahr is the wage for intimacy, and giving it is either handing it over immediately or naming it in the contract.

There is a difference regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿We have made lawful for you your wives﴾. Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said: Allah made lawful for him to marry every woman to whom he gives her mahr, so the verse permits all women except those within the prohibited degrees.

The majority said: the intended meaning is: We have made lawful for you your wives who are with you, because they chose you over the world and its adornment; and this is the apparent meaning, because His saying "We have made lawful" and "you have given" are in the past tense, and restricting the lawfulness by the giving of the wages is not because the permission depends on it, since a contract is valid without a named dowry, and the mahr of the like (mahr al-mithl) is due with intercourse, and enjoyment without it; so it seems to be for the purpose of guiding to what is better. ﴿And what your right hand possesses from what Allah has returned to you﴾, i.e., the captive women who entered his possession through spoils of war.

The meaning of ﴿from what Allah has returned to you﴾ is: from what Allah has returned to you from the unbelievers as booty, for their women taken by force and dominance. This restriction is not intended to exclude what he owns by other than spoils, for it makes lawful to him a purchased or gifted concubine and the like; rather it is an indication of what is better, like the first restriction that explicitly mentions giving the wages. Similarly the restriction of emigration in His saying: ﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who have emigrated with you﴾, for it is an indication of what is better, and an announcement of the nobility of emigration and of those who emigrated. The meaning of "with you" here is sharing in the emigration, not in the companionship in it.

It was also said: this restriction, I mean emigration, is considered, and that those among these who did not emigrate are not lawful to him, as in His saying: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you owe them no guardianship until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. This is supported by the hadith of Umm Hani', which will come at the end of this discussion, if Allah wills. The reason for the singular of paternal uncle and maternal uncle and the plural of paternal aunt and maternal aunt is what al-Qurtubi mentioned: that "uncle" and "maternal uncle" in general usage are collective nouns (ism jins), like "the poet" and "the reciter," whereas "paternal aunt" and "maternal aunt" are not so.

He said: This is a linguistic convention, so the speech came in accordance with it, with complete clarity. He related this from Ibn al-'Arabi.

Ibn Kathir said: He made the word for the male singular because of its nobility, and pluralized the female, like His saying: ﴿on the right and the left﴾ [al-Nahl: 48], and His saying: ﴿He brings them out from the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and it has many similar examples. End of quote.

Al-Naysaburi said: He did not pluralize "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" being content with their generic nature, although the plural of the daughters indicates that, because two sisters cannot be under one man; and this abbreviation did not sound good for paternal aunt and maternal aunt, since it could occur to the mind that the ta' in them denotes unity. End of quote.

Each of these explanations is open to objection by counter-argument and opposition, and the best of them is the explanation of pluralizing paternal aunt and maternal aunt by the thought occurring that the ta' is for unity; yet nothing in "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" leads the mind to think that unity is intended by them, except the mere singular form, and that does not require it after its addition to a noun, given the generality of genitive-constructed generic nouns. Moreover, even this best explanation is not free from the taint of objection.

﴿And a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾. This is coordinated with the object of "We have made lawful", i.e., and We have made lawful for you a woman who affirms the Oneness of God, if she gives herself to you without a dowry.

As for one who is not a believer, she is not lawful to you merely by her giving herself to you; but this is not obligatory upon you, such that you must accept it, rather it is conditional upon your will. For this reason He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾, i.e., to make her a wife to him and to take possession of her intimacy by that gift without a dowry.

It has been said: the Prophet (ﷺ) did not marry any of the women who gave themselves, and none of them was with him.

It was said: there was with him of them Khawlah bint Hakim, as in Sahih al-Bukhari from 'A'ishah. Qatadah said: she was Maymunah bint al-Harith. al-Sha'bi said: she was Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Ansariyyah, Umm al-Masakin. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: she was Umm Sharik bint Jabir al-Asadiyyah. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: she was Umm Hakim bint al-Awqas al-Sulamiyyah.

Then He, glory be to Him, made clear that this type of marriage is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and is not lawful for anyone else of his community. He said: ﴿as a special privilege for you, not for the [other] believers﴾, i.e., this pure permission is specific to you, to the exclusion of other believers.

The word khalisah is either a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "woman", as said by al-Zajjaj, or an emphatic infinitive like "the promise of Allah", i.e., it is purely yours, a purity.

al-Jumhur read wamra'atan with the accusative. Abu Haywah read it in the nominative as a subject. al-Jumhur read "in wahabat" with kasrah on in; Ubayy, al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with fathah on it as a subject.

al-Jumhur read khalisatan with the accusative, and it was read in the nominative as an attribute of "woman" according to the reading of whoever read "woman" in the nominative. The scholars have agreed that this is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it is not permissible for anyone else, and that marriage is not concluded by a woman giving herself in gift, except what is related from Abu Hanifah and his two companions, that marriage is valid if she gives herself and he calls witnesses on himself to a dowry. As for without a dowry, there is no disagreement that this is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason He said: ﴿We know what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives﴾, i.e., what Allah, glory be to Him, has enjoined upon the believers regarding the rights of their wives from the conditions and rights of the contract, for that is an obligatory right upon them that is not lawful for them to neglect, nor to imitate the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what Allah specifically granted him as an ease and honor, so they shall not marry except four, with a dowry, a witness and a guardian. ﴿And what your right hands possess﴾, i.e., and We know what We have enjoined upon them concerning what their right hands possess, of those women who may lawfully be taken captive and fought, not those who may not be taken captive, or who have a covenant with the Muslims. ﴿So that there will be no discomfort upon you﴾.

The commentators said: this refers back to the beginning of the verse, i.e., We have made lawful for you your wives, and what your right hand possesses, and the gifted woman, so that there will be no discomfort upon you; so the lam is connected to "We have made lawful." It was said: it is connected to "khalisatan," and the first is preferable. The discomfort (haraj) is constriction, i.e., We widened the permission for you in the lawful things, so that your breast would not be constricted, and you would not think that you had sinned in some of the women you married. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, who forgives sins and has mercy on His servants, and for this reason He widened the matter and did not restrict it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 49–52 (part 2 of 3):

﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾. It is read as *turji* with the hamza (*turji'*) and without it, and both are dialectal forms. *Al-irja'* means delay: one says *arja'tu al-amr* and *arjaytuhu* when one postpones a matter. ﴿And you may take to yourself whom you will﴾: that is, you may draw her to you. One says *awahu ilayhi* (with the long vowel) meaning he drew him to himself, and *awa* (short form) meaning he was drawn to him. The meaning is that God gave the Messenger (ﷺ) latitude and left the choice to him regarding his wives. He may defer whom he wishes of them, postponing her turn and leaving her without visiting her, without divorcing her. And he may take to himself whom he wishes, lie with her and spend the night with her. The division of nights had been obligatory for him until this verse was revealed; the obligation was lifted, and the choice became his. Among those whom he took to himself were ʿĀ'isha, Ḥafṣa, Umm Salama and Zaynab. Among those whom he deferred were Sawda, Juwayriyya, Umm Ḥabība, Maymūna and Ṣafiyya. The Messenger (ﷺ) would treat equally those whom he took to himself in the division of nights, and he would divide [his time] for those whom he had deferred as he wished.

This is the view of the majority of the exegetes regarding the meaning of the verse, and it is what the established evidence in the Ṣaḥīḥ (the authentic collections) and elsewhere indicates.

It has been said that this verse concerns only the women who gave themselves in marriage to the Prophet (ﷺ), and not the other wives. This was said by al-Shaʿbī and others.

It has been said that the meaning of the verse concerns divorce: that he divorces whom he wishes of them and keeps whom he wishes.

Al-Ḥasan said that the meaning is: you may marry whom you wish of the women of your community and leave marrying whom you wish of them.

It has been said that this verse abrogates (*nāsikha*, i.e. naskh: the cancelling of a earlier ruling by a later one) His words: ﴿Women are not lawful to you hereafter﴾. Its explanation will come later.

﴿And whomever you seek from those whom you had set aside, there is no blame upon you﴾. *Al-ibtighāʾ* means seeking, and *al-ʿazl* means removing. The meaning is that if he wishes to take to himself a woman from among those whom he had set aside from the division and draw her to himself, there is no fault upon him in that.

In summary, God, glorified is He, entrusted the matter to His Messenger, who may do with his wives whatever he wishes: advancing or delaying, setting aside or keeping, taking to himself those he had deferred and deferring those he had taken to himself, and doing whatever he wishes concerning them, as a broadening upon him and a removal of hardship from him.

The root of *al-junāḥ* (blame) is inclination; one says *janaḥat al-safīna* when the ship leaned.

The meaning is: there is no inclination (of blame) upon you through reproach or rebuke for what you did. The reference in His words ﴿that﴾ is to what preceded of entrusting the matter to his will. It is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿that their eyes may be comforted﴾, that is: that delegation which We have entrusted to you is closer to their being pleased, because it is the ruling of God, glorified is He.

Qatāda said: that is, that choice which We gave you regarding their companionship is closer to their being pleased, since it comes from Us; for when they know that it is from God, their eyes are comforted.

The majority read *taqarra* (with the verb in the active voice, its subject being *aʿyunuhunna*, "their eyes"). Ibn Muḥayṣin read *tuqirra* with a *ḍamma* on the *tāʾ*, from *aqarra*, whose subject is the pronoun of the addressee, and *aʿyunahunna* in the accusative as object. It was also read in the passive voice.

The explanation of the meaning of "comfort of the eye" has already been given in Surat Maryam. As for ﴿and that they may not grieve﴾, its meaning is that no grief arises among them through your favouring some of them over others. ﴿And that they may all be pleased with what you have given them﴾, that is: that they may all be pleased together with what you have given them of bringing near, deferring, setting aside, and taking to oneself.

The majority read *kulluhunna* with a *ḍamma* as an emphatic (*tawkīd*) of the subject of *yarḍayna* ("they are pleased"). Abū Iyās read it with a *fatḥa* as an emphatic of the object pronoun in *ātaytahunna*.

﴿And God knows what is in your hearts﴾, of everything you conceal, and of that is what you conceal regarding the affairs of women. ﴿And God is ever Knowing, Forbearing﴾: Knowing of everything, nothing hidden from Him, Forbearing, who does not hasten to punish the disobedient.

﴿Women are not lawful to you hereafter﴾. The majority read *lā yaḥillu* with a *yāʾ* (third person), because the verb is separated from its feminine subject. Ibn Kathīr read it with a *tāʾ*.

The people of knowledge have differed over the interpretation of this verse, in several opinions.

The first is that it is *muḥkam* (definitive, not abrogated), and that God forbade the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to marry any other woman in addition to his wives, as a recompense to them for what they did in choosing God, His Messenger and the Last Abode, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by God's command to him, gave them the choice. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Jarīr.

Abū Umāma ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf said: when God forbade them to marry after him, He forbade him to marry anyone other than them.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿIkrima and Abū Razīn said that the meaning is: women are not lawful to you after the categories which God has named.

Al-Qurṭubī said: this is the choice of Ibn Jarīr.

It has been said: the Jewish and Christian women are not lawful to you, because they cannot be described as "Mothers of the Believers".

This view is far-fetched, because it would mean: "women are not lawful to you after the believing women," and there has been no mention of believing women.

It has been said: this verse is abrogated by the Sunna and by His words: ﴿You may defer whom you will of them, and take to yourself whom you will﴾. This is the view of ʿĀ'isha, Umm Salama, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, and others. This is the preferred view, and the evidence indicating it will come at the end of the discussion.

﴿Nor that you should exchange them for other wives﴾: that is, that you should exchange them (*tatabaddala*, with one of the two *tāʾs* elided). That is, it is not permitted for you to divorce one or more of them and marry in exchange for whomever you divorced. The *min* in His words ﴿for other wives﴾ is superfluous, for emphasis.

Ibn Zayd said: this is something the Arabs used to do. One would say: "Take my wife and give me your wife." An-Naḥḥās and Ibn Jarīr rejected what Ibn Zayd mentioned.

Ibn Jarīr said: the Arabs never did this at all.

What refutes this rejection by the two of them is what al-Dāraquṭnī narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: the exchange in the Jāhiliyya (pre-Islamic period) was that a man would say to another: "Step down for me from your wife, and I will step down for you from my wife." So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾.

Al-Bazzār and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from him.

The clause ﴿even if their beauty pleased you﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *tabaddala*. The meaning is that exchanging your wives is not permitted, even if the beauty of others pleased you, others whom you wished to make a replacement for one of them. This exchange is also among the things God abrogated regarding His Messenger, according to the preferred view.

His words ﴿except what your right hand possesses﴾ are an exception from "women", because the term includes both free women and slave-girls.

The scholars have differed over the permissibility of a non-Muslim slave-girl. The first view is that she is lawful to the Prophet (ﷺ) by the generality of this verse. This is the view of Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥakam.

The second view is that she is not lawful to him, out of glorifying his station and keeping him from intimacy with an unbeliever.

The first view is preferred by the generality of this verse. The argument for prohibition on the basis of purity is weak, for nothing that God, glorified is He, has made lawful is impure. What He has made lawful is good, not foul, with regard to matters of marriage, and not with regard to other matters. The polytheists are impure by the explicit text of the Qur'an.

The second view could be preferred by His words, glorified is He: ﴿And do not hold on to marriage ties with unbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], for it is a general prohibition.

﴿And God is ever Watchful over all things﴾: that is, Observer, Guardian, Overseer, to whom nothing is hidden and from whom nothing escapes.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿When you marry believing women﴾, that he said: this concerns a man who marries a woman and then divorces her before he has touched her. When he divorces her once, she is separated from him, and she has no waiting period (*ʿidda*), so she may marry whomever she wishes. Then he said: ﴿So provide for them and release them with a fair release﴾: that is, if he had named a dowry for her, she is entitled only to half; and if he had not named a dowry for her, he provides for her according to his means, poor or well-off, and that is the fair release.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them﴾ is abrogated; it was abrogated by the verse in al-Baqara: ﴿then half of what you have specified﴾ [al-Baqara: 237].

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated the same from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from al-Ḥasan and Abū al-ʿĀliya, who both said: it is not abrogated; she is entitled to half the dowry, and she is entitled to the provision (*matāʿ*).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: it reached Ibn ʿAbbās that Ibn Masʿūd used to say: if a man divorces before he has consummated the marriage, it is valid. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he was wrong in this; God says: ﴿When you marry believing women, then divorce them before you have touched them﴾, and He did not say: "When you divorce believing women, then marry them."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he recited this verse and said: there is no divorce until there is marriage.

There are hadiths to this effect, among them: "There is no divorce except after marriage," and they are well known.

Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Rāhawayh, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who rated it *ḥasan* (good), Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Umm Hāniʾ bint Abī Ṭālib, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) proposed to me, and I excused myself to him, and he excused me. Then God revealed: ﴿O Prophet, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾. She said: so I was not lawful to him, because I had not emigrated with him; I was among the Freed ones (*al-ṭulaqāʾ*, those freed at the Conquest).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated by another route from her, who said: this verse was revealed concerning me: ﴿And the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts . . . who emigrated with you﴾. The Prophet wished to marry me, but was forbidden from me, since I had not emigrated.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾, that he said: God forbade to him other women besides those. Before that he could marry whichever women he wished, and it was not forbidden to him. His wives were extremely distressed that he might marry whichever women he loved. So when it was revealed: "I have forbidden to you women other than what I have related to you," this pleased his wives.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Sunan* narrated from ʿĀ'isha, who said: the woman who gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ) was Khawla bint Ḥakīm.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhārī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Bayhaqī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUrwa that Khawla bint Ḥakīm was among those women who gave themselves to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Ibn Abī Shayba and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥakam and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayda, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married thirteen women: six from Quraysh: Khadīja, ʿĀ'isha, Ḥafṣa, Umm Ḥabība, Sawda and Umm Salama; three from the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa; two women from the Banū Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir: Maymūna bint al-Ḥārith, who is the one who gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Zaynab Umm al-Masākīn; al-ʿĀmiriyya, who is the one who chose this world; a woman from the Banū al-Jawn, who is the one who sought refuge from him; Zaynab bint Jaḥsh al-Asadiyya; and the two captive women: Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy and Juwayriyya bint al-Ḥārith al-Khuzāʿiyya.

Al-Bukhārī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, do you have any need of me?" Anas's daughter said: "How little modesty she had!" He said: "She is better than you; she desired the Prophet (ﷺ) and offered herself to him."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and offered herself to him in marriage, and he remained silent. [He then continued,] the hadith in its full length.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar concerning His saying: ﴿We already know what We have made obligatory upon them concerning their wives﴾, that he said: Allah made it obligatory upon them that there is no marriage except with a guardian (wali) and two witnesses.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas the like of it, and added "and a dowry (mahr)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from 'Ali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that a pregnant woman be approached (sexually) until she gives birth, and that a woman who is not pregnant be approached until she has been cleansed (istibra') by one menstrual cycle (hayd)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, that he said: "You may delay (tu'akhkhir)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning the saying ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, that he said: "Whomever you wish, you may release her from them, and whomever you wish, you may keep of them."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "I used to be jealous of those women who had given themselves to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I would say, 'Does a woman give herself [in marriage]?' Then when Allah revealed ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾ up to the verse, I said: 'I see that your Lord only hastens to satisfy your desire.'"

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Razin, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to divorce some of his wives. When they saw that, they came to him and said: 'Do not release us, and you are free in what is between us and you. Assign for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish.' So Allah revealed ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, meaning: you may set aside whom you will; so he postponed some of them and sheltered others."

Among those he postponed were Maymunah, Juwayriyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Sawdah, and he would allot to them from himself and his wealth whatever he wished. Among those he sheltered were 'A'ishah, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab, and his allotment from himself and his wealth to them was equal.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'ishah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to ask permission (to stay) on the day of any one of us after this verse was revealed: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾. I said to her: 'What did you used to say?' She said: 'I used to say: If that is up to me, then I do not want to give preference to anyone over you.'"

Al-Ruyani, al-Darimi, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ziyad, a man of the Ansar, who said: I said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Tell me, if the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) died, would it not be lawful for him to marry?" He said: "What would prevent him from that?" I said: "[Allah's] saying: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾." He said: "He only made lawful for him a certain kind of women and described for him a quality, saying: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and a believing woman﴾. Then He said: Women are not lawful for you after this description."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was forbidden from [marrying] categories of women except those who were believing emigrants. He said: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this, nor is it [permissible] that you exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except what your right hand possesses﴾. So He made lawful for him believing slave-girls, and [a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet]. And He forbade every woman of a religion other than Islam. He said: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a privilege for you, apart from the believers﴾. And He forbade whatever else of categories of women."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden to marry any [new women] after his first wives."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him concerning the verse: "Allah confined him to them, just as He confined them to him."

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Anas, who said: "When he gave them the choice and they chose Allah and His Messenger, He restricted him to them, saying: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Umm Salamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until Allah made lawful for him to marry whatever women he wished, except those forbidden by kinship (dhat mahram). This is the saying of Allah: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and shelter whom you will﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated through 'Ata' from 'A'ishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until Allah made lawful for him to marry whatever women he wished, except those forbidden by kinship, due to His saying: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and shelter whom you will﴾."

Ibn Sa'd narrated the like of it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Razin concerning ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾, that he said: "[Except] from among the polytheist women, except what you capture, so that your right hand possesses them."

al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The exchange (badal) in the Jahiliyyah was that a man would say to another man: 'Exchange your wife with me and I will exchange my wife with you,' meaning: 'Give me your wife and I will give you my wife.' So Allah revealed: ﴿nor is it [permissible] that you exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you﴾." He said: "Then 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while 'A'ishah was with him, and he entered without permission. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Where is the seeking of permission?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have not sought permission from any man of the Ansar since I reached [maturity].' Then he said: 'Who is this Humayra' beside you?' The Messenger of Allah said: 'This is 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers.' He said: 'Shall I not give you in exchange for her the best of Allah's creation?' He said: 'O 'Uyaynah, indeed Allah has forbidden that.' When he left, 'A'ishah said: 'Who is this?' He said: 'A foolish man who is obeyed, and he is, as you see, the chief of his people.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verse 49–52 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the story of Zayd and his divorce of Zaynab, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had consummated the marriage with her and proposed to her after the completion of her waiting period, as has preceded, He addressed the believers, explaining to them the ruling concerning a wife whose husband divorces her before consummation, and said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women﴾, meaning: when you contract marriage with them. The word nikah (marriage) in the Book of Allah occurs only in the sense of contract, as stated by the author of al-Kashshaf, al-Qurtubi and others.

There is a difference of opinion as to whether the word nikah is literally (haqiqah) used for sexual intercourse (wat'), or for the contract ('aqd), or for both by way of homonymy (ishtirak). The discourse of the author of al-Kashshaf at this point suggests that it is literally used for intercourse, for he (p-1175) said: "Nikah is intercourse, and calling the contract nikah is because of its connection to it, insofar as it is a means to it. Its parallel is calling wine sin, because it is a cause of committing sin."

﴿Before you touch them﴾, meaning before you have intercourse with them; He referred to that by the word touching (mass). ﴿Then you have no waiting period for them to count﴾. This is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir related. The meaning of ta'taddunaha is: you complete their number, from "I counted the dirhams (ʿadadtu al-darahim), so I calculate them (a'taddu-ha)."

The attribution of this to men indicates that the waiting period is a right for them, as the phrase ﴿you have no waiting period for them﴾ implies. The majority (al-Jumhur) read ta'taddunaha with a doubled dal (tashdid), while Ibn Kathir, in one narration from him, and the people of Makkah read it with a single dal (takhfif).

For this reading there are two possibilities: first, that it has the same meaning as the former, derived from i'tidad, i.e., you complete their number, but they omitted the doubling for the purpose of lightening.

Al-Razi said: If it were from i'tida', which is injustice, it would be weak, because i'tida' is transitive with ʿala.

It was also said: it is permissible that it be from i'tida' with the preposition omitted, i.e., ta'tadunna ʿalayha: i.e., ʿalā al-ʿidda, figuratively, and similar to it is his saying:
"She yearns and reveals what is in her of ardent love, and I conceal what, were it not for grief, would have killed me."
i.e., would have decided against me (laqada 'alayya).

The second possibility is that the meaning is ta'tadūna fīhā (you transgress in it), and the intended sense of transgression here is that found in His saying: ﴿And do not keep them in marriage to harm them, so that you transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. Thus the meaning of the verse on the latter reading is: ﴿you have no waiting period for them that you count against them in it, by harming them.﴾

Ibn 'Atiyyah denied the soundness of this reading from Ibn Kathir and said: al-Bazzi made a mistake regarding it. This verse specifies the generality of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], and His saying: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. The provision of enjoyment (mut'ah) mentioned here has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the enjoyment mentioned here is abrogated by the verse in Surah al-Baqarah, which is His saying: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already set a dowry for them, then half of what you have set﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. It was also said: the enjoyment here is more general than being half the dowry, or the enjoyment is specific if no dowry was named for her. So with the naming of the dowry she is entitled to half of what was named, acting upon His saying: "then half of what you have set for them," and without naming she is entitled to enjoyment, acting upon this verse. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them a dowry; but provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236]. This harmonization is necessary, and it takes precedence over preference (tarjih) and over the claim of abrogation.

The widow whose husband has died is specified out of this verse, for if he dies after contracting marriage with her and before consummation, death is like consummation, so she observes a waiting period of four months and ten days.

Ibn Kathir said: by consensus. So the specifier is consensus. Those who take this verse as evidence that there is no divorce before marriage, namely the majority, have relied upon it. Malik and Abu Hanifah held that divorce before marriage is valid if he says: "If I marry so-and-so, she is divorced," so she is divorced when he marries her.

The basis of the evidence of the verse for what the majority said is that He said: ﴿When you marry believing women, then you divorce them﴾, so He followed the divorce with the marriage by the particle thumma (then), which indicates sequence and an interval, ﴿and release them with a fair release﴾, i.e., send them out of your homes, since you have no waiting period for them. The "fair release" here is a metaphor for divorce, but this is far-fetched, because divorce has already been mentioned, followed by the provision of enjoyment, and the fair release is joined to it by conjunction, so it must mean something other than divorce.

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whose bridal payments you have given﴾. In this verse He mentioned the kinds of marriages which He made lawful for His Messenger, and He began with his wives whose dowries (ujur) he had given, i.e., their mahr (bridal gift), for the mahr is the wage for intimacy, and giving it is either handing it over immediately or naming it in the contract.

There is a difference regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿We have made lawful for you your wives﴾. Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said: Allah made lawful for him to marry every woman to whom he gives her mahr, so the verse permits all women except those within the prohibited degrees.

The majority said: the intended meaning is: We have made lawful for you your wives who are with you, because they chose you over the world and its adornment; and this is the apparent meaning, because His saying "We have made lawful" and "you have given" are in the past tense, and restricting the lawfulness by the giving of the wages is not because the permission depends on it, since a contract is valid without a named dowry, and the mahr of the like (mahr al-mithl) is due with intercourse, and enjoyment without it; so it seems to be for the purpose of guiding to what is better. ﴿And what your right hand possesses from what Allah has returned to you﴾, i.e., the captive women who entered his possession through spoils of war.

The meaning of ﴿from what Allah has returned to you﴾ is: from what Allah has returned to you from the unbelievers as booty, for their women taken by force and dominance. This restriction is not intended to exclude what he owns by other than spoils, for it makes lawful to him a purchased or gifted concubine and the like; rather it is an indication of what is better, like the first restriction that explicitly mentions giving the wages. Similarly the restriction of emigration in His saying: ﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who have emigrated with you﴾, for it is an indication of what is better, and an announcement of the nobility of emigration and of those who emigrated. The meaning of "with you" here is sharing in the emigration, not in the companionship in it.

It was also said: this restriction, I mean emigration, is considered, and that those among these who did not emigrate are not lawful to him, as in His saying: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you owe them no guardianship until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. This is supported by the hadith of Umm Hani', which will come at the end of this discussion, if Allah wills. The reason for the singular of paternal uncle and maternal uncle and the plural of paternal aunt and maternal aunt is what al-Qurtubi mentioned: that "uncle" and "maternal uncle" in general usage are collective nouns (ism jins), like "the poet" and "the reciter," whereas "paternal aunt" and "maternal aunt" are not so.

He said: This is a linguistic convention, so the speech came in accordance with it, with complete clarity. He related this from Ibn al-'Arabi.

Ibn Kathir said: He made the word for the male singular because of its nobility, and pluralized the female, like His saying: ﴿on the right and the left﴾ [al-Nahl: 48], and His saying: ﴿He brings them out from the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and it has many similar examples. End of quote.

Al-Naysaburi said: He did not pluralize "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" being content with their generic nature, although the plural of the daughters indicates that, because two sisters cannot be under one man; and this abbreviation did not sound good for paternal aunt and maternal aunt, since it could occur to the mind that the ta' in them denotes unity. End of quote.

Each of these explanations is open to objection by counter-argument and opposition, and the best of them is the explanation of pluralizing paternal aunt and maternal aunt by the thought occurring that the ta' is for unity; yet nothing in "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" leads the mind to think that unity is intended by them, except the mere singular form, and that does not require it after its addition to a noun, given the generality of genitive-constructed generic nouns. Moreover, even this best explanation is not free from the taint of objection.

﴿And a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾. This is coordinated with the object of "We have made lawful", i.e., and We have made lawful for you a woman who affirms the Oneness of God, if she gives herself to you without a dowry.

As for one who is not a believer, she is not lawful to you merely by her giving herself to you; but this is not obligatory upon you, such that you must accept it, rather it is conditional upon your will. For this reason He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾, i.e., to make her a wife to him and to take possession of her intimacy by that gift without a dowry.

It has been said: the Prophet (ﷺ) did not marry any of the women who gave themselves, and none of them was with him.

It was said: there was with him of them Khawlah bint Hakim, as in Sahih al-Bukhari from 'A'ishah. Qatadah said: she was Maymunah bint al-Harith. al-Sha'bi said: she was Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Ansariyyah, Umm al-Masakin. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: she was Umm Sharik bint Jabir al-Asadiyyah. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: she was Umm Hakim bint al-Awqas al-Sulamiyyah.

Then He, glory be to Him, made clear that this type of marriage is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and is not lawful for anyone else of his community. He said: ﴿as a special privilege for you, not for the [other] believers﴾, i.e., this pure permission is specific to you, to the exclusion of other believers.

The word khalisah is either a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "woman", as said by al-Zajjaj, or an emphatic infinitive like "the promise of Allah", i.e., it is purely yours, a purity.

al-Jumhur read wamra'atan with the accusative. Abu Haywah read it in the nominative as a subject. al-Jumhur read "in wahabat" with kasrah on in; Ubayy, al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with fathah on it as a subject.

al-Jumhur read khalisatan with the accusative, and it was read in the nominative as an attribute of "woman" according to the reading of whoever read "woman" in the nominative. The scholars have agreed that this is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it is not permissible for anyone else, and that marriage is not concluded by a woman giving herself in gift, except what is related from Abu Hanifah and his two companions, that marriage is valid if she gives herself and he calls witnesses on himself to a dowry. As for without a dowry, there is no disagreement that this is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason He said: ﴿We know what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives﴾, i.e., what Allah, glory be to Him, has enjoined upon the believers regarding the rights of their wives from the conditions and rights of the contract, for that is an obligatory right upon them that is not lawful for them to neglect, nor to imitate the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what Allah specifically granted him as an ease and honor, so they shall not marry except four, with a dowry, a witness and a guardian. ﴿And what your right hands possess﴾, i.e., and We know what We have enjoined upon them concerning what their right hands possess, of those women who may lawfully be taken captive and fought, not those who may not be taken captive, or who have a covenant with the Muslims. ﴿So that there will be no discomfort upon you﴾.

The commentators said: this refers back to the beginning of the verse, i.e., We have made lawful for you your wives, and what your right hand possesses, and the gifted woman, so that there will be no discomfort upon you; so the lam is connected to "We have made lawful." It was said: it is connected to "khalisatan," and the first is preferable. The discomfort (haraj) is constriction, i.e., We widened the permission for you in the lawful things, so that your breast would not be constricted, and you would not think that you had sinned in some of the women you married. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾, who forgives sins and has mercy on His servants, and for this reason He widened the matter and did not restrict it.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 49–52 (part 2 of 3):

﴿You may defer whom you will of them﴾. It is read as *turji* with the hamza (*turji'*) and without it, and both are dialectal forms. *Al-irja'* means delay: one says *arja'tu al-amr* and *arjaytuhu* when one postpones a matter. ﴿And you may take to yourself whom you will﴾: that is, you may draw her to you. One says *awahu ilayhi* (with the long vowel) meaning he drew him to himself, and *awa* (short form) meaning he was drawn to him. The meaning is that God gave the Messenger (ﷺ) latitude and left the choice to him regarding his wives. He may defer whom he wishes of them, postponing her turn and leaving her without visiting her, without divorcing her. And he may take to himself whom he wishes, lie with her and spend the night with her. The division of nights had been obligatory for him until this verse was revealed; the obligation was lifted, and the choice became his. Among those whom he took to himself were ʿĀ'isha, Ḥafṣa, Umm Salama and Zaynab. Among those whom he deferred were Sawda, Juwayriyya, Umm Ḥabība, Maymūna and Ṣafiyya. The Messenger (ﷺ) would treat equally those whom he took to himself in the division of nights, and he would divide [his time] for those whom he had deferred as he wished.

This is the view of the majority of the exegetes regarding the meaning of the verse, and it is what the established evidence in the Ṣaḥīḥ (the authentic collections) and elsewhere indicates.

It has been said that this verse concerns only the women who gave themselves in marriage to the Prophet (ﷺ), and not the other wives. This was said by al-Shaʿbī and others.

It has been said that the meaning of the verse concerns divorce: that he divorces whom he wishes of them and keeps whom he wishes.

Al-Ḥasan said that the meaning is: you may marry whom you wish of the women of your community and leave marrying whom you wish of them.

It has been said that this verse abrogates (*nāsikha*, i.e. naskh: the cancelling of a earlier ruling by a later one) His words: ﴿Women are not lawful to you hereafter﴾. Its explanation will come later.

﴿And whomever you seek from those whom you had set aside, there is no blame upon you﴾. *Al-ibtighāʾ* means seeking, and *al-ʿazl* means removing. The meaning is that if he wishes to take to himself a woman from among those whom he had set aside from the division and draw her to himself, there is no fault upon him in that.

In summary, God, glorified is He, entrusted the matter to His Messenger, who may do with his wives whatever he wishes: advancing or delaying, setting aside or keeping, taking to himself those he had deferred and deferring those he had taken to himself, and doing whatever he wishes concerning them, as a broadening upon him and a removal of hardship from him.

The root of *al-junāḥ* (blame) is inclination; one says *janaḥat al-safīna* when the ship leaned.

The meaning is: there is no inclination (of blame) upon you through reproach or rebuke for what you did. The reference in His words ﴿that﴾ is to what preceded of entrusting the matter to his will. It is the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿that their eyes may be comforted﴾, that is: that delegation which We have entrusted to you is closer to their being pleased, because it is the ruling of God, glorified is He.

Qatāda said: that is, that choice which We gave you regarding their companionship is closer to their being pleased, since it comes from Us; for when they know that it is from God, their eyes are comforted.

The majority read *taqarra* (with the verb in the active voice, its subject being *aʿyunuhunna*, "their eyes"). Ibn Muḥayṣin read *tuqirra* with a *ḍamma* on the *tāʾ*, from *aqarra*, whose subject is the pronoun of the addressee, and *aʿyunahunna* in the accusative as object. It was also read in the passive voice.

The explanation of the meaning of "comfort of the eye" has already been given in Surat Maryam. As for ﴿and that they may not grieve﴾, its meaning is that no grief arises among them through your favouring some of them over others. ﴿And that they may all be pleased with what you have given them﴾, that is: that they may all be pleased together with what you have given them of bringing near, deferring, setting aside, and taking to oneself.

The majority read *kulluhunna* with a *ḍamma* as an emphatic (*tawkīd*) of the subject of *yarḍayna* ("they are pleased"). Abū Iyās read it with a *fatḥa* as an emphatic of the object pronoun in *ātaytahunna*.

﴿And God knows what is in your hearts﴾, of everything you conceal, and of that is what you conceal regarding the affairs of women. ﴿And God is ever Knowing, Forbearing﴾: Knowing of everything, nothing hidden from Him, Forbearing, who does not hasten to punish the disobedient.

﴿Women are not lawful to you hereafter﴾. The majority read *lā yaḥillu* with a *yāʾ* (third person), because the verb is separated from its feminine subject. Ibn Kathīr read it with a *tāʾ*.

The people of knowledge have differed over the interpretation of this verse, in several opinions.

The first is that it is *muḥkam* (definitive, not abrogated), and that God forbade the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to marry any other woman in addition to his wives, as a recompense to them for what they did in choosing God, His Messenger and the Last Abode, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by God's command to him, gave them the choice. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, Abū Bakr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām, Ibn Zayd, and Ibn Jarīr.

Abū Umāma ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf said: when God forbade them to marry after him, He forbade him to marry anyone other than them.

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿIkrima and Abū Razīn said that the meaning is: women are not lawful to you after the categories which God has named.

Al-Qurṭubī said: this is the choice of Ibn Jarīr.

It has been said: the Jewish and Christian women are not lawful to you, because they cannot be described as "Mothers of the Believers".

This view is far-fetched, because it would mean: "women are not lawful to you after the believing women," and there has been no mention of believing women.

It has been said: this verse is abrogated by the Sunna and by His words: ﴿You may defer whom you will of them, and take to yourself whom you will﴾. This is the view of ʿĀ'isha, Umm Salama, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, and others. This is the preferred view, and the evidence indicating it will come at the end of the discussion.

﴿Nor that you should exchange them for other wives﴾: that is, that you should exchange them (*tatabaddala*, with one of the two *tāʾs* elided). That is, it is not permitted for you to divorce one or more of them and marry in exchange for whomever you divorced. The *min* in His words ﴿for other wives﴾ is superfluous, for emphasis.

Ibn Zayd said: this is something the Arabs used to do. One would say: "Take my wife and give me your wife." An-Naḥḥās and Ibn Jarīr rejected what Ibn Zayd mentioned.

Ibn Jarīr said: the Arabs never did this at all.

What refutes this rejection by the two of them is what al-Dāraquṭnī narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: the exchange in the Jāhiliyya (pre-Islamic period) was that a man would say to another: "Step down for me from your wife, and I will step down for you from my wife." So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾.

Al-Bazzār and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from him.

The clause ﴿even if their beauty pleased you﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the subject of *tabaddala*. The meaning is that exchanging your wives is not permitted, even if the beauty of others pleased you, others whom you wished to make a replacement for one of them. This exchange is also among the things God abrogated regarding His Messenger, according to the preferred view.

His words ﴿except what your right hand possesses﴾ are an exception from "women", because the term includes both free women and slave-girls.

The scholars have differed over the permissibility of a non-Muslim slave-girl. The first view is that she is lawful to the Prophet (ﷺ) by the generality of this verse. This is the view of Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥakam.

The second view is that she is not lawful to him, out of glorifying his station and keeping him from intimacy with an unbeliever.

The first view is preferred by the generality of this verse. The argument for prohibition on the basis of purity is weak, for nothing that God, glorified is He, has made lawful is impure. What He has made lawful is good, not foul, with regard to matters of marriage, and not with regard to other matters. The polytheists are impure by the explicit text of the Qur'an.

The second view could be preferred by His words, glorified is He: ﴿And do not hold on to marriage ties with unbelieving women﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], for it is a general prohibition.

﴿And God is ever Watchful over all things﴾: that is, Observer, Guardian, Overseer, to whom nothing is hidden and from whom nothing escapes.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿When you marry believing women﴾, that he said: this concerns a man who marries a woman and then divorces her before he has touched her. When he divorces her once, she is separated from him, and she has no waiting period (*ʿidda*), so she may marry whomever she wishes. Then he said: ﴿So provide for them and release them with a fair release﴾: that is, if he had named a dowry for her, she is entitled only to half; and if he had not named a dowry for her, he provides for her according to his means, poor or well-off, and that is the fair release.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them﴾ is abrogated; it was abrogated by the verse in al-Baqara: ﴿then half of what you have specified﴾ [al-Baqara: 237].

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn Jarīr narrated the same from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from al-Ḥasan and Abū al-ʿĀliya, who both said: it is not abrogated; she is entitled to half the dowry, and she is entitled to the provision (*matāʿ*).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: it reached Ibn ʿAbbās that Ibn Masʿūd used to say: if a man divorces before he has consummated the marriage, it is valid. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he was wrong in this; God says: ﴿When you marry believing women, then divorce them before you have touched them﴾, and He did not say: "When you divorce believing women, then marry them."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he recited this verse and said: there is no divorce until there is marriage.

There are hadiths to this effect, among them: "There is no divorce except after marriage," and they are well known.

Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Rāhawayh, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who rated it *ḥasan* (good), Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī narrated from Umm Hāniʾ bint Abī Ṭālib, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) proposed to me, and I excused myself to him, and he excused me. Then God revealed: ﴿O Prophet, We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to His words ﴿who emigrated with you﴾. She said: so I was not lawful to him, because I had not emigrated with him; I was among the Freed ones (*al-ṭulaqāʾ*, those freed at the Conquest).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated by another route from her, who said: this verse was revealed concerning me: ﴿And the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts . . . who emigrated with you﴾. The Prophet wished to marry me, but was forbidden from me, since I had not emigrated.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words ﴿We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾, that he said: God forbade to him other women besides those. Before that he could marry whichever women he wished, and it was not forbidden to him. His wives were extremely distressed that he might marry whichever women he loved. So when it was revealed: "I have forbidden to you women other than what I have related to you," this pleased his wives.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in *al-Sunan* narrated from ʿĀ'isha, who said: the woman who gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ) was Khawla bint Ḥakīm.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Saʿd, Ibn Abī Shayba, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhārī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Bayhaqī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from ʿUrwa that Khawla bint Ḥakīm was among those women who gave themselves to the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Ibn Abī Shayba and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥakam and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUbayda, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) married thirteen women: six from Quraysh: Khadīja, ʿĀ'isha, Ḥafṣa, Umm Ḥabība, Sawda and Umm Salama; three from the Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa; two women from the Banū Hilāl ibn ʿĀmir: Maymūna bint al-Ḥārith, who is the one who gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Zaynab Umm al-Masākīn; al-ʿĀmiriyya, who is the one who chose this world; a woman from the Banū al-Jawn, who is the one who sought refuge from him; Zaynab bint Jaḥsh al-Asadiyya; and the two captive women: Ṣafiyya bint Ḥuyayy and Juwayriyya bint al-Ḥārith al-Khuzāʿiyya.

Al-Bukhārī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, do you have any need of me?" Anas's daughter said: "How little modesty she had!" He said: "She is better than you; she desired the Prophet (ﷺ) and offered herself to him."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi that a woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and offered herself to him in marriage, and he remained silent. [He then continued,] the hadith in its full length.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Umar concerning His saying: ﴿We already know what We have made obligatory upon them concerning their wives﴾, that he said: Allah made it obligatory upon them that there is no marriage except with a guardian (wali) and two witnesses.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas the like of it, and added "and a dowry (mahr)."

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from 'Ali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade that a pregnant woman be approached (sexually) until she gives birth, and that a woman who is not pregnant be approached until she has been cleansed (istibra') by one menstrual cycle (hayd)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, that he said: "You may delay (tu'akhkhir)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning the saying ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, that he said: "Whomever you wish, you may release her from them, and whomever you wish, you may keep of them."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'ishah, who said: "I used to be jealous of those women who had given themselves to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I would say, 'Does a woman give herself [in marriage]?' Then when Allah revealed ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾ up to the verse, I said: 'I see that your Lord only hastens to satisfy your desire.'"

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Razin, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) resolved to divorce some of his wives. When they saw that, they came to him and said: 'Do not release us, and you are free in what is between us and you. Assign for us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish.' So Allah revealed ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, meaning: you may set aside whom you will; so he postponed some of them and sheltered others."

Among those he postponed were Maymunah, Juwayriyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Sawdah, and he would allot to them from himself and his wealth whatever he wished. Among those he sheltered were 'A'ishah, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab, and his allotment from himself and his wealth to them was equal.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from 'A'ishah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to ask permission (to stay) on the day of any one of us after this verse was revealed: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾. I said to her: 'What did you used to say?' She said: 'I used to say: If that is up to me, then I do not want to give preference to anyone over you.'"

Al-Ruyani, al-Darimi, Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ziyad, a man of the Ansar, who said: I said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Tell me, if the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) died, would it not be lawful for him to marry?" He said: "What would prevent him from that?" I said: "[Allah's] saying: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾." He said: "He only made lawful for him a certain kind of women and described for him a quality, saying: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and a believing woman﴾. Then He said: Women are not lawful for you after this description."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was forbidden from [marrying] categories of women except those who were believing emigrants. He said: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this, nor is it [permissible] that you exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except what your right hand possesses﴾. So He made lawful for him believing slave-girls, and [a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet]. And He forbade every woman of a religion other than Islam. He said: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a privilege for you, apart from the believers﴾. And He forbade whatever else of categories of women."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden to marry any [new women] after his first wives."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him concerning the verse: "Allah confined him to them, just as He confined them to him."

Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Anas, who said: "When he gave them the choice and they chose Allah and His Messenger, He restricted him to them, saying: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾."

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Umm Salamah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until Allah made lawful for him to marry whatever women he wished, except those forbidden by kinship (dhat mahram). This is the saying of Allah: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and shelter whom you will﴾."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his Nasikh, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated through 'Ata' from 'A'ishah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until Allah made lawful for him to marry whatever women he wished, except those forbidden by kinship, due to His saying: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and shelter whom you will﴾."

Ibn Sa'd narrated the like of it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Razin concerning ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾, that he said: "[Except] from among the polytheist women, except what you capture, so that your right hand possesses them."

al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The exchange (badal) in the Jahiliyyah was that a man would say to another man: 'Exchange your wife with me and I will exchange my wife with you,' meaning: 'Give me your wife and I will give you my wife.' So Allah revealed: ﴿nor is it [permissible] that you exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you﴾." He said: "Then 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while 'A'ishah was with him, and he entered without permission. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Where is the seeking of permission?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have not sought permission from any man of the Ansar since I reached [maturity].' Then he said: 'Who is this Humayra' beside you?' The Messenger of Allah said: 'This is 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers.' He said: 'Shall I not give you in exchange for her the best of Allah's creation?' He said: 'O 'Uyaynah, indeed Allah has forbidden that.' When he left, 'A'ishah said: 'Who is this?' He said: 'A foolish man who is obeyed, and he is, as you see, the chief of his people.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verse 49–52 (part 1 of 3):

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the story of Zayd and his divorce of Zaynab, and the Prophet (ﷺ) had consummated the marriage with her and proposed to her after the completion of her waiting period, as has preceded, He addressed the believers, explaining to them the ruling concerning a wife whose husband divorces her before consummation, and said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women﴾, meaning: when you contract marriage with them. The word nikah (marriage) in the Book of Allah occurs only in the sense of contract, as stated by the author of al-Kashshaf, al-Qurtubi and others.

There is a difference of opinion as to whether the word nikah is literally (haqiqah) used for sexual intercourse (wat'), or for the contract ('aqd), or for both by way of homonymy (ishtirak). The discourse of the author of al-Kashshaf at this point suggests that it is literally used for intercourse, for he (p-1175) said: "Nikah is intercourse, and calling the contract nikah is because of its connection to it, insofar as it is a means to it. Its parallel is calling wine sin, because it is a cause of committing sin."

﴿Before you touch them﴾, meaning before you have intercourse with them; He referred to that by the word touching (mass). ﴿Then you have no waiting period for them to count﴾. This is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir related. The meaning of ta'taddunaha is: you complete their number, from "I counted the dirhams (ʿadadtu al-darahim), so I calculate them (a'taddu-ha)."

The attribution of this to men indicates that the waiting period is a right for them, as the phrase ﴿you have no waiting period for them﴾ implies. The majority (al-Jumhur) read ta'taddunaha with a doubled dal (tashdid), while Ibn Kathir, in one narration from him, and the people of Makkah read it with a single dal (takhfif).

For this reading there are two possibilities: first, that it has the same meaning as the former, derived from i'tidad, i.e., you complete their number, but they omitted the doubling for the purpose of lightening.

Al-Razi said: If it were from i'tida', which is injustice, it would be weak, because i'tida' is transitive with ʿala.

It was also said: it is permissible that it be from i'tida' with the preposition omitted, i.e., ta'tadunna ʿalayha: i.e., ʿalā al-ʿidda, figuratively, and similar to it is his saying:
"She yearns and reveals what is in her of ardent love, and I conceal what, were it not for grief, would have killed me."
i.e., would have decided against me (laqada 'alayya).

The second possibility is that the meaning is ta'tadūna fīhā (you transgress in it), and the intended sense of transgression here is that found in His saying: ﴿And do not keep them in marriage to harm them, so that you transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. Thus the meaning of the verse on the latter reading is: ﴿you have no waiting period for them that you count against them in it, by harming them.﴾

Ibn 'Atiyyah denied the soundness of this reading from Ibn Kathir and said: al-Bazzi made a mistake regarding it. This verse specifies the generality of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], and His saying: ﴿And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. The provision of enjoyment (mut'ah) mentioned here has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the enjoyment mentioned here is abrogated by the verse in Surah al-Baqarah, which is His saying: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already set a dowry for them, then half of what you have set﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. It was also said: the enjoyment here is more general than being half the dowry, or the enjoyment is specific if no dowry was named for her. So with the naming of the dowry she is entitled to half of what was named, acting upon His saying: "then half of what you have set for them," and without naming she is entitled to enjoyment, acting upon this verse. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them a dowry; but provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236]. This harmonization is necessary, and it takes precedence over preference (tarjih) and over the claim of abrogation.

The widow whose husband has died is specified out of this verse, for if he dies after contracting marriage with her and before consummation, death is like consummation, so she observes a waiting period of four months and ten days.

Ibn Kathir said: by consensus. So the specifier is consensus. Those who take this verse as evidence that there is no divorce before marriage, namely the majority, have relied upon it. Malik and Abu Hanifah held that divorce before marriage is valid if he says: "If I marry so-and-so, she is divorced," so she is divorced when he marries her.

The basis of the evidence of the verse for what the majority said is that He said: ﴿When you marry believing women, then you divorce them﴾, so He followed the divorce with the marriage by the particle thumma (then), which indicates sequence and an interval, ﴿and release them with a fair release﴾, i.e., send them out of your homes, since you have no waiting period for them. The "fair release" here is a metaphor for divorce, but this is far-fetched, because divorce has already been mentioned, followed by the provision of enjoyment, and the fair release is joined to it by conjunction, so it must mean something other than divorce.

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whose bridal payments you have given﴾. In this verse He mentioned the kinds of marriages which He made lawful for His Messenger, and He began with his wives whose dowries (ujur) he had given, i.e., their mahr (bridal gift), for the mahr is the wage for intimacy, and giving it is either handing it over immediately or naming it in the contract.

There is a difference regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿We have made lawful for you your wives﴾. Ibn Zayd and al-Dahhak said: Allah made lawful for him to marry every woman to whom he gives her mahr, so the verse permits all women except those within the prohibited degrees.

The majority said: the intended meaning is: We have made lawful for you your wives who are with you, because they chose you over the world and its adornment; and this is the apparent meaning, because His saying "We have made lawful" and "you have given" are in the past tense, and restricting the lawfulness by the giving of the wages is not because the permission depends on it, since a contract is valid without a named dowry, and the mahr of the like (mahr al-mithl) is due with intercourse, and enjoyment without it; so it seems to be for the purpose of guiding to what is better. ﴿And what your right hand possesses from what Allah has returned to you﴾, i.e., the captive women who entered his possession through spoils of war.

The meaning of ﴿from what Allah has returned to you﴾ is: from what Allah has returned to you from the unbelievers as booty, for their women taken by force and dominance. This restriction is not intended to exclude what he owns by other than spoils, for it makes lawful to him a purchased or gifted concubine and the like; rather it is an indication of what is better, like the first restriction that explicitly mentions giving the wages. Similarly the restriction of emigration in His saying: ﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts, and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who have emigrated with you﴾, for it is an indication of what is better, and an announcement of the nobility of emigration and of those who emigrated. The meaning of "with you" here is sharing in the emigration, not in the companionship in it.

It was also said: this restriction, I mean emigration, is considered, and that those among these who did not emigrate are not lawful to him, as in His saying: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate, you owe them no guardianship until they emigrate﴾ [al-Anfal: 72]. This is supported by the hadith of Umm Hani', which will come at the end of this discussion, if Allah wills. The reason for the singular of paternal uncle and maternal uncle and the plural of paternal aunt and maternal aunt is what al-Qurtubi mentioned: that "uncle" and "maternal uncle" in general usage are collective nouns (ism jins), like "the poet" and "the reciter," whereas "paternal aunt" and "maternal aunt" are not so.

He said: This is a linguistic convention, so the speech came in accordance with it, with complete clarity. He related this from Ibn al-'Arabi.

Ibn Kathir said: He made the word for the male singular because of its nobility, and pluralized the female, like His saying: ﴿on the right and the left﴾ [al-Nahl: 48], and His saying: ﴿He brings them out from the darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257], ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1], and it has many similar examples. End of quote.

Al-Naysaburi said: He did not pluralize "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" being content with their generic nature, although the plural of the daughters indicates that, because two sisters cannot be under one man; and this abbreviation did not sound good for paternal aunt and maternal aunt, since it could occur to the mind that the ta' in them denotes unity. End of quote.

Each of these explanations is open to objection by counter-argument and opposition, and the best of them is the explanation of pluralizing paternal aunt and maternal aunt by the thought occurring that the ta' is for unity; yet nothing in "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" leads the mind to think that unity is intended by them, except the mere singular form, and that does not require it after its addition to a noun, given the generality of genitive-constructed generic nouns. Moreover, even this best explanation is not free from the taint of objection.

﴿And a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾. This is coordinated with the object of "We have made lawful", i.e., and We have made lawful for you a woman who affirms the Oneness of God, if she gives herself to you without a dowry.

As for one who is not a believer, she is not lawful to you merely by her giving herself to you; but this is not obligatory upon you, such that you must accept it, rather it is conditional upon your will. For this reason He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾, i.e., to make her a wife to him and to take possession of her intimacy by that gift without a dowry.

It has been said: the Prophet (ﷺ) did not marry any of the women who gave themselves, and none of them was with him.

It was said: there was with him of them Khawlah bint Hakim, as in Sahih al-Bukhari from 'A'ishah. Qatadah said: she was Maymunah bint al-Harith. al-Sha'bi said: she was Zaynab bint Khuzaymah al-Ansariyyah, Umm al-Masakin. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: she was Umm Sharik bint Jabir al-Asadiyyah. 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: she was Umm Hakim bint al-Awqas al-Sulamiyyah.

Then He, glory be to Him, made clear that this type of marriage is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and is not lawful for anyone else of his community. He said: ﴿as a special privilege for you, not for the [other] believers﴾, i.e., this pure permission is specific to you, to the exclusion of other believers.

The word khalisah is either a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "woman", as said by al-Zajjaj, or an emphatic infinitive like "the promise of Allah", i.e., it is purely yours, a purity.

al-Jumhur read wamra'atan with the accusative. Abu Haywah read it in the nominative as a subject. al-Jumhur read "in wahabat" with kasrah on in; Ubayy, al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with fathah on it as a subject.

al-Jumhur read khalisatan with the accusative, and it was read in the nominative as an attribute of "woman" according to the reading of whoever read "woman" in the nominative. The scholars have agreed that this is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that it is not permissible for anyone else, and that marriage is not concluded by a woman giving herself in gift, except what is related from Abu Hanifah and his two companions, that marriage is valid if she gives herself and he calls witnesses on himself to a dowry. As for without a dowry, there is no disagreement that this is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ).
