Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words, ﴿There is no blame upon them﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: "This was revealed specifically concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)—and His words 'the wives of the Prophet' mean the wives of the believing women—﴿nor upon what their right hands possess﴾, from among the male slaves and female slaves. And they were permitted to see them after the hijab had been imposed upon them."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 53–55 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet﴾. This is a general prohibition for every believer against entering the houses of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except with his permission.

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was what occurred from some of the Companions at the wedding feast (walimah) of Zaynab, and the explanation of that will come at the end of the discussion, God willing.

His saying: ﴿except when permission is given to you﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances, meaning: do not enter them in any circumstance except in the circumstance of being given permission. It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning: except accompanied by permission; or by omitting the preposition (naz' al-khafid), meaning: except that permission is given to you; or it is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyyah), meaning: except at the time when permission is given to you. His saying: ﴿to a meal﴾ is connected to yu'dhana (is given permission), on the basis of its being implicitly construed with the meaning of invitation (al-du'a'), meaning: except that permission is given to you, being invited to a meal. The accusative of ﴿not waiting for its preparation﴾ is as a circumstantial qualifier, and its governing element is yu'dhana or an implied verb, meaning: enter, not waiting for it. The meaning of "waiting" (nazirin) is awaiting, and its "preparation" (inahu) is its cooking and its ripening. It is said: anā yaʾnī anan, when it has come near and ripened.

The majority of readers recite ﴿not waiting﴾ with the accusative (ghayra). Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited ghayri with the genitive, as a qualifier of ta'am (food). The grammarians considered this reading weak, because the pronoun does not appear (in the required form), since it applies to other than the one to whom it belongs; the correct form would have been: ghayra nazirina inahu antum (you not waiting for its preparation). Then He, glorified is He, explained to them what is appropriate in that matter, saying: ﴿But when you are invited, then enter﴾. This contains an emphasis of the prohibition and a clarification of the time at which entering is permitted, which is at the time of permission.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: The implied sense of the statement is: "But when you are invited and permission is given to you, then enter," for otherwise the invitation itself is not sufficient permission for entering. It has been said that in this there is clear evidence that the intended meaning of "permission to the meal" is the invitation to it. ﴿And when you have eaten, then disperse﴾. He, glorified is He, commanded them to disperse after eating, which means to separate, and what is intended is an obligation to leave the house to which the invitation was made once the purpose of eating has been fulfilled. ﴿Nor remaining for conversation in familiarity﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿not waiting﴾, or with an implied element, meaning: do not enter and do not remain, being familiar (in conversation).

The meaning: a prohibition for them against sitting after the meal conversing familiarly with one another.

Al-Razi said regarding His saying ﴿except when permission is given to you to a meal﴾: either there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, its implied sense being: "Do not enter for a meal except when you are given permission," so that it is not a prohibition of entering at a time other than the meal without permission; or there is no inversion in it, and its meaning is: "Do not enter except when permission is given to you for a meal," so that the permission is conditional upon it being for a meal, and if one is not given permission for a meal, then entering is not permitted; so if one is permitted to enter to listen to a speech and not to eat a meal, that is not permitted. We say the intended meaning is the second, so that the prohibition on entering is general.

As for its being impermissible except with permission for a meal, that is due to what is mentioned in the occasion of revelation, that the address was with a people who would watch for the time of the meal and enter without permission, so they were forbidden to enter at their time without permission.

Ibn 'Adil said: It is preferable to say that the intended meaning is the second, because inversion is contrary to the original form, and His saying ﴿to a meal﴾ is of the type of specification by mention, so it does not indicate the negation of what is other than it, especially when its like is known, for whoever is permitted to enter his house by permission for his meal is permitted to enter by permission for other than the meal, end of quote.

The better way to express this meaning that he intended is to say: the evidences have established the permissibility of entering the houses of the Prophet (ﷺ) by his permission for other than a meal, and that is known beyond doubt, for the Companions and others would ask his permission to enter for other than a meal, and he would grant them permission. That necessitates restricting this verse to the cause for which it was revealed, namely the people who would watch for the Prophet's (ﷺ) meal, enter, and sit waiting for it to be ready, and those like them. So it does not indicate a prohibition on entering with permission for something other than that, for otherwise it would not be permissible for anyone to enter his house with his permission for other than a meal, and the implication is false, so the implicate is likewise false.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It was the custom of the people, when they had a feast or the like, that whoever wished would come early to the invitation, waiting for the food to be cooked and ripened, and likewise when they had finished they would sit in the same manner. So God forbade the believers from doing that in the house of the Prophet (ﷺ), and this prohibition extends to all the believers, and people adopted the discipline (adab) that God set for them in this matter. He forbade them from entering except with permission, at the time of eating and not before it, for waiting for the food to ripen. The reference in His saying "that is" refers to the waiting and the familiar conversation, and these two are referred to with the demonstrative used for a single thing, by interpreting them as the thing mentioned, as in His saying: ﴿neither old nor young, but between that﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68], meaning: that which is mentioned of the two matters. ﴿That was causing harm to the Prophet﴾, because they would crowd the house upon him and his family and would talk about what he did not wish.

Al-Zajjaj said: The Prophet (ﷺ), out of generosity, would tolerate their prolonging their stay, so he would endure the harm in that. God taught those who attend him this discipline, which became a discipline for them and for those who came after them. ﴿But he is shy of you﴾, meaning: he is shy to say to you, "Stand up" or "Leave." ﴿But Allah is not shy of the truth﴾ (p-1180), meaning: He does not refrain from making clear to you what the truth is, nor does He withhold from its clarification and manifestation, and the expression of that by "not being shy" is for the sake of parallelism (al-mushakalah).

The majority recited "yastahyi" with two yas'; and it is narrated from Ibn Kathir that he recited with one ya', which is the dialect of Tamim, who say istaha yastahi, like istaqa yastaqi. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned another discipline connected with the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And when you ask them for an article﴾, meaning: something to be used, of household goods and other things, ﴿then ask them from behind a screen﴾, meaning: from behind a curtain between you and them.

The word mata' (article/provision) applies to everything that is used for enjoyment, so there is no basis for what has been said: that it means a loan, or a legal ruling, or the Qur'an (mushaf). The reference in His saying "that" is to asking for an article from behind a screen. It has been said that the reference is to all that has been mentioned: not entering without permission, not remaining in familiar conversation upon entering, and asking for an article. The first is preferable. The demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾, meaning: more purifying for them from doubt and evil thoughts that come to men regarding women and to women regarding men.

In this there is a discipline for every believer and a warning to him not to trust himself to be alone with one who is not lawful to him, nor to converse without a screen with one who is forbidden to him.

﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾, meaning: it is not proper or right for you to harm him in any way whatsoever, and among that is entering his houses without his permission, remaining in them in a manner other than what he wishes, and speaking with his wives without a screen. ﴿Nor to marry his wives after him, ever﴾, meaning: nor was it permissible for you to do that after his death, for they are the mothers of the believers, and it is not lawful for sons to marry their mothers. The reference in His saying "that" is to marrying his wives after him, ﴿that would be in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾, meaning: a great sin and a tremendous, severe matter.

The occasion of revelation of the verse was that someone said: "If Muhammad dies, we will marry his wives," and that explanation will come.

﴿Whether you disclose a thing or conceal it, indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾, He knows everything, and among that is what you display regarding the affairs of the wives of His Messenger, and what you conceal in your breasts.

In this is a severe warning, for His encompassing knowledge of all knowable things entails recompense for their good and their evil.

Then He, glorified is He, explained who is not subject to the veil, saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers, their sons, their brothers, the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters﴾. These are not required to be veiled from, neither by the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) nor by other women. He did not mention the paternal uncle and maternal uncle, because they are treated like parents.

Al-Zajjaj said: The paternal and maternal uncles may describe the woman to their sons, for a woman is lawful to the son of her paternal uncle and the son of her maternal uncle, so he disliked for them to see her. This is very weak, for permitting a woman to be described to one for whom she is lawful is possible from others who are permitted to look at her, especially the sons of brothers and the sons of sisters, and the implication is false, so the implicate is likewise false. Likewise, it would necessitate that it is not permissible for non-Muslim women to look at her, because they would describe her, and the implication is false, so the implicate is likewise false. Likewise, there is no basis for what al-Sha'bi and Ikrimah said: that it is disliked for a woman to remove her headcover in front of her paternal uncle or maternal uncle. The better view is that He, glorified is He, limited Himself here to some of the unmarriageable relatives (mahram) mentioned in Surah al-Nur, relying on what preceded.

﴿Nor their women﴾. This addition implies that the intended "women" are believing women, for non-believing women cannot be trusted with private parts, and all women are an awrah. ﴿Nor what their right hands possess﴾, from male and female slaves. It has been said: female slaves specifically, and young male slaves who have not reached puberty; the disagreement on this is well known. This was already discussed in Surah al-Nur, where there is sufficiency.

Then He, glorified is He, commanded them to have taqwa, which is the foundation of the whole matter. And the meaning: fear Allah in all affairs, of which what is mentioned here is part. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾, nothing escapes Him of all things, whatever they may be, so He will recompense the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Anas, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: O Messenger of Allah, indeed both the righteous and the wicked enter upon your wives, so if you veiled them [it would be better]. So Allah revealed the veil."

In another wording, that "'Umar said: O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon you, so if you ordered the Mothers of the Believers to veil, then Allah revealed the verse of the veil."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Anas, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh, he invited the people, and they ate, then they sat conversing, and he appeared as if he were preparing to stand, but they did not stand. When he saw that, he stood up; when he stood, some of them stood and three persons remained seated. The Prophet (ﷺ) came to enter, but behold, the people were still sitting. Then they got up, and I went and informed the Prophet (ﷺ) that they had left, so he came and entered. I went to enter, but he placed the curtain between me and him. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 56–58 (part 1 of 2):

The majority of reciters read "wa-malā'ikatahu" (and His angels) with the accusative (naṣb) on al-Malā'ika, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the form (lafẓ) of the noun of inna. Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-malā'ikatuhu" with the nominative (raf'), as a conjunction on the position (maḥall) of the noun of inna. The pronoun in His saying "yuṣallūna" (they send blessings) refers to Allah and to the angels.

In this there is a great honour for the angels, in that He made the pronoun refer to them and to Allah, glorified is He, as one. Therefore the objection is not raised based on what was established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, when "he heard the speaker saying: Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has been guided aright, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray. He said: Wretched is the orator of the people. You should say: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger." The reason for this is that it is not permissible for anyone to join the mention of Allah, glorified is He, with another in a single pronoun. This hadith is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

It is also established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, commanded a caller who called out on the day of Khaybar: Indeed Allah and His Messenger forbid you the flesh of domestic donkeys."

The people of knowledge have discussions on reconciling the two hadiths, which is not the place to mention them. The verse supports the permissibility of making the pronoun in it refer to Allah and His angels as one. The reasoning based on honouring the angels can be applied similarly to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. The censure of that speaker who combined the two is to be understood as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, understanding from him the intention of equating Allah, glorified is He, with His Messenger, so the prohibition applies specifically to such a case. This is the best of what has been said regarding the combination.

A group said: there is an elision (ḥadhf) here, and the estimate is: "Indeed Allah sends blessings, and His angels send blessings."

According to this view, the verse is not one in which the mention of Allah and the mention of another are combined in a single pronoun, and the objection that "blessing from Allah is mercy, and blessing from His angels is supplication, so how can these two different meanings be combined in the word yuṣallūna" is also not raised. It may be said: according to the first view, a figurative meaning (maʿnā majāzī) was intended by yuṣallūna which encompasses both meanings, namely that by His saying yuṣallūna is meant: they are concerned with displaying his honour, or they magnify his status, or they take care of his affair.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu al-ʿĀliya that the blessing of Allah, glorified is He, is His praise of him in the presence of His angels, and the blessing of the angels is supplication.

al-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan from Sufyan al-Thawri and other than one of the people of knowledge that they said: the blessing of the Lord is mercy, and the blessing of the angels is seeking forgiveness.

al-Wahidi related from Muqatil that he said: As for the blessing of the Lord, it is forgiveness, and as for the blessing of the angels, it is seeking forgiveness.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabāḥ said: His blessing, blessed and exalted is He, is: "Subbūḥ, Quddūs, my mercy has preceded my wrath."

The purpose of this verse is that Allah, glorified is He, informed His servants of the station of His Prophet with Him in the Highest Assembly, that He praises him in the presence of His angels, and that the angels send blessings upon him, and He commanded His servants to follow that and send blessings upon him.

The people of knowledge have differed regarding sending blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, whether it is obligatory (wājib) or recommended (mustaḥabb), after their agreement that sending blessings upon him is an obligation (farḍ) once in a lifetime.

al-Qurtubi related this consensus in his tafsir. Some people of knowledge said: it is obligatory whenever he is mentioned, and some said: it is obligatory once in every gathering.

Hadiths have been related explicitly censuring one who hears the mention of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and does not send blessings upon him.

The scholars differed regarding sending blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, in the tashahhud of the obligatory prayer, whether it is obligatory or not. The majority went to the view that in it, it is a emphasized sunnah (sunna muʾakkada), not obligatory.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is recommended that no one prays a prayer except that he sends blessings upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, in it. If someone leaves that, his prayer is valid according to the school of Malik, the people of Madina, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of Kufa among the Ahl al-Ra'y, and others, and it is the saying of the majority of the people of knowledge.

He said: al-Shafi'i stood alone, obligating on the one who leaves it the repetition of the prayer if he deliberately leaves it, not out of forgetfulness. This saying from al-Shafi'i was not related from him except by Harmala ibn Yahya, and nothing is found from al-Shafi'i except through his narration.

al-Tahawi said: No one among the people of knowledge said this except al-Shafi'i.

Al-Khattabi, who was of the Shafi'is, said: It is not obligatory in the prayer. He said: This is the saying of a group of jurists except al-Shafi'i, and I know of no precedent for him in that, end of quote.

A group of people of knowledge held the view of al-Shafi'i, among them al-Sha'bi, al-Baqir, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal went to it at the end, as related by Abu Zur'a al-Dimashqi, and Ibn Rahwayh and Ibn al-Mawwaz of the Malikis said it.

I have compiled in this question a separate treatise in which I mentioned what those who held it obligatory argued with, and what the majority answered with. The strongest thing used as evidence for obligation is the established hadith with the wording: "Indeed Allah has commanded us to send blessings upon you, so how shall we send blessings upon you in our prayer? He said: Say..." The hadith.

Indeed this command is suitable to be used as evidence for obligation.

As for the invalidation of the prayer by omitting it and the necessity of repeating it, that does not follow, because the absence of obligatory acts does not necessarily entail the absence of the prayer, as the absence of conditions and pillars does.

Know that many hadiths have come concerning the virtue of sending blessings upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. If they were collected they would fill an independent work, and even if there were nothing among them except the hadith established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from His saying, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace: "Whoever sends one blessing upon me, Allah sends ten blessings upon him for it."

Let this suffice you as to this great virtue and noble honour. As for the manner of sending blessings upon him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, many descriptions have come with established hadiths in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, some of which are restricted to the manner of sending blessings upon him in the prayer, and some of which are unrestricted. They are well known in the books of hadith, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

What achieves compliance with the general command in this verse is that the speaker says: "O Allah, send blessings and peace upon Your Messenger," or "upon Muhammad," or "upon the Prophet," or "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and grant peace."

Whoever wishes to send blessings upon him and greet him with one of the descriptions that were taught and guided to, that is more complete. These are many descriptions, which the books of the pure Sunna contain, and some of them will come at the end of the discussion. The discussion of blessing upon the family (āl) will also come.

The apparent meaning of this command to send blessings and peace in the verse would be that the speaker says: "I sent blessings upon him and I greeted him with peace," or "the blessing upon him and the peace upon him," or "upon him be the blessing and the greeting," because Allah, glorified is He, commanded us to bring about blessing upon him and peace from us. Compliance is that it be in what we have mentioned. So how is compliance with Allah's command to us in that to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon him and grant him peace," in exchange for Allah's command to us, with our command to Him to send blessings upon him and grant him peace?

This has been answered by saying that these blessing and peace, since they are a great emblem (shiʿār) of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and a noble honour, we entrusted that to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and returned it to Him. This answer is very weak.

The best answer is to say: the blessing and peace commanded in the verse are that we say, "O Allah, send blessings upon him and grant him peace," or something similar that conveys its meaning, as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, explained to us. The explanation in the many hadiths required that this is the legislated blessing.

Know that this blessing from Allah upon His Messenger, although its meaning is mercy, has become an emblem specific to him to the exclusion of others, so it is not permissible for us to send blessings upon anyone else from his community, as it is permissible for us to say: "O Allah, have mercy upon so-and-so," or "May Allah have mercy upon so-and-so." The majority of scholars held this, while differing on whether it is forbidden, or greatly disliked, or disliked as a matter of abstention (tanzīh), according to three sayings.

Ibn ʿAbbas said, as related from him by Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab: It is not proper to send blessings upon anyone except the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, but rather one prays for the Muslim men and women with forgiveness.

Others said that this is permissible, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And send blessings upon them; indeed your blessings are a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawba: 103], and His saying: ﴿Those—upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾ [al-Baqara: 157], and His saying: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], and the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, who said: "When a people came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, with their charity, he would say: O Allah, send blessings upon them. Then my father came to him with his charity, and he said: O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abu Awfa."

This is answered by saying that this emblem established for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, is for him to bestow upon whom he wills, and it is not for us to apply it to others.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], and His saying: ﴿Those—upon them are blessings from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 157], this contains only that Allah, glorified is He, sends blessings upon groups of His servants, just as He sends blessings ten times upon whoever sends a blessing upon His Messenger once. There is in that no command for us, nor did Allah legislate it for us. Rather He legislated for us only the blessing and peace upon His Messenger.

Just as the phrase "blessing upon the Messenger of Allah" is an emblem of him, so too the phrase "peace upon him" is.

The custom of the majority of this community and its great body, from its predecessors and successors, has been to invoke Allah's pleasure upon the Companions, to ask mercy for those after them, and to supplicate for them for Allah's forgiveness and pardon, as He guided us to that by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancour toward those who believed﴾ [al-Hashr: 10].

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned what is due to His Messenger of veneration, He mentioned the severe threat to those who harm him, saying: ﴿Indeed those who harm Allah and His Messenger—Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾. It was said: the meaning of harm here is doing what they both dislike of sins, since harm cannot reach Allah, glorified is He.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said they are the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians, who attributed offspring to Allah, saying: ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, and the Messiah is the son of Allah, and the angels are the daughters of Allah, and they denied the Messenger of Allah, and wounded his face, and broke his incisor, and said: a madman, a poet, a liar, a sorcerer.

al-Qurtubi said: This is also the saying of the majority of scholars.

ʿIkrima said: The harm to Allah, glorified is He, is by image-making and attempting to do what only Allah does, by carving images and other things.

A group said: the verse contains an elision of a modifier (muḍāf), and the estimate is: "Indeed those who harm the friends of Allah." As for harming His Messenger, it is everything that harms him of sayings and deeds. The meaning of curse (laʿna) is expulsion and distancing from His mercy. He made it in this world and the Hereafter so that the curse would encompass them in both, such that no time of their life or death would pass without the curse befalling them and accompanying them. ﴿And He has prepared for them﴾ along with that curse ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾, by which they become in humiliation in the Hereafter, because of what the sense of "preparing" conveys, namely that it is in the Hereafter.

Then, when he had finished censuring those who harm Allah and His Messenger, he mentioned harm directed at His righteous servants, saying: ﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women﴾ in any of the ways of harm, by word or by deed. The meaning of ﴿without their having earned it﴾ is that it was not for any cause they had committed which made harm obligatory upon them and made them deserving of it. As for harming a believing man or believing woman for what they have earned that makes a hadd (prescribed punishment) or a ta'zir (discretionary punishment) or the like obligatory upon them, that is a right which the Law has established, and a matter Allah has commanded us to and encouraged us toward. Likewise, if believers begin by insulting a believing man or woman, or causing them harm, then retaliation against the doer is not part of the forbidden harm in any form, so long as it does not exceed what Allah has prescribed.

Then he informed of what awaits those who harm believing men and believing women without their having earned it, saying: ﴿then they have born a slander and a manifest sin﴾, i.e., something apparent and clear, with no doubt that it is of the nature of slander (buhtan) and sin (ithm). The reality of buhtan and the reality of ithm have already been explained.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾: they bless him.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Children of Israel said to Musa: Does your Lord send blessings (yusalli)? So his Lord called out to him: O Musa, they have asked you, 'Does your Lord send blessings?' So say: Yes, I send blessings, and My angels, upon My prophets and My messengers. Then Allah revealed to His Prophet ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾," and the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: The blessing of Allah upon the Prophet is forgiveness; Allah does not "send blessings" but He forgives. As for the blessings of people upon the Prophet, it is seeking forgiveness for him.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace, a greeting" (ṣallū 'alayhi wa-sallimū taslīmā).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah that he said: "When the verse ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ was revealed, we said: O Messenger of Allah, we already know the greeting of peace upon you; so how is the blessing upon you?" He said: "Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated it from his hadith with the wording: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace upon you, we know it; so how is the blessing upon you? He said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, how is the blessing upon you? He said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

There is variation among the hadiths: in some, it is "upon Ibrahim" only; in some, "upon the family of Ibrahim" only; and in some, a combination of both, as in this hadith of Talhah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi that they "said: O Messenger of Allah, how should we send blessings upon you? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

The hadiths on this subject are very numerous. In some of them the blessing is restricted to the prayer, as in the hadith of Abu Mas'ud in Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace upon you, we have known it; so how shall we send blessings upon you when we send blessings upon you in our prayer?" — the hadith.

Al-Shafi'i in his Musnad narrated a similar report from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. All the instructions that came from him (ﷺ) regarding sending blessings upon him include sending blessings upon his family along with him, except for rare and few hadiths. Therefore, the one who sends blessings upon him should include his family with him in his blessing. A group of scholars has said so, and Imam al-Haramayn and al-Ghazali reported it as an opinion from al-Shafi'i, as Ibn Kathir narrated from them in his tafsir. There is no need to adhere to the saying of one speaker in such a matter when the authentic hadiths explicitly state it. Nor is there any basis for the view of those who say that these instructions from him (ﷺ) about the manner of sending blessings upon him are restricted to blessing within the prayer, by applying the unrestricted hadiths to the restricted one with that condition, since in the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah and others, that question to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked at the time the verse was revealed.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets of Allah and His messengers, for Allah sent them as He sent me."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾, the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning those who slandered the Prophet (ﷺ) when he took Safiyyah bint Huyayy (as a wife). It is also reported from him that it was revealed concerning those who falsely accused 'A'ishah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 56–58 (part 1 of 2):

The majority of reciters read "wa-malā'ikatahu" (and His angels) with the accusative (naṣb) on al-Malā'ika, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the form (lafẓ) of the noun of inna. Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-malā'ikatuhu" with the nominative (raf'), as a conjunction on the position (maḥall) of the noun of inna. The pronoun in His saying "yuṣallūna" (they send blessings) refers to Allah and to the angels.

In this there is a great honour for the angels, in that He made the pronoun refer to them and to Allah, glorified is He, as one. Therefore the objection is not raised based on what was established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, when "he heard the speaker saying: Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has been guided aright, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray. He said: Wretched is the orator of the people. You should say: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger." The reason for this is that it is not permissible for anyone to join the mention of Allah, glorified is He, with another in a single pronoun. This hadith is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

It is also established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, commanded a caller who called out on the day of Khaybar: Indeed Allah and His Messenger forbid you the flesh of domestic donkeys."

The people of knowledge have discussions on reconciling the two hadiths, which is not the place to mention them. The verse supports the permissibility of making the pronoun in it refer to Allah and His angels as one. The reasoning based on honouring the angels can be applied similarly to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. The censure of that speaker who combined the two is to be understood as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, understanding from him the intention of equating Allah, glorified is He, with His Messenger, so the prohibition applies specifically to such a case. This is the best of what has been said regarding the combination.

A group said: there is an elision (ḥadhf) here, and the estimate is: "Indeed Allah sends blessings, and His angels send blessings."

According to this view, the verse is not one in which the mention of Allah and the mention of another are combined in a single pronoun, and the objection that "blessing from Allah is mercy, and blessing from His angels is supplication, so how can these two different meanings be combined in the word yuṣallūna" is also not raised. It may be said: according to the first view, a figurative meaning (maʿnā majāzī) was intended by yuṣallūna which encompasses both meanings, namely that by His saying yuṣallūna is meant: they are concerned with displaying his honour, or they magnify his status, or they take care of his affair.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu al-ʿĀliya that the blessing of Allah, glorified is He, is His praise of him in the presence of His angels, and the blessing of the angels is supplication.

al-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan from Sufyan al-Thawri and other than one of the people of knowledge that they said: the blessing of the Lord is mercy, and the blessing of the angels is seeking forgiveness.

al-Wahidi related from Muqatil that he said: As for the blessing of the Lord, it is forgiveness, and as for the blessing of the angels, it is seeking forgiveness.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabāḥ said: His blessing, blessed and exalted is He, is: "Subbūḥ, Quddūs, my mercy has preceded my wrath."

The purpose of this verse is that Allah, glorified is He, informed His servants of the station of His Prophet with Him in the Highest Assembly, that He praises him in the presence of His angels, and that the angels send blessings upon him, and He commanded His servants to follow that and send blessings upon him.

The people of knowledge have differed regarding sending blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, whether it is obligatory (wājib) or recommended (mustaḥabb), after their agreement that sending blessings upon him is an obligation (farḍ) once in a lifetime.

al-Qurtubi related this consensus in his tafsir. Some people of knowledge said: it is obligatory whenever he is mentioned, and some said: it is obligatory once in every gathering.

Hadiths have been related explicitly censuring one who hears the mention of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and does not send blessings upon him.

The scholars differed regarding sending blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, in the tashahhud of the obligatory prayer, whether it is obligatory or not. The majority went to the view that in it, it is a emphasized sunnah (sunna muʾakkada), not obligatory.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is recommended that no one prays a prayer except that he sends blessings upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, in it. If someone leaves that, his prayer is valid according to the school of Malik, the people of Madina, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of Kufa among the Ahl al-Ra'y, and others, and it is the saying of the majority of the people of knowledge.

He said: al-Shafi'i stood alone, obligating on the one who leaves it the repetition of the prayer if he deliberately leaves it, not out of forgetfulness. This saying from al-Shafi'i was not related from him except by Harmala ibn Yahya, and nothing is found from al-Shafi'i except through his narration.

al-Tahawi said: No one among the people of knowledge said this except al-Shafi'i.

Al-Khattabi, who was of the Shafi'is, said: It is not obligatory in the prayer. He said: This is the saying of a group of jurists except al-Shafi'i, and I know of no precedent for him in that, end of quote.

A group of people of knowledge held the view of al-Shafi'i, among them al-Sha'bi, al-Baqir, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal went to it at the end, as related by Abu Zur'a al-Dimashqi, and Ibn Rahwayh and Ibn al-Mawwaz of the Malikis said it.

I have compiled in this question a separate treatise in which I mentioned what those who held it obligatory argued with, and what the majority answered with. The strongest thing used as evidence for obligation is the established hadith with the wording: "Indeed Allah has commanded us to send blessings upon you, so how shall we send blessings upon you in our prayer? He said: Say..." The hadith.

Indeed this command is suitable to be used as evidence for obligation.

As for the invalidation of the prayer by omitting it and the necessity of repeating it, that does not follow, because the absence of obligatory acts does not necessarily entail the absence of the prayer, as the absence of conditions and pillars does.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated it from his hadith with the wording: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace upon you, we know it; so how is the blessing upon you? He said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, how is the blessing upon you? He said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

There is variation among the hadiths: in some, it is "upon Ibrahim" only; in some, "upon the family of Ibrahim" only; and in some, a combination of both, as in this hadith of Talhah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi that they "said: O Messenger of Allah, how should we send blessings upon you? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

The hadiths on this subject are very numerous. In some of them the blessing is restricted to the prayer, as in the hadith of Abu Mas'ud in Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace upon you, we have known it; so how shall we send blessings upon you when we send blessings upon you in our prayer?" — the hadith.

Al-Shafi'i in his Musnad narrated a similar report from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. All the instructions that came from him (ﷺ) regarding sending blessings upon him include sending blessings upon his family along with him, except for rare and few hadiths. Therefore, the one who sends blessings upon him should include his family with him in his blessing. A group of scholars has said so, and Imam al-Haramayn and al-Ghazali reported it as an opinion from al-Shafi'i, as Ibn Kathir narrated from them in his tafsir. There is no need to adhere to the saying of one speaker in such a matter when the authentic hadiths explicitly state it. Nor is there any basis for the view of those who say that these instructions from him (ﷺ) about the manner of sending blessings upon him are restricted to blessing within the prayer, by applying the unrestricted hadiths to the restricted one with that condition, since in the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah and others, that question to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked at the time the verse was revealed.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets of Allah and His messengers, for Allah sent them as He sent me."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾, the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning those who slandered the Prophet (ﷺ) when he took Safiyyah bint Huyayy (as a wife). It is also reported from him that it was revealed concerning those who falsely accused 'A'ishah.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 33, verses 56–58 (part 1 of 2):

The majority of reciters read "wa-malā'ikatahu" (and His angels) with the accusative (naṣb) on al-Malā'ika, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the form (lafẓ) of the noun of inna. Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-malā'ikatuhu" with the nominative (raf'), as a conjunction on the position (maḥall) of the noun of inna. The pronoun in His saying "yuṣallūna" (they send blessings) refers to Allah and to the angels.

In this there is a great honour for the angels, in that He made the pronoun refer to them and to Allah, glorified is He, as one. Therefore the objection is not raised based on what was established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, when "he heard the speaker saying: Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has been guided aright, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray. He said: Wretched is the orator of the people. You should say: And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger." The reason for this is that it is not permissible for anyone to join the mention of Allah, glorified is He, with another in a single pronoun. This hadith is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ.

It is also established in the Ṣaḥīḥ that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, commanded a caller who called out on the day of Khaybar: Indeed Allah and His Messenger forbid you the flesh of domestic donkeys."

The people of knowledge have discussions on reconciling the two hadiths, which is not the place to mention them. The verse supports the permissibility of making the pronoun in it refer to Allah and His angels as one. The reasoning based on honouring the angels can be applied similarly to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. The censure of that speaker who combined the two is to be understood as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, understanding from him the intention of equating Allah, glorified is He, with His Messenger, so the prohibition applies specifically to such a case. This is the best of what has been said regarding the combination.

A group said: there is an elision (ḥadhf) here, and the estimate is: "Indeed Allah sends blessings, and His angels send blessings."

According to this view, the verse is not one in which the mention of Allah and the mention of another are combined in a single pronoun, and the objection that "blessing from Allah is mercy, and blessing from His angels is supplication, so how can these two different meanings be combined in the word yuṣallūna" is also not raised. It may be said: according to the first view, a figurative meaning (maʿnā majāzī) was intended by yuṣallūna which encompasses both meanings, namely that by His saying yuṣallūna is meant: they are concerned with displaying his honour, or they magnify his status, or they take care of his affair.

Al-Bukhari related from Abu al-ʿĀliya that the blessing of Allah, glorified is He, is His praise of him in the presence of His angels, and the blessing of the angels is supplication.

al-Tirmidhi related in his Sunan from Sufyan al-Thawri and other than one of the people of knowledge that they said: the blessing of the Lord is mercy, and the blessing of the angels is seeking forgiveness.

al-Wahidi related from Muqatil that he said: As for the blessing of the Lord, it is forgiveness, and as for the blessing of the angels, it is seeking forgiveness.

ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabāḥ said: His blessing, blessed and exalted is He, is: "Subbūḥ, Quddūs, my mercy has preceded my wrath."

The purpose of this verse is that Allah, glorified is He, informed His servants of the station of His Prophet with Him in the Highest Assembly, that He praises him in the presence of His angels, and that the angels send blessings upon him, and He commanded His servants to follow that and send blessings upon him.

The people of knowledge have differed regarding sending blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, whether it is obligatory (wājib) or recommended (mustaḥabb), after their agreement that sending blessings upon him is an obligation (farḍ) once in a lifetime.

al-Qurtubi related this consensus in his tafsir. Some people of knowledge said: it is obligatory whenever he is mentioned, and some said: it is obligatory once in every gathering.

Hadiths have been related explicitly censuring one who hears the mention of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and does not send blessings upon him.

The scholars differed regarding sending blessings upon the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, in the tashahhud of the obligatory prayer, whether it is obligatory or not. The majority went to the view that in it, it is a emphasized sunnah (sunna muʾakkada), not obligatory.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: It is recommended that no one prays a prayer except that he sends blessings upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, in it. If someone leaves that, his prayer is valid according to the school of Malik, the people of Madina, Sufyan al-Thawri, the people of Kufa among the Ahl al-Ra'y, and others, and it is the saying of the majority of the people of knowledge.

He said: al-Shafi'i stood alone, obligating on the one who leaves it the repetition of the prayer if he deliberately leaves it, not out of forgetfulness. This saying from al-Shafi'i was not related from him except by Harmala ibn Yahya, and nothing is found from al-Shafi'i except through his narration.

al-Tahawi said: No one among the people of knowledge said this except al-Shafi'i.

Al-Khattabi, who was of the Shafi'is, said: It is not obligatory in the prayer. He said: This is the saying of a group of jurists except al-Shafi'i, and I know of no precedent for him in that, end of quote.

A group of people of knowledge held the view of al-Shafi'i, among them al-Sha'bi, al-Baqir, and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal went to it at the end, as related by Abu Zur'a al-Dimashqi, and Ibn Rahwayh and Ibn al-Mawwaz of the Malikis said it.

I have compiled in this question a separate treatise in which I mentioned what those who held it obligatory argued with, and what the majority answered with. The strongest thing used as evidence for obligation is the established hadith with the wording: "Indeed Allah has commanded us to send blessings upon you, so how shall we send blessings upon you in our prayer? He said: Say..." The hadith.

Indeed this command is suitable to be used as evidence for obligation.

As for the invalidation of the prayer by omitting it and the necessity of repeating it, that does not follow, because the absence of obligatory acts does not necessarily entail the absence of the prayer, as the absence of conditions and pillars does.

Know that many hadiths have come concerning the virtue of sending blessings upon the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. If they were collected they would fill an independent work, and even if there were nothing among them except the hadith established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from His saying, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace: "Whoever sends one blessing upon me, Allah sends ten blessings upon him for it."

Let this suffice you as to this great virtue and noble honour. As for the manner of sending blessings upon him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, many descriptions have come with established hadiths in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, some of which are restricted to the manner of sending blessings upon him in the prayer, and some of which are unrestricted. They are well known in the books of hadith, so we will not lengthen by mentioning them.

What achieves compliance with the general command in this verse is that the speaker says: "O Allah, send blessings and peace upon Your Messenger," or "upon Muhammad," or "upon the Prophet," or "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and grant peace."

Whoever wishes to send blessings upon him and greet him with one of the descriptions that were taught and guided to, that is more complete. These are many descriptions, which the books of the pure Sunna contain, and some of them will come at the end of the discussion. The discussion of blessing upon the family (āl) will also come.

The apparent meaning of this command to send blessings and peace in the verse would be that the speaker says: "I sent blessings upon him and I greeted him with peace," or "the blessing upon him and the peace upon him," or "upon him be the blessing and the greeting," because Allah, glorified is He, commanded us to bring about blessing upon him and peace from us. Compliance is that it be in what we have mentioned. So how is compliance with Allah's command to us in that to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon him and grant him peace," in exchange for Allah's command to us, with our command to Him to send blessings upon him and grant him peace?

This has been answered by saying that these blessing and peace, since they are a great emblem (shiʿār) of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and a noble honour, we entrusted that to Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and returned it to Him. This answer is very weak.

The best answer is to say: the blessing and peace commanded in the verse are that we say, "O Allah, send blessings upon him and grant him peace," or something similar that conveys its meaning, as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, explained to us. The explanation in the many hadiths required that this is the legislated blessing.

Know that this blessing from Allah upon His Messenger, although its meaning is mercy, has become an emblem specific to him to the exclusion of others, so it is not permissible for us to send blessings upon anyone else from his community, as it is permissible for us to say: "O Allah, have mercy upon so-and-so," or "May Allah have mercy upon so-and-so." The majority of scholars held this, while differing on whether it is forbidden, or greatly disliked, or disliked as a matter of abstention (tanzīh), according to three sayings.

Ibn ʿAbbas said, as related from him by Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab: It is not proper to send blessings upon anyone except the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, but rather one prays for the Muslim men and women with forgiveness.

Others said that this is permissible, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And send blessings upon them; indeed your blessings are a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawba: 103], and His saying: ﴿Those—upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾ [al-Baqara: 157], and His saying: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], and the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and others, who said: "When a people came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, with their charity, he would say: O Allah, send blessings upon them. Then my father came to him with his charity, and he said: O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abu Awfa."

This is answered by saying that this emblem established for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, is for him to bestow upon whom he wills, and it is not for us to apply it to others.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], and His saying: ﴿Those—upon them are blessings from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 157], this contains only that Allah, glorified is He, sends blessings upon groups of His servants, just as He sends blessings ten times upon whoever sends a blessing upon His Messenger once. There is in that no command for us, nor did Allah legislate it for us. Rather He legislated for us only the blessing and peace upon His Messenger.

Just as the phrase "blessing upon the Messenger of Allah" is an emblem of him, so too the phrase "peace upon him" is.

The custom of the majority of this community and its great body, from its predecessors and successors, has been to invoke Allah's pleasure upon the Companions, to ask mercy for those after them, and to supplicate for them for Allah's forgiveness and pardon, as He guided us to that by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancour toward those who believed﴾ [al-Hashr: 10].

Then, when He, glorified is He, mentioned what is due to His Messenger of veneration, He mentioned the severe threat to those who harm him, saying: ﴿Indeed those who harm Allah and His Messenger—Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾. It was said: the meaning of harm here is doing what they both dislike of sins, since harm cannot reach Allah, glorified is He.

al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said they are the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians, who attributed offspring to Allah, saying: ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, and the Messiah is the son of Allah, and the angels are the daughters of Allah, and they denied the Messenger of Allah, and wounded his face, and broke his incisor, and said: a madman, a poet, a liar, a sorcerer.

al-Qurtubi said: This is also the saying of the majority of scholars.

ʿIkrima said: The harm to Allah, glorified is He, is by image-making and attempting to do what only Allah does, by carving images and other things.

A group said: the verse contains an elision of a modifier (muḍāf), and the estimate is: "Indeed those who harm the friends of Allah." As for harming His Messenger, it is everything that harms him of sayings and deeds. The meaning of curse (laʿna) is expulsion and distancing from His mercy. He made it in this world and the Hereafter so that the curse would encompass them in both, such that no time of their life or death would pass without the curse befalling them and accompanying them. ﴿And He has prepared for them﴾ along with that curse ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾, by which they become in humiliation in the Hereafter, because of what the sense of "preparing" conveys, namely that it is in the Hereafter.

Then, when he had finished censuring those who harm Allah and His Messenger, he mentioned harm directed at His righteous servants, saying: ﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women﴾ in any of the ways of harm, by word or by deed. The meaning of ﴿without their having earned it﴾ is that it was not for any cause they had committed which made harm obligatory upon them and made them deserving of it. As for harming a believing man or believing woman for what they have earned that makes a hadd (prescribed punishment) or a ta'zir (discretionary punishment) or the like obligatory upon them, that is a right which the Law has established, and a matter Allah has commanded us to and encouraged us toward. Likewise, if believers begin by insulting a believing man or woman, or causing them harm, then retaliation against the doer is not part of the forbidden harm in any form, so long as it does not exceed what Allah has prescribed.

Then he informed of what awaits those who harm believing men and believing women without their having earned it, saying: ﴿then they have born a slander and a manifest sin﴾, i.e., something apparent and clear, with no doubt that it is of the nature of slander (buhtan) and sin (ithm). The reality of buhtan and the reality of ithm have already been explained.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾: they bless him.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "the Children of Israel said to Musa: Does your Lord send blessings (yusalli)? So his Lord called out to him: O Musa, they have asked you, 'Does your Lord send blessings?' So say: Yes, I send blessings, and My angels, upon My prophets and My messengers. Then Allah revealed to His Prophet ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾," and the verse.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him that he said: The blessing of Allah upon the Prophet is forgiveness; Allah does not "send blessings" but He forgives. As for the blessings of people upon the Prophet, it is seeking forgiveness for him.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace, a greeting" (ṣallū 'alayhi wa-sallimū taslīmā).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah that he said: "When the verse ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ was revealed, we said: O Messenger of Allah, we already know the greeting of peace upon you; so how is the blessing upon you?" He said: "Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated it from his hadith with the wording: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace upon you, we know it; so how is the blessing upon you? He said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, how is the blessing upon you? He said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

There is variation among the hadiths: in some, it is "upon Ibrahim" only; in some, "upon the family of Ibrahim" only; and in some, a combination of both, as in this hadith of Talhah.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi that they "said: O Messenger of Allah, how should we send blessings upon you? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim, and bless Muhammad and his wives and his descendants, as You blessed the family of Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious."

The hadiths on this subject are very numerous. In some of them the blessing is restricted to the prayer, as in the hadith of Abu Mas'ud in Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting of peace upon you, we have known it; so how shall we send blessings upon you when we send blessings upon you in our prayer?" — the hadith.

Al-Shafi'i in his Musnad narrated a similar report from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. All the instructions that came from him (ﷺ) regarding sending blessings upon him include sending blessings upon his family along with him, except for rare and few hadiths. Therefore, the one who sends blessings upon him should include his family with him in his blessing. A group of scholars has said so, and Imam al-Haramayn and al-Ghazali reported it as an opinion from al-Shafi'i, as Ibn Kathir narrated from them in his tafsir. There is no need to adhere to the saying of one speaker in such a matter when the authentic hadiths explicitly state it. Nor is there any basis for the view of those who say that these instructions from him (ﷺ) about the manner of sending blessings upon him are restricted to blessing within the prayer, by applying the unrestricted hadiths to the restricted one with that condition, since in the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah and others, that question to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked at the time the verse was revealed.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets of Allah and His messengers, for Allah sent them as He sent me."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾, the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning those who slandered the Prophet (ﷺ) when he took Safiyyah bint Huyayy (as a wife). It is also reported from him that it was revealed concerning those who falsely accused 'A'ishah.

When al-Shawkani had finished with the rebuke for those among His servants who harm His Messenger and the believing men and women, Allah (glorified is He) commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to instruct some of those who had suffered harm to take a measure that would ward off what befalls them from it. So He said: (p-1184) ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers that they should draw their outer garments (jalabib) over themselves﴾. The word "min" (from) in ﴿min jalabibihinna﴾ is for partitive meaning (li-l-tab'id, "some of"). The word jalabib is the plural of jilbab, which is a garment larger than the khimar (headcover).

Al-Jawhari said: the jilbab is a mulhafa (a wrap or covering cloth). It is also said to be a qina' (veil), and it is also said to be a garment that covers the whole body of the woman, as is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Umm 'Atiyyah, that she said: "O Messenger of Allah, one of us may not have a jilbab." He said: "Let her sister clothe her with one of her jilbabs."

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said, they should cover their faces and their heads, except one eye, so that it is known that they are free women and they are not molested.

Al-Hasan said: she covers half of her face.

Qatadah said: she wraps it over the forehead and fastens it, then folds it over the nose; even if her eyes appear, it covers the chest and most of the face.

The reference in His words ﴿dhalika﴾ (that) is to the drawing of the jalabib. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿adna an yu'rafna﴾ (more suitable that they be recognized), meaning: more likely that they will be recognized, so that they are distinguished from slave women, and it becomes apparent to people that they are free women. ﴿So that they will not be harmed﴾ by the people of lewdness through being accosted, with them being watched over, and their families as well. The intended meaning of His words ﴿that they will be recognized﴾ is not that a particular one of them be identified as who she is; rather the meaning is that they be known as free women and not slave women, because they have put on a style of dress that is specific to free women. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of what has passed from them of neglecting to draw their jalabib, ﴿Merciful﴾ to them; or, He is Forgiving to the sinners and Merciful to them, so they enter into this by primary inclusion.

Then Allah (glorified is He) threatened the people of hypocrisy and of spreading false rumours, and He said: ﴿If the hypocrites desist not﴾ from what they are upon of hypocrisy, ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning doubt and suspicion about what they are upon of instability, ﴿and those who spread rumours in Al-Madinah﴾ regarding what proceeds from them of spreading rumours, by mentioning false reports that contain the weakening of the side of the Muslims and the ascendancy of the polytheists over them.

Al-Qurtubi said: the exegetes are agreed that the three descriptions refer to one thing, and the meaning is that the hypocrites combined hypocrisy, disease of the hearts, and spreading rumours against the Muslims. So it is, on this view, of the type of the saying:

"To the king, the leader, son of the chief, the lion of the battalion in the crowd"

meaning: to the king, the leader, son of the chief, the lion of the battalion.

'Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: those in whose hearts is a disease are the fornicators (al-zunat).

Al-irjaf in the language is the spreading of lies and falsehood. It is said: arjafa bi-kadha, when he reports it without basis in truth, because it is a report that is unsteady and unestablished, from al-rajfah, which is the earthquake.

It is said: the earth quaked (rajafat al-ard), meaning it moved and convulsed, yartajifu rajfan; and al-rajafan is severe agitation. The sea was named rajjaf because of its agitation. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Those who feed meat every evening, until the sun sets in the rajjaf."

Al-irjaf is the singular of al-arajif (rumours), and arjafu fi al-shay' means they plunged into it. From it is the saying of a poet:

"Though you reproach us with our small number, and a rebel and an envier spread rumours against Islam."

And the saying of another:

"With rumours, O son of baseness, do you threaten me? And in rumours I thought baseness and cowardice."

That is because these spreaders of rumours used to report about the expeditions (saraya) of the Muslims that they had been defeated, and at times that they had been killed, and at times that they had been overcome, and similar things by which the hearts of the Muslims are broken from reports. So Allah (glorified is He) threatened them with His words: ﴿Then We will surely incite you against them﴾, meaning: We will surely empower you over them with killing and dispersal by Our command to you to do so.

Al-Mubarrad said: Allah has indeed incited him against them in His words after this verse:

﴿Cursed; wherever they are found, they shall be seized and massacred with slaughter﴾. So in this there is the meaning of a command to kill them and seize them, meaning: this is their ruling when they remain upon hypocrisy and spreading rumours.

Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best of what has been said regarding the verse.

I say: this is not good, nor is it the best, for His words "cursed..." etc. are merely a supplication against them, not a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to fight them, nor an empowerment of him over them. It has been said that they desisted after the revelation of this verse from spreading rumours, so Allah did not incite him against them. The clause ﴿We will surely incite you against them﴾ is the answer of the oath (jawab al-qasam), and the clause ﴿Then they will not remain your neighbours therein except briefly﴾ is conjoined to the clause that is the answer of the oath, meaning: they will not be your neighbours therein except for a brief neighbourhood until they perish. The accusative state of mal'unin is a circumstantial accusative (hal), as al-Mubarrad and others said, and the meaning is: expelled, wherever they are found and overtaken. ﴿Seized and massacred﴾ is a supplication against them that they be seized and slain with slaughter. It has been said: this is the ruling regarding them, and it is not a supplication against them; the first is preferable.

It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that they persisted in hypocrisy; for them there was no residence in Al-Madinah except that they were expelled.

﴿A way of Allah with those who passed before, and you will not find for the way of Allah any change﴾. Meaning: Allah has established that in the past nations, namely the cursing of the hypocrites, their seizure, and their slaughter, and likewise the ruling for the spreaders of rumours. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar).

The accusative of qarib (near) is adverbial of time (zarfiyyah). The masculine form is used because the Hour is in the sense of "the day" or "the time," while the feminine of "al-sa'ah" is not real (haqiqi). The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to clarify that if it is hidden from him, he does not know its time, and he is the Messenger of Allah, then how about other people? In this there is a great threat to them.

The word "yawma" (the day) in His words ﴿the Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾ is an adverbial accusative (zarf) for His words "they will not find," and it has been said: for "abiding," and it has been said: for "a helper," and it has been said: for an implied verb, which is "remember."

Al-Jumhur read tuqallabu (are turned) with a damma on the ta' and fatha on the lam, in the passive form.

'Isa al-Hamdani and Ibn Abi Ishaq read nuqallibu (We turn) with the nun and a kasra on the lam, in the active form, the agent being Allah (glorified is He).

'Isa also read (p-1185) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the lam, meaning: the blaze turns their faces.

Abu Haywah, Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read with a fatha on the ta' and the lam, meaning: tatagallabu (they turn about). The meaning of this turning mentioned in the verse is: its turning them at times on one side and at other times on another side, back to belly; or the change of their colours by the scorching of the fire, so that they blacken at times and turn green at others; or the replacement of their skins with other skins. Then at that time ﴿they will say: "O would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger"﴾. The clause is resumptive (mustanafah), as if it was said: what is their state? The intended meaning of His words ﴿that they will be recognized﴾ is not that a particular one of them be identified as who she is; rather the meaning is that they be known as free women and not slave women, because they have put on a style of dress that is specific to free women. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾ of what has passed from them of neglecting to draw their jalabib, ﴿Merciful﴾ to them; or, He is Forgiving to the sinners and Merciful to them, so they enter into this by primary inclusion.

Then Allah (glorified is He) threatened the people of hypocrisy and of spreading false rumours, and He said: ﴿If the hypocrites desist not﴾ from what they are upon of hypocrisy, ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning doubt and suspicion about what they are upon of instability, ﴿and those who spread rumours in Al-Madinah﴾ regarding what proceeds from them of spreading rumours, by mentioning false reports that contain the weakening of the side of the Muslims and the ascendancy of the polytheists over them.

Al-Qurtubi said: the exegetes are agreed that the three descriptions refer to one thing, and the meaning is that the hypocrites combined hypocrisy, disease of the hearts, and spreading rumours against the Muslims. So it is, on this view, of the type of the saying:

"To the king, the leader, son of the chief, the lion of the battalion in the crowd"

meaning: to the king, the leader, son of the chief, the lion of the battalion.

'Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab said: those in whose hearts is a disease are the fornicators (al-zunat).

Al-irjaf in the language is the spreading of lies and falsehood. It is said: arjafa bi-kadha, when he reports it without basis in truth, because it is a report that is unsteady and unestablished, from al-rajfah, which is the earthquake.

It is said: the earth quaked (rajafat al-ard), meaning it moved and convulsed, yartajifu rajfan; and al-rajafan is severe agitation. The sea was named rajjaf because of its agitation. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Those who feed meat every evening, until the sun sets in the rajjaf."

Al-irjaf is the singular of al-arajif (rumours), and arjafu fi al-shay' means they plunged into it. From it is the saying of a poet:

"Though you reproach us with our small number, and a rebel and an envier spread rumours against Islam."

And the saying of another:

"With rumours, O son of baseness, do you threaten me? And in rumours I thought baseness and cowardice."

That is because these spreaders of rumours used to report about the expeditions (saraya) of the Muslims that they had been defeated, and at times that they had been killed, and at times that they had been overcome, and similar things by which the hearts of the Muslims are broken from reports. So Allah (glorified is He) threatened them with His words: ﴿Then We will surely incite you against them﴾, meaning: We will surely empower you over them with killing and dispersal by Our command to you to do so.

Al-Mubarrad said: Allah has indeed incited him against them in His words after this verse:

﴿Cursed; wherever they are found, they shall be seized and massacred with slaughter﴾. So in this there is the meaning of a command to kill them and seize them, meaning: this is their ruling when they remain upon hypocrisy and spreading rumours.

Al-Nahhas said: this is among the best of what has been said regarding the verse.

I say: this is not good, nor is it the best, for His words "cursed..." etc. are merely a supplication against them, not a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to fight them, nor an empowerment of him over them. It has been said that they desisted after the revelation of this verse from spreading rumours, so Allah did not incite him against them. The clause ﴿We will surely incite you against them﴾ is the answer of the oath (jawab al-qasam), and the clause ﴿Then they will not remain your neighbours therein except briefly﴾ is conjoined to the clause that is the answer of the oath, meaning: they will not be your neighbours therein except for a brief neighbourhood until they perish. The accusative state of mal'unin is a circumstantial accusative (hal), as al-Mubarrad and others said, and the meaning is: expelled, wherever they are found and overtaken. ﴿Seized and massacred﴾ is a supplication against them that they be seized and slain with slaughter. It has been said: this is the ruling regarding them, and it is not a supplication against them; the first is preferable.

It has been said: the meaning of the verse is that they persisted in hypocrisy; for them there was no residence in Al-Madinah except that they were expelled.

﴿A way of Allah with those who passed before, and you will not find for the way of Allah any change﴾. Meaning: Allah has established that in the past nations, namely the cursing of the hypocrites, their seizure, and their slaughter, and likewise the ruling for the spreaders of rumours. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar).

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah has explained concerning those who act hypocritically toward the prophets and spread rumours against them that they should be slain wherever they are found. ﴿And you will not find for the way of Allah any alteration﴾, meaning: any transformation or change; rather it is established and enduring regarding such people among later and earlier generations.
